blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 2:56pm

Senator Robinhood Padilla on Friday arrived at the Department of Justice (DOJ) for the preliminary investigation for the obstruction of justice complaint filed against him by the Philippine National Police (PNP).
This was in relation to Senator Ronald Bato Dela Rosa’s departure from the Senate premises amid an ICC warrant against him.
Padilla was greeted by his supporters already awaiting his arrival at Padre Faura in Manila.
“Una po maraming salamat po sa lahat ng mga kapatid na Muslim, lahat na kapatid na mga Kristiyano, na nagpunta po dito at nagbigay ng suporta sa akin kahit na napaka-sikip natin,” Padilla said.
(First off, I want to thank our fellow Muslims and Christians, who went here to give their support.)
“Nandito po tayo para i-file po namin yung counter-affidavit namin. Kasama ko po yung mga abogado ko,” Padilla said.
(We are here to file our counter-affidavit. I am with my lawyers.)

articles.title: Pacquiao to 'Filipino traitors': Come to Pagasa Island
articles.summary: PAGASA ISLAND, KALAYAAN, Palawan — Renowned boxer and former Sen. Manny Pacquiao challenged critics he labeled “Filipino traitors” to visit this island to experience the realities…

blocks.text: PAGASA ISLAND, KALAYAAN, Palawan — Renowned boxer and former Sen. Manny Pacquiao challenged critics he labeled “Filipino traitors” to visit this island to experience the realities of living in a maritime dispute with China.
Pacquiao, now chair and lead convenor of the National Anti-Poverty Commission, was here on Friday to join the celebration of Maritime and Archipelagic Nation Awareness Month (Mana Mo).
The NAPC chair said the Filipino people should unite and strengthen their resolve in the country’s sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

“Ang masasabi ko lang sa ating mga kababayan, magkaisa tayo. (What I can say to my fellow citizens is we should unite),” he told covering newsmen, conceding that the trip gave him better perspective on what the country is asserting. “I’m happy to be here in Pagasa Island. Nakita ko yung mga barko ng China (I now see those Chinese ships), ” he said.
“Kailangan siguro pagtibayin natin yung samahan natin, ipakita natin sa kanila na hindi tayo basta-basta gi-give up sa sariling atin,” Pacquiao said.
(We need to reinforce this unity and show them we will not give up what is rightfully ours)
“Hindi naman tayo nakikipag-away, gusto natin makipagkaibigan, pero huwag naman to the point na kukuhanin yung sa’yo,” he added.
(We are not at war; we seek friendship but not at the expense of them taking from us)
Pacquiao said he finds the presence of Chinese vessels, which are anchored just a few kilometers away from the Pag Asa community, “insulting.”
“This is our territory, nandyan sila so parang nabu-bully tayo, ini-intimidate tayo (but they surround us like bullies and we will not be intimidated),” he said.
Pacquiao said he is looking forward to these differences between the Philippines and China being ironed out soon.

“Doon sa mga Pilipino na medyo traydor, dapat pumunta kayo dito para maranasan niyo (yung buhay). Sa mga Pilipinong traydor, dapat mag-isip silang mabuti, Atin ‘to. Hindi maganda na sarili mong tahanan tapos kukunin,” he said.

( Filipinos who are a bit traitorous should come here and experience life on the island. Filipino traitors should think things over. This is ours, and it’s not good that our own house is being taken from us.)
Pacquiao turned over P500,000 to the local government of Kalayaan, saying he showed up to honor the troops standing vigil in this part of Philippine territory./coa

articles.title: Legarda camp wants plunder complaint reconsidered
articles.summary: Legarda camp wants plunder complaint reconsidered

blocks.text: Senator Loren Legarda’s spokesperson, Atty. Tony La Viña, called on the Office of the Ombudsman to reconsider the plunder and graft complaints filed against the senator and her son, Congressman Leandro Leviste, saying there is "insufficient evidence" against them.
“We would like the government… especially the Ombudsman to reconsider at wag na nilang ituloy ito (not pursue this anymore),” La Viña said at a news forum on Friday.

According to La Viña, filing a case against Legarda and Leviste would fail to meet the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) new policy standard, which requires prima facie evidence with a reasonable certainty of conviction before a case can be filed.
“Yan din naman ang ano ni Ombudsman Remulla sa DOJ, ‘yung kanyang binago na standard—you do not file a case unless may reasonable certainty ka na maco-convict mo,” La Vina said.
(That’s also Ombudsman Remulla’s standard—or rather, the standard he changed at the DOJ: you do not file a case unless you have a reasonable certainty of winning a conviction.)
“Ito talagang walang certainty, walang reasonable certainty, walang possibility na ma-convict,” he added.
(In this situation, there is simply no certainty, no reasonable certainty, and no possibility of a conviction.)
'Benefit of the doubt'
La Viña previously described the Ombudsman’s probe into Legarda and Leviste as “lawfare,” or the weaponization of the law against government critics or opposition figures.
He noted that the timing of the complaint against Leviste is not dismissible, as it seems connected to, or triggered by, his earlier exposé on government corruption.

“Kung magpatuloy sila, I have to say, clearly political ito, di ba? This is lawfare, this is weaponization of the law… This is actually to stop Leandro Leviste speaking about corruption. And parang nag-succeed sila, ‘di ba? Kasi napatahimik nila right now, “ La Vina said.

(If they proceed, I have to say this is clearly political, right? This is lawfare; this is the weaponization of the law… This is actually intended to stop Leandro Leviste from speaking out about corruption. And it seems they succeeded, right? Because they managed to silence him for now.)
He added that they are currently giving the government the benefit of the doubt, assuming it merely made an error regarding the issue.

“So, lahat ito, sa tingin namin, benefit of the doubt, nagkamali lang sila. Please reconsider. Please look at your invoices, please look at your bills, please look at the documents. ‘Yun ang una naming hinihingi,” the spokesperson said.

(So, considering all this, we are giving them the benefit of the doubt that they just made a mistake. Please reconsider. Please look at your invoices, please look at your bills, please look at the documents. That is what we are asking for first.)

Legarda and Leviste are facing plunder and graft complaints in connection with the latter’s solar energy projects valued at P10.44 billion. They have both denied the allegations and filed a counter-affidavit answering the complaint.
Legarda has been on medical leave since August 3 to undergo treatment for a lung illness.
She requested to extend her leave until October 9 as she continues her treatment in France, where she is currently being cared for by Leviste.
‘No criminal act'

La Viña also denounced allegations that Leviste should be held accountable for the non-implementation of the Solar para sa Bayan project, explaining that he never received the required implementing rules and regulations from the Department of Energy (DOE), which subsequently led to the revocation of his solar project’s franchise.
“Totoo ba na hindi na-implement yung Solar ng Bayan? Totoo, kasi ‘di naglabas ‘yung DOE ng rules and regulations and ng places ng mga lugar kung saan ito i-implement,” La Viña said.
(Is it true that Solar para sa Bayan was not implemented? Yes, that’s true, because the DOE failed to issue the rules, regulations, and specified locations where it should be implemented.)

“Because the law provided na once na in 2 years kung ‘di mo siya maimplement… automatically revoked ang franchise mo. Na-revoke siya. Uulitin ko, hindi kasalanan ni Leandro Leviste [at]... hindi kasama si Loren Legarda sa pag-approve, in fact, nag-inhibit siya,” he added.

(Because the law specifies that if you fail to implement the project within two years… your franchise is automatically revoked. So it was revoked. I repeat: this is not Leandro Leviste’s fault, [and] Loren Legarda had no part in approving it—in fact, she inhibited herself.

La Viña also denied claims that Leandro owes P10 billion or P24 billion in debt, adding that he does not hold a monopoly on renewable energy contracts, as his projects account for only about 10% of the market.
He reiterated his previous stance that the lawmaker is an out-of-the-box innovator whose sole intention is to accelerate the country's solar energy industry.

“I want to make it clear: walang kasalanan, walang criminal act na kinommit ‘yung bata, innovator lang siya out-of-the-box lang siya, minsan hindi naiintindihan yung mga moves niya kasi panibagong mga moves, pero importante yung motivation niya to accelerate the solar transition or the just energy transition in the Philippines,” La Vina said.

(I want to make it clear: the young man committed no crime, no criminal act. He is simply an out-of-the-box innovator. Sometimes his actions aren't immediately understood because they are novel approaches, but what matters is his motivation to accelerate the solar transition or a just energy transition in the Philippines.)
Regarding Legarda, he emphasized that the senator should not be implicated simply because she is Leviste’s mother.
“Having said that, the only accusation against Loren Legarda is nanay ka ng bata,” La Vina said.
(Having said that, the only accusation against Loren Legarda is that she happens to be the young man's mother.)
Investors

The spokesperson also stressed that this issue is crucial for renewable energy investors looking to invest in the country, warning that these cases could discourage investors who might fear prosecution if a project does not push through—a common outcome if a project proves unviable after assessment.

“These cases, if they are filed, will be a signal to all the renewable energy investors, ‘Wag na kayong pupunta sa Pilipinas, kasi mapa-plunder kayo ‘pag ‘di kayo magpatuloy sa project ninyo,’” La Vina said.
(If these cases are filed, it will send a signal to all renewable energy investors: ‘Do not go to the Philippines, because you will be charged with plunder if you fail to complete your project.’)

“And natural ’yon na consequence… regular ‘yon na sitwasyon na ‘di magpapatuloy beyond predevelopment kasi hindi siya viable— walang lupa, walang araw, walang hangin, may katutubo, may magsasaka hindi maka-connect sa grid, maraming dahilan bakit hindi tumutuloy,” he added.

(And that is a natural consequence… it is a normal occurrence for a project not to move past the pre-development stage if it turns out not to be viable—whether due to lack of land, lack of sunlight or wind, issues with indigenous communities, farmers, or grid connectivity challenges. There are many reasons why projects do not proceed.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Martin Romualdez likely to testify in plunder case, says lawyer
articles.summary: Former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will likely take the witness stand to defend himself in the P7.4 billion plunder charge he is facing over his alleged involvement in the flood control…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 2:37pm

Former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will likely take the witness stand to defend himself in the P7.4 billion plunder charge he is facing over his alleged involvement in the flood control project kickback scheme, his lawyer Ade Fajardo said Friday.
Fajardo said this after the pre-trial conference, a court process wherein evidence for both the prosecution and the defense are marked, was terminated.
“Ang pinakaimportante ay ang akusado mismo, si Congressman Romualdez. He wants his day to defend himself in court, and he will most likely testify,” Fajardo said.

“’He’s about to be listed as an actual witness when it is the turn of the defense to present evidence. For the bail hearing, normally the presentation of evidence is just on the part of the prosecution," he added.
"It is merely an option for the defense to present counter evidence. But as to the presentation of evidence in chief, likelier than not, tetestigo po si Congressman Romualdez,” Fajardo said.
Fajardo said that Romualdez will file his petition for bail on Monday, September 28.
“The petition for bail, this has been ready for some time now. We were only waiting for the actual filing once the pre-trial conference is terminated," he said.
Romualdez’s camp told the Sandiganbayan Third Division that they intend to present 40 witnesses for the bail hearing.
Fajardo, however, said that the fielding of witnesses will depend on the merits, or lack of, of the prosecution’s witnesses.
“If we feel that the evidence of the prosecution is weak, then there might be no need to present all those [40] witnesses,” Fajardo said.
Romualdez attended the pre-trial conference online from his cell in New Quezon City jail due to his current heart- and brain-related ailments. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: AMLC pushes for anti-money laundering law overhaul
articles.summary: The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) is pushing for a legislative reform to overhaul the country's financial crime laws, emphasizing its urgency, as pending amendments to the Anti-Money…

blocks.text: AHEAD OF FATF EVALUATION
Published September 25, 2026 2:32pm

The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) is pushing for a legislative reform to overhaul the country's financial crime laws, emphasizing its urgency, as pending amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA) must be passed before the Philippines faces a critical international evaluation in 2027.

During a forum organized by SGV & Co. in Makati City on Friday, AMLC executive director Ronel Buenaventura said strengthening the anti-dirty money watchdog’s legal framework is crucial as the country prepares for the upcoming Financial Action Task Force (FATF) mutual evaluation next year.
To recall, in 2025, the Philippines was removed from the FATF’s so-called anti-dirty money “grey list.”

When the FATF places a nation under “grey list” or increased monitoring, it means that a country committed to resolving the identified strategic deficiencies within agreed timeframes and is subject to increased monitoring.

For Buenaventura, however, the Philippines’ non-inclusion in the grey list was “not destination” as the government must keep the country from being under the watch of an international body for money laundering and countering financing of terrorism.
“We did not exit the gray list only to return to it," the AMLC chief said.
"The 2027 mutual evaluation timing is critical," he said, noting that FATF methodology, assessors only consider laws and measures actually enforced by the end of an on-site visit.
"An amendment still pending when the assessors complete their visit earns the country no credit,” he said.

The AMLC outlined three key objectives behind the proposed amendments —aligning the national legal framework with evolving FATF standards, addressing operational and legal gaps, and enhancing investigative, supervisory, and enforcement capabilities.
To achieve this, the AMLC is pushing for expansive revisions to the 2001 law, currently backed by at least five Senate bills and nine House bills pending before their respective banking committees.
The measures have been included among the top priority legislation targeted for passage.
The proposed amendments include the following:

items: Explicitly including Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs) and trusts as covered persons under the law
Updating and adding new felonies and offenses to the list of predicate crimes.
Granting the AMLC non-court-based subpoena power and expanding its authority to inquire into bank deposits without a court order, aimed at accelerating evidence-gathering in financial investigations.

Empowering the AMLC with the authority to temporarily suspend transactions, freeze criminal assets, and directly file petitions for freeze orders and civil forfeitures without requiring an initial court order

Setting the threshold for customer due diligence by casinos to P150,000, aligning it directly with FATF-prescribed standards, and explicitly establishing the AMLC's authority to inspect and examine covered persons based on risk-based supervision.

blocks.text: For covered institutions, Buenaventura said that the reforms could translate to faster, more direct requests from the regulator, requiring compliance and response processes to be fully prepared. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No basis to claim that Villar siblings, Padilla face arrest to force VP Sara’s ouster
articles.summary: Graft complaints against the Villars exist, but these are related to a water utility deal, not to Duterte's impeachment. Padilla, meanwhile, faces an obstruction of justice complaint over Dela Rosa’s…

blocks.text: Claim: Senators Mark Villar, Camille Villar, and Robin Padilla will be jailed as part of an effort to remove Vice President Sara Duterte from office.
Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video posted on September 21 by the channel “News Update Files,” credited to “Banat By,” makes the claim.

Its thumbnail shows images of the three senators along with the text, “3 senador makukulong na? Ikulong para mapatalsik si VP Sara?” (3 senators about to be jailed? Jail them to oust VP Sara?) and “Minority bloc, bawas na naman ulit” (Minority bloc, reduced yet again.)
The video’s title reads, “Pwersahan na! Magkapatid na Villar at Sen Padilla makukulong na? Ikukulong kahit walang kaso?”
(By force now! Villar siblings and Senator Padilla about to be jailed? Jailed even without a case?)

The video appears to imply that the three senators are set to be arrested to further reduce the number of senator-judges voting in Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial. As of writing, the video has now garnered nearly 6,000 views and over 400 likes.

The facts: There are no arrest orders against the Villars. Although the Villars face graft complaints, these have not yet reached the courts. These complaints concern PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation’s agreements with local water districts and have no connection to Duterte’s impeachment trial.

On September 18, the Office of the Ombudsman filed criminal and administrative complaints against Senators Mark and Camille Villar, former senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, and businessman Paolo Villar. Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said the complaints concern allegations that PrimeWater failed to meet its obligations to some water districts.

The complaints are currently under preliminary investigation, meaning no charges have been filed in court and no one has been arrested or detained as prosecutors have yet to determine if there’s enough evidence against the respondents.

Padilla is not among the respondents in the Ombudsman complaints. His connection to the misleading video’s narrative appears to come from a separate announcement that he does not intend to seek reelection in 2028.

He does, however, face a separate obstruction of justice complaint over his alleged role in helping Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa evade authorities. The Department of Justice has subpoenaed Padilla to appear before prosecutors on September 25 and October 9. Padilla has denied helping Dela Rosa escape and said he would attend the proceedings.

The video offers no evidence linking the Villar graft complaints or Padilla’s obstruction of justice complaint to Duterte’s impeachment trial, or showing that either was filed to influence how senators vote.

VP trial: The three senators are among the senator-judges in Duterte’s impeachment trial. The Senate recently voted to lower the voting threshold for convicting the Vice President. Senators Camille Villar and Robin Padilla did not participate in the voting, while Senator Mark Villar voted yes to lowering the threshold. (READ: A Villar split: Why is Mark Villar breaking ranks with sister Camille?)

Duterte faces four articles of impeachment covering allegations including misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

items: Philippine Airlines plans to launch nonstop flights from Manila to Delhi and Mumbai in December 2026, pending approval from the Indian government.
Flights to Delhi will operate three times a week, while flights to Mumbai will run four times weekly, using Airbus A321neo aircraft.
The new routes aim to strengthen PAL's network in India, providing opportunities for travel and cargo capacity between the two countries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Philippine Airlines (PAL) plans to launch nonstop flights from Manila to Delhi and Mumbai in December 2026, opening direct links between the Philippines and two of India’s biggest cities.
The new routes remain subject to approval from the Indian government, PAL said.

Flights between Manila and Delhi will operate three times a week, departing Manila every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 10:40 pm. Return flights will leave Delhi every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at 8:15 am.

Flights between Manila and Mumbai will run four times weekly, with departures from the Philippines every Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday at 10:40 pm. Return flights will operate every Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday at 7:15 am.
Both routes will use PAL’s 168-seat Airbus A321neo, configured with 12 lie-flat Business Class seats and 156 Economy Class seats.

“Opening services to Delhi and Mumbai strengthens PAL’s network in one of Asia’s most dynamic economies,” PAL president Richard Nuttall said. “These routes will create new opportunities for Filipinos to explore India while supporting the growing movement of travelers, businesses and goods between our two countries.”
Delhi is India’s capital and a gateway to northern India, while Mumbai is the country’s financial and commercial center. PAL said the flights would also add cargo capacity between the two countries.

The India expansion comes as PAL adds destinations and services across its network. In April, the flag carrier launched twice-weekly nonstop Manila-Palau flights while restoring service to Saipan, expanding its routes to the Pacific islands. PAL is also scheduled to begin nonstop Manila-Chicago flights on November 9, which would make Chicago its eighth destination in the United States and its territories.

Closer to home, PAL expanded its FurPAL program in September to allow passengers to bring small cats as well as dogs inside the cabin on eligible domestic flights. The service costs P2,500 one way, subject to aircraft capacity and pet travel requirements. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why Sara Duterte ally is taking impeachment vote threshold fight to SC
articles.summary: 'The Senate possesses the power to try and decide. It does not possess the power to determine its own constitutional voting threshold,' says lawyer and former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threats case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
'The Senate possesses the power to try and decide. It does not possess the power to determine its own constitutional voting threshold,' says lawyer and former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez

items: Vic Rodriguez, former executive secretary and ally of Vice President Sara Duterte, is challenging the Senate impeachment court's ruling that lowered the threshold for impeachment convictions before the Supreme Court.

Rodriguez filed a certiorari petition arguing that the Senate's ruling alters the constitutional requirement for conviction, which mandates a two-thirds majority of all Senate members, and claims that the Senate cannot change this threshold through procedural rules.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Vic Rodriguez, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s former executive secretary and now Vice President Sara Duterte’s ally, is challenging the lowered impeachment conviction threshold before the Supreme Court (SC).

On Thursday night, September 24, the High Court confirmed that Rodriguez filed a certiorari petition against the Senate impeachment court’s ruling. A certiorari petition is filed to review another body’s decision or grave abuse of discretion.
Rodriguez also asked for the issuance of a temporary restraining order, which if granted, can stop an application or implementation of an order.

A challenge for Rodriguez, however, is to prove that he has locus standi or the legal standing to file the petition, even if he is not directly a party to the case. This is a requirement to prove that a petitioner has a stake in the issue being sought for review. Petitions could be dismissed by the court due to the lack of a petitioner’s legal standing.
Rodriguez, however, said in his pleading: “Petitioner is a taxpayer with a direct interest in preventing the expenditure of public funds pursuant to an allegedly unconstitutional governmental act.”

With 13 affirmative votes, the Senate impeachment court voted to lower the voting threshold on Wednesday, September 23. Presiding officer Chiz Escudero, who ruled on July 6 that the votes needed to convict Duterte is fixed at 16, was the lone negative vote.

Based on the ruling, the court will count only the vote of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings at the time of the vote. With 20 active senators at present, two-thirds (or the required number of conviction votes) would mean 14.
Assuming Rodriguez’s petition will not be dismissed outright, how is he trying to convince the SC that the Senate impeachment court was wrong about its ruling?

In the petition, Rodriguez said the ruling did not only change a procedure in impeachment, but also the constitutional threshold for conviction itself. He argued that the ruling added a qualification to the phrase “all the Members of the Senate” found under Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution.
“No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate,” the provision says.

Rodriguez argued that there are ways to change what’s written in the Constitution, such as through constitutional convention or people’s initiative. But nothing in the Constitution, according to the former Malacañang official, says that the impeachment court can modify a provision through a ruling, or alter the conviction denominator.

Under Article XI, Section 3(8), Congress — the House of Representatives and the Senate — has the power to make its own impeachment rules. The House has the mandate to endorse a complaint and impeach an official, while the Senate serves as the impeachment court.
But Rodriguez argued that a procedural rule cannot change what’s written in the Constitution, adding that an implementing rule must follow the principles declared in the highest law of the land.

“The Tribunal’s interpretation effectively substitutes one phrase for another. The Constitution says: ‘all the Members of the Senate.’ The Tribunal’s rule operates as though the Constitution said: ‘all Members of the Senate who are legally and factually capable of participating in the impeachment proceedings,'” the lawyer argued.
“Those are not equivalent phrases. The latter contains substantive qualifications that the formerdoes not,” he added.

The petition also argued that the Senate, under the Constitution, is composed of 24 senators. Rodriguez said Senate membership is a legal status, while participation is an act related to the exercise of the membership.
He claimed that the absence of a senator does not make him or her a non-member of the upper chamber.

“If the constitutional denominator were allowed to fluctuate with attendance, incapacity, recusal, or other circumstances, the threshold for conviction would cease to be fixed by the Constitution. It would instead depend upon factual determinations made by the Tribunal. Such a mechanism is not found in Article XI, Section 3(6),” Rodriguez said.

Rodriguez also argued that the Senate’s power to try and decide impeachment cases is subject to constitutional limitations. He claimed that, yes, the upper chamber has the said mandate, but this provision should be interpreted along with the phrase “no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”

“The Senate possesses the power to try and decide. It does not possess the power to determine its ownconstitutional voting threshold. The latter is fixed by the Constitution,” the former Marcos official said.
“Because the Tribunal’s ruling effectively modifies an express constitutional provision without constitutional authority to do so, it should be annulled for grave abuse of discretion,” he added.
The Vice President’s camp said they will seek an SC intervention themselves, but did not provide specific details as to when they will do so.

“[We] Will issue a statement once we’ve filed. However, there won’t be a need to cover because petitions filed before the Supreme Court are done electronically — they are not physically filed,” defense spokesperson Michael Poa said on Wednesday.

For the House prosecution team, it is too early to file a petition before the SC because the issue is not yet justiciable or a legal issue that needs to be decided by a court. The Senate has yet to vote whether to acquit or convict Duterte as the trial is ongoing.

“Magiging justiciable and ripe lang ito for purposes of filing a petition [with] the Supreme Court after voting on the verdict, which means the conviction or acquittal,” lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro said. (The case will only be justiciable and ripe for filing a petition with the Supreme Court after the voting on the verdict, which means the conviction or acquittal.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Chinese vessels hindered PH resupply mission to Ayungin Shoal --NTF-WPS
articles.summary: The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) on Friday said Chinese vessels interfered with the Philippine rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal on Thursday.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 2:12pm
The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) on Friday said Chinese vessels interfered with the Philippine rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal on Thursday.
In a statement, the task force said China Coast Guard (CCG) and People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) hindered the delivery of essential supplies to Filipino crew aboard BRP Sierra Madre.
“In doing so, they put Filipino personnel at risk and obstructed a legitimate humanitarian and sustainment operation,” the NTF-WPS said.
“The NTF-WPS calls on the China Coast Guard and the PLA Navy to immediately cease interfering with lawful Philippine RoRe missions,” it added.
According to the task force, the PLA Navy’s and CCG’s actions are inconsistent with the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the 2016 Arbitral Award.
These laws and ruling affirmed the Philippines' sovereign rights and jurisdiction in its exclusive economic zone, including Ayungin Shoal, the task force added.
“The Philippines will continue to conduct lawful operations in the West Philippine Sea and exercise its sovereign rights and jurisdiction in accordance with international law,” the NTF-WPS said.
GMA News Online has sought comment from the Chinese Embassy in Manila but the office has yet to provide a statement as of posting time.

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —VAL, GMA News

Senator Loren Legarda is eager to return home from her medical treatment, where she has been under the care of her son, Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, her spokesperson Atty. Tony La Viña said Friday.
Legarda extended her medical leave to October 9, 2026. She has been on leave since August 3 to undergo treatment for a lung illness, having last attended a Senate plenary session on July 29.
La Viña said Legarda is undergoing medical treatment in France and taking time to rest, as her condition worsens under stress or tension.
“Aggravated siya when there’s stress, when there’s tension. So that’s why she’s taking the opportunity to have this,” La Vina said.
(Her condition is aggravated when there’s stress or tension. That’s why she’s taking the opportunity to rest.)
“... Kasama niya si Leandro, who’s the one assisting her sa medical needs niya. As you know, Leandro is her main family now, so ‘yon ang ginagawa nila,” he added.
(... Leandro is with her, assisting with her medical needs. As you know, Leandro is her main family now, so that’s what they’re doing.)
La Viña noted that Legarda’s return to the Senate by November is not ruled out, as she remains eager to return home from treatment.
He emphasized that Legarda has no reason to avoid coming home or to flee the country, pointing out that no cases have been filed against her yet.

“She wants to come, she’s eager to come home. And very important ito ha, walang reason kung why she can't come home or why she can't be stopped if she wants to leave. There's no reason [dahil] wala namang kasong nakasampa sa kanya… Hindi totoo na tumakbo siya kasi huhulihin siya the next day, hindi ganon ang proseso,” La Viña said.

(She wants to come back; she’s eager to come home. And this is very important: there is no reason why she can't come home, nor can anyone stop her if she wants to leave. There's no reason because no case has been filed against her… It is not true that she ran away to avoid arrest the next day—that is not how the process works.)
Legarda and Leviste both face plunder and graft complaints in connection with incomplete solar energy projects valued at P10.44 billion.
They have previously denied the allegations, with Legarda dismissing them as “false and baseless.”

La Viña previously described the Office of the Ombudsman’s probe into Legarda and Leviste as “lawfare” and “political persecution,” or the weaponization of the law that has traditionally been used against government critics and opposition figures. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Gilas Women earn shot at Asian Games 3×3 gold; Gilas Men drop to bronze match
articles.summary: Gilas Women stay unbeaten after a low-scoring win over Thailand in the semifinals and assure the Philippines its first-ever 3x3 basketball medal in the Asian Games

blocks.text: ANCHOR. Kacey dela Rosa in action for Gilas Women 3x3 in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Gilas Women stay unbeaten after a low-scoring win over Thailand in the semifinals and assure the Philippines its first-ever 3x3 basketball medal in the Asian Games

items: Gilas Women secured a spot in the women's 3x3 basketball gold medal match at the 2026 Asian Games after defeating Thailand 13-8 in the semifinals.
Kacey dela Rosa and Maria Pasilang led the team, with Pasilang contributing 5 points and 7 rebounds, ensuring the Philippines will win its first-ever 3x3 basketball medal in the Asian Games.
In contrast, Gilas Men lost to South Korea 21-9 and will compete for the bronze medal against Iran later on the same day.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Gilas Women will fight for the women’s 3×3 basketball gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, after a 13-8 win over Thailand in the semifinals at the Kinjo Futo Station Square Venue on Friday, September 25.
Kacey dela Rosa and Maria Pasilang showed the way in the low-scoring affair as the Filipinas stayed unbeaten and assured themselves of at least a silver.
Regardless of the color, it will be the Philippines’ first-ever 3×3 basketball medal in the Asian Games.

Pasilang finished with 5 points and 7 rebounds, including the free throw that gave Gilas Women a commanding 12-4 lead with just under four minutes remaining — more than enough time, but still too little for Thailand to recover.

Dela Rosa backstopped Pasilang with 4 points and 3 rebounds, Kennah Ka added 3 points, while Amyah Espanol chipped in 1 point and 5 rebounds in the victory that allowed the Filipinas to arrange a title clash with host Japan later on Friday.
After a 2-2 deadlock, Gilas Women pulled away with a 10-2 run, with all four players contributing baskets during the surge.
Unlike their female counterparts, Gilas Men were denied a place in the final following a rough 21-9 loss to South Korea.
A sizzling 13-2 start by the Koreans spelled the difference as the Filipinos failed to mount a comeback and found themselves relegated to the bronze-medal game.

Luis Pablo put up 3 points and 6 rebounds in the loss, which marked the Philippines’ first after it won its first four games of the tournament, sweeping the group stage and dethroning Chinese Taipei in the quarterfinals.
Koji Buenaflor added 3 points and 3 rebounds for Gilas Men, Nic Cabañero tallied 2 points and 2 rebounds, while Doy Dungo had 1 point and 3 rebounds.
Kim Seung-woo and Lee Ju-yeong both proved to be a thorn in the side of the Philippines, firing 8 and 6 points, respectively, and knocking down two long bombs apiece.
Gilas Men can still end their campaign on a high note as they shoot for the bronze against Iran later on Friday. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film
articles.summary:
Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen

Liam…

blocks.text: Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.

It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign by Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.

“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”

blocks.caption: Liam Neeson, the producer of The Lost Children of Tuam, says he felt a deep sense of obligation to expose the truth. Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb

blocks.text: It prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.

The result, nine years later, is The Lost Children of Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.

The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961.

blocks.caption: Catherine Corless at the site of the former mother and baby home in Tuam, County Galway, where it is believed 796 infants were buried. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

blocks.text: An international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children since starting work last year – the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died.

It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions across Ireland. Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it.

blocks.caption: Monica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, in a scene from The Lost Children of Tuam. Photograph: Element Pictures

blocks.text: In her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.”

The film, based on the New York Times article by Dan Barry, tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished.

Early reviews of the film, which was written by Rebecca Lenkiewicz and directed by Frank Berry, say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actor Monica Dolan giving a powerful central performance.

blocks.caption: Director Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson promote The Lost Children of Tuam in Toronto. Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb

blocks.text: “She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?”
Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said.

Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said.

blocks.caption: Andrew Bennett and Monica Dolan, who play Aidan and Catherine Corless. The actors have captured their personality and relationship, says Corless. Photograph: Element Pictures

blocks.text: “We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.”

Berry, the director, said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.”

articles.title: ‘Filipiñana’ team appeals for support as lead star Jorrybell Agoto battles cancer
articles.summary: Just over a week after Filipiñana’ earned the Philippines’ Oscar nod, lead actress Jorrybell Agoto is now in critical care following lung surgery

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The team behind the film Filipiñana called for support for actress Jorrybell Agoto as she battles lymphoma, a type of blood cancer that affects the immune system.
On an Instagram post on Thursday, September 24, Filipiñana’s official account sought financial assistance and prayers for Agoto and her family.
“The mounting medical expenses have become overwhelming, and we are asking for your help to give her the strength to keep fighting,” the Filipiñana team wrote.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Filipiñana (@filipiniana.film)

Agoto is currently confined at St. Luke’s Hospital and is under critical care after undergoing lung surgery. According to the post, the indie star is relying on a Blake drain to “manage fluid in her lungs and help her breathe.”
Film Development Council of the Philippines CEO and chairman Joey Javier Reyes also expressed support for Agoto as she recovers in the hospital.

“Heartbroken. Life can be so unfair,” Reyes wrote in response to Agoto’s confinement. “But who are we to question? In the end, all that happens serves a purpose. In the end, we will understand. We are with you, Jorrybell. You are meant for greater things. Laban lang (Keep fighting).”
Agoto’s friends have started an Instagram account called “Jorrybell Beats It,” which is dedicated to crowdsourcing funds to help cover her growing medical expenses.

Producer Jane Danting also mentioned in an Instagram post that those who would like to help Agoto can directly message her or her other friends, Chen Mangle-Saez, Camille Lipnica, and Juan Karlos, who have all promised to help the actress attend to other matters as she seeks treatment in the hospital.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by jane danting (@__jjanerose)
“This is a heartbreaking and challenging time for Jorrybell. Her treatment, hospital stay, procedures, medications, and other medical needs continue to bring significant expenses,” Lipnica said.
Agoto’s medical battle comes just over a week after Filipiñana was announced as the Philippines’ official entry to the 2027 Oscars in the Best International Feature Film category.

In Rappler’s recent interview with Agoto on the sidelines of the Film Academy of the Philippines’ Oscars announcement, she had expressed deep gratitude to her team and the people who continuously support her in her career.
“Ako po, sobrang saya ko lagi at sobrang suwerte ko sa mga nakaka-work ko, lalo na mga directors (I’m always happy and lucky with the people I work with, especially the directors),” Agoto said.
In the black comedy film directed by Rafael Manuel, Agoto plays 17-year-old Isabel, a tee girl at an exclusive golf club in the Philippines. It offers a critique of the country’s class divide.
The 2020 short film version of Filipiñana was only Agoto’s second short film project since she started acting in 2019. She then reprised the same role for the 2026 feature-length adaptation.
Her career breakthrough in 2023 included significant roles as complex characters under working-class narratives, showcasing her ability to portray political themes.

She also starred in other feature films such as When This Is All Over by Kevin Mayuga, Tether by Gian Arre, and Sam Manacsa’s labor drama Cross My Heart and Hope to Die where she earned her Best Actress award at the 2024 Tokyo Film Festival. – Angel Camille Dio/Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

articles.title: Pope Leo heads to France with AI, apologies for clergy abuse on agenda
articles.summary: Pope Leo is likely to draw large crowds on the September 25 to 28 visit, which includes stops in Paris, at the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, and in a city on the German border central to the…

blocks.text: POPE LEO. Pope Leo XIV holds a Jubilee audience on the occasion of the Jubilee of Catechists in St.Peter's Square at the Vatican, September 27, 2025.
Francesco Fotia/REUTERS

Pope Leo is likely to draw large crowds on the September 25 to 28 visit, which includes stops in Paris, at the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, and in a city on the German border central to the founding of the EU

items: Pope Leo is visiting France from September 25 to 28 to address the Catholic Church's reputation following abuse scandals and to advocate for global AI regulations.
The visit includes significant events such as an outdoor Mass in Paris with an expected attendance of 600,000 and meetings with French leaders, including President Macron.
Pope Leo will also meet with abuse survivors and lead a prayer service at Notre-Dame cathedral, marking the first papal visit to France in nearly 20 years.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo leaves on Friday, September 25, for a weekend visit to France, where he is hoping to repair the Catholic Church’s standing after abuse scandals and is expected to renew calls for global rules on AI development while laying out a vision for Europe’s future.

Leo is likely to draw large crowds on the September 25 to 28 visit, which includes stops in Paris, at the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, in the southwest, and in Metz, a city on the German border central to the founding of the European Union.
Some 600,000 people have registered to join an outdoor Mass in central Paris with Leo on Saturday, September 26, with throngs expected to stretch down the famed Avenue des Champs-Élysées.
“Pope Leo’s visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave” of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters.

Leading Leo’s agenda on Friday are speeches to President Emmanuel Macron and other French leaders at the Élysée Palace and to staff at the headquarters of the UN culture and education body, UNESCO, which is facing budget shortfalls after US President Donald Trump withdrew from the agency in 2025.
The first US pope attracted Trump’s ire earlier this year after criticizing the Iran war.

blocks.caption: For Pope Leo, the risk of an AI apocalypse is a major concern

blocks.text: Leo, who has made the risks spurred by AI a major concern of his papacy and has called on world leaders for global rules to oversee the industry, is expected to address the issue at UNESCO.

In a speech at the Vatican on Thursday, the pope said AI could benefit humanity, but has introduced “new dangers to security and international peace.” He urged global leaders to “govern wisely” in overseeing the technology.

Leo’s visit comes as Catholic leaders in France have been at odds with the government over the 2024 enshrining of a right to abortion in the French constitution, a world first, and the passage of a law earlier this year legalizing assisted dying for adults with incurable illnesses.
The Catholic Church teaches that all human life is sacred and opposes abortion, assisted dying and capital punishment.
Leo will also lead a prayer service in Paris on Friday at the restored Notre-Dame cathedral, in the first visit by a pope since a devastating fire nearly destroyed the Gothic masterpiece in 2019.

Leo is the first pope to make an official visit to France in nearly 20 years. Local Church leaders hope the trip will repair the Church’s standing after a crushing 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
French bishops have since introduced compensation and safeguarding measures, but survivors have continued to press Church leaders to demonstrate accountability.
“Leo bears the immense responsibility of ‘declaring enough is enough,'” Alain Esquerre, 66, a spokesperson for victims at the Notre-Dame de Bétharram Catholic institution, told Reuters.

The pope will meet seven French victims of abuse by Catholic clergy on Sunday in Lourdes. The Vatican, which usually only issues statements about the pope’s meetings with abuse victims afterwards, has not provided further details.
Leo’s French tour will culminate in Metz on Sunday, September 27, with a speech on “the roots of Europe for peace and unity.”
Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU member states to attend but it is unclear who will come. – Rappler.com

articles.title: AI might run your first job interview as JobStreet launches new hiring tools
articles.summary: ‘AI is there to support, but the decision is always on the employer and on the candidate. What AI will do is give you recommendations,’ JobStreet managing director Dannah Majarocon tells Rappler

blocks.text: ‘AI is there to support, but the decision is always on the employer and on the candidate. What AI will do is give you recommendations,’ JobStreet managing director Dannah Majarocon tells Rappler

items: JobStreet is introducing AI tools for conducting initial voice interviews with job applicants, allowing them to complete pre-screening on their own devices and time.
The AI technology aims to streamline the hiring process by automating tasks such as ranking applicants and conducting reference checks, potentially saving recruiters significant time each week.
While AI is being adopted rapidly in the Philippines, JobStreet emphasizes the importance of governance and transparency to ensure fair hiring practices and mitigate bias in AI systems.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Your next job interview might begin without a human recruiter on the other end.

JobStreet by SEEK is rolling out artificial intelligence tools that can conduct initial voice interviews with applicants, asking about their experience, motivations, availability, and other questions relevant to the job. Candidates can complete the pre-screening interview on their own device and on their own time, before a human recruiter eventually steps in.

It’s one of the more striking features of seekAi, JobStreet’s employment-focused AI engine unveiled at its JobStreet Connect conference on Thursday, September 24. Beyond interviews, the technology can rank applicants, suggest recruiters’ next steps, automate reference checks, and help identify candidates likely to fit a particular employer.

According to the online job board, AI can take over much of the busywork in hiring, freeing HR practitioners to spend more time engaging with applicants instead of getting bogged down by repetitive tasks. (READ: 59% of Filipino workers happy with salary, 45% say pay falls short – Jobstreet)

During the conference, JobStreet illustrated how going from posting a job advertisement to producing a shortlist could involve roughly 3,000 button presses across different tools for screening, rating, pre-interviewing, and managing applicants. Bringing more of those steps together through AI could save recruiters around 10 to 12 hours of work each week, according to JobsStreet managing director Dannah Majarocon.

Its Personalized Targeting feature, for instance, learns what a strong candidate looks like for an individual company based on the job, employer preferences, and previous hiring activity rather than relying mainly on broad keyword searches. JobStreet said candidates identified by the system as likely interested are up to five times more likely to apply.

Applicants could benefit as well. Better matching could help qualified workers surface for openings that actually fit them rather than having their résumés disappear into a large generic pool. An AI pre-screening interview also removes some of the friction of coordinating schedules just to clear an early stage of recruitment.

blocks.caption: MAP: Where Filipino families earn the most and least

blocks.text: In an interview with Rappler, Majarocon said that guardrails and governance have to accompany those systems, particularly because hiring decisions can determine whether a person gets an economic opportunity in the first place.

While the JobStreet head highlighted the company’s nearly three decades of hiring information, job descriptions, and candidate behavior, she also acknowledged that having more data does not mean handing the decision over to a machine.

“We are continuously asking ourselves if we have the right systems, tools, and structures in place to ensure that we guarantee no bias within the systems that we have,” she told Rappler on Thursday. “We constantly regulate that to make sure that we do provide for fair opportunities for Filipinos and for people around the world that we look for.”
For applicants uncomfortable with the idea that AI might parse their résumé or conduct the first stage of an interview, Majarocon said that explanability and transparency were key.

“What we aim to do is to make sure that there is explanability, that you understand the type of AI that we use, and most importantly, you understand the benefits that it provides for you and how we’re storing data,” she said.

All this becomes even more important here in the Philippines, which is adopting AI in HR faster than its peers. JobStreet said 39% of the country’s employers in its 2025 Hiring, Compensation, & Benefits Report already used AI tools in recruitment, higher than the 27% average across Southeast Asia.

At the end of the day, recruiters are not the only ones using AI. Applicants are using it too, including to tailor their CVs for automated screening systems, and some employers are finding that the best way to balance that out is to bring the process back to humans.

DITO Telecommunity chief human resources officer Holy Ampaguey said the technology company still handles much of recruitment the “old school” way, with people reviewing applicants individually. One reason, she said, is that candidates can now use AI to optimize their CVs for the systems that screen them.

“In our own hiring process, a lot of it is still done by our team. We’re kind of old school that way, but we also feel like it is more meaningful,” the chief officer said. “We’re trying to game AI by not using AI.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: AFP suspends Ayungin resupply mission after Chinese vessels interfere
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) suspended a rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal after Chinese coast guard and naval vessels…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) suspended a rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal after Chinese coast guard and naval vessels interfered with the Philippine convoy, citing the risk of escalation.

AFP spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Roy Vincent Trinidad (Reserve) said on Friday that three People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) warships and five China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels interfered with the routine mission on Thursday.
The M/V Lapu-Lapu and three Philippine Navy and Philippine Coast Guard support vessels were still about 111 kilometers from Ayungin Shoal when they were hindered by the Chinese vessels.
“Given the possibility of escalation that could endanger our personnel and vessels, the RoRe mission was temporarily suspended,” Trinidad said in a statement.
The mission was meant to deliver supplies and rotate personnel stationed aboard the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal.
‘Legitimate humanitarian mission’
In a separate statement Friday, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) also denounced the interference by the CCG and PLAN.

“Navy vessels hindered a routine mission to deliver essential supplies to, and rotate the personnel stationed aboard BRP Sierra Madre (LS57),” the task force said. “They put Filipino personnel at risk and obstructed a legitimate humanitarian and sustainment operation.”
“The NTF-WPS calls on the China Coast Guard and the PLA Navy to immediately cease interfering with lawful Philippine RoRe missions,” it added.

It said the actions were inconsistent with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) and the 2016 arbitral award, which affirmed the Philippines’ sovereign rights and jurisdiction in its exclusive economic zone, including Ayungin Shoal.
Trinidad, meanwhile, described the Chinese vessels’ actions as “irresponsible” and “reckless,” saying they were also inconsistent with collision-prevention rules at sea.
“The safety of our personnel remains paramount, nevertheless these actions will not deter the AFP from performing its mission,” Trinidad said.
The AFP said it would continue to sustain personnel aboard the BRP Sierra Madre and called on the PLAN and CCG to “cease these dangerous actions and exercise restraint.”
The Philippines deliberately grounded the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal in 1999 and has since maintained troops aboard the vessel to assert its claim over the feature.
Ayungin Shoal lies about 194 kilometers west of Palawan within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone and continental shelf.

Manila and Beijing reached a provisional understanding in July 2024 aimed at managing differences over rotation and resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre following a series of confrontations at the shoal.
The Philippines has maintained that the arrangement does not require China’s permission to conduct its missions at Ayungin.
The 2016 arbitral tribunal ruled that Ayungin Shoal is a low-tide elevation within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone and continental shelf. China has rejected the ruling. /mr

articles.title: US and China must act as responsible powers together, Xi says as Trump toasts friendship at state dinner
articles.summary: Trump said he and Xi had "never gotten along better" as he hosted the Chinese president at the lavish White House event.
articles.byline: Bernd Debusmann, Max Matza, Ione Wells

blocks.text: Trump thanked Xi for making the long trip to the US, and said the relationship between the two men was strong.
"We've never gotten along better," Trump said.
He praised the long history of US-China relations, although he did take an unscripted detour to praise his ongoing ballroom project.
In the off-the-cuff moment, he said as a "special treat" the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first to enter the ballroom, which is still a year away from completion.
"Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkling, it's our honour to have you do so," he said.
He also presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America".
"We hope it will find a nice, wonderful place in Beijing. It's your honour," he said.
Trump added that he and First Lady Melania had participated in the design of the sculpture.
Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration", making them "feel truly at home".
He said the two leaders are "making history in our bilateral engagements".

"We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Xi said, adding that the two shared "sincere and in-depth exchanges" that will strengthen relations between the two countries.
Like Trump's, Xi's remarks were heavy on flattery, focusing on cultural ties and shared history between the US and China.

The relationship between the two countries was "forged in blood and fire" during the fight against Japan in the Second World War, before being furthered during the "ping pong" diplomacy of the Nixon administration, he said.
Towards the end of his speech, Xi said the US and China's goals can be "mutually reinforcing". He urged both sides to explore a "new approach for major countries to get along".

When the BBC entered the dining hall for the dinner, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was standing over a table and appeared to be telling an entertaining story that had two others nearby barreled over with laughter.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was at another table, with a serious look on his face. His wife is sat beside him, with Jared Kushner and White House chief of staff Monica Crowley nearby.
The White House invited scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and other corporate executives.
Attendees included members of Trump's cabinet, as well as family members like his children Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany.
Bosses from the tech industry in attendance included Apple's Tim Cook, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Both Cook and Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi. As was Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government.
Other companies whose leaders were in attendance include General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance, ExxonMobil and more.
Social media mogul Mark Zuckerberg also attended, as well as Jeff Yaas, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.
"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more."
But one notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there.

articles.title: Allies unite behind Saudi Arabia as Houthis step up attacks
articles.summary: The Houthis launch strikes on the Saudi-backed government in Yemen and repeatedly fire into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East…

blocks.text: HOUTHIS. File photo shows participants taking the oath of allegiance to the Houthi movement during a parade in a show of force amid a standoff in the Red Sea and US-led airstrikes on Houthi targets, in Sanaa, Yemen, February 8, 2024.
Khaled Abdullah/REUTERS

The Houthis launch strikes on the Saudi-backed government in Yemen and repeatedly fire into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war

items: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan are convening a high-level meeting to discuss support for Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks, with Saudi's Grand Mufti urging troops to prepare for battle.

The Houthis have intensified their missile strikes against Saudi targets, prompting emergency alerts in key Saudi cities, while the foreign ministers of the three nations condemned these attacks and affirmed Saudi Arabia's right to self-defense.

Iran's President distanced the country from the Houthis, while Tehran proposed a peace plan to the US, aiming to end hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, amidst ongoing tensions and sanctions affecting Iran's economy.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold an urgent, high-level meeting under a joint defense pact to discuss ways to support the kingdom amid attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, while Saudi’s top religious authority told troops to be ready to lay down their lives to fight their Iran-aligned enemy.

The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government in Yemen and repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

The Houthis said they had fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets on Thursday, September 24, while authorities in Saudi Arabia said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Houthi fighters.

blocks.caption: Houthis pushing to model Iran’s Hormuz control in Red Sea – Yemeni foreign chief

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia earlier had issued emergency alerts for areas including the holy city of Mecca, Jeddah and Yanbu, the main Saudi Red Sea oil port.

Saudi Arabia’s Grand Mufti, the kingdom’s top religious authority, called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis until the group is ousted from power, according to a statement posted by the Saudi state news agency late on Thursday.

Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met within the framework of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement. They condemned the attacks targeting Mecca and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia’s right to defend itself, the statement said.

“The ministers also discussed arrangements for holding an urgent meeting of the chiefs of staff of the three countries to discuss ways to support Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which stipulates that an attack against any one of the parties constitutes an attack against all parties,” read part of the statement.
The meeting was announced shortly after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sought to distance Iran from the Houthis in an American television interview on Thursday.
“The Houthis are responsible for their own actions,” Pezeshkian told the Fox News program “Special Report with Bret Baier” a day after he appeared before the UN General Assembly in New York.

The Pezeshkian interview and speech took place amid a pause in fighting between the US and Iran and a brief attempt at diplomacy in New York, with Qatar serving as intermediary between the warring parties.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal to the United States via intermediaries under which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened if Tehran’s conditions were met.

Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, he said.
“The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the last day,” Araqchi said, adding that talks with the United States on other issues, including Iran’s nuclear issue, would then start.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday, September 23, that Tehran was reviewing Washington’s response to its peace proposals.

Oil prices fell on Friday, September 25, as markets weighed the possibility of a truce, even as the number of ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropped to nine on Thursday, half the 10-day average.
The war, which US President Donald Trump launched alongside Israel in February, has killed thousands of people and disrupted global energy supplies.
While the US and Iran have largely stood down from direct combat, Iranian allies are engaged in the region with Hezbollah confronting Israel in Lebanon and the Houthis advancing in Yemen.

Iran and its allies have significantly pressured oil exports from Saudi Arabia, a US ally. The Houthis have disrupted ship traffic at the mouth of the Red Sea while Iran has effectively limited tanker traffic at the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for 20% of the world’s oil exports before the start of the war. An attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq also temporarily knocked Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline out of service.

Security experts have debated exactly how much Iran directly influences the Houthis, a Shi’ite Islamist movement that evolved from a local insurgency into a powerful armed group controlling much of northern Yemen.
However, Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources have said the Houthis’ advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast was carried out with direct guidance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

With the US-Israeli war against Iran largely stalemated for months on the battlefield, Washington has announced a shift in tactics to extend the reach of its financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms, a practice known as “secondary sanctions.”

Iranian airlines were barred from neighboring countries including the UAE and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of a shift in US policy to target companies in third countries that do business with Iran.
A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran’s isolation and worsen an economic crisis in the country, which is already facing a US blockade of its ports at sea.
“We are living in an open-air prison,” a retired teacher in Tehran told Reuters by text message on condition her name not be used. – Rappler.com
