articles.title: Comelec expects SC petitions vs BSKE postponement
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) is expecting the filing of petitions before the Supreme Court (SC) challenging the postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) in…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 1:20pm

The Commission on Elections (Comelec) is expecting the filing of petitions before the Supreme Court (SC) challenging the postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) in November 2026.

“Ang problem po talaga namin ay paano nga kung may pumunta sa Korte Suprema at magkaroon ng tinatawag na injunctive restraining order,” Comelec Chairman George Garcia told Super Radyo dzBB in an interview.
(Our problem is what if someone goes to the Supreme Court and gets an injunctive restraining order.
Canceled COC filing, preps
“Samantala, ika-cancel na rin po namin ang filing ng certificates of candidacy at ibang aktibidad bilang isang natural consequence,” he added.
(Meanwhile, we are already canceling the filing of certificates of candidacy and other activities as a natural consequence..)
Garcia said the poll body has moved to halt all election preparations, including the filing of Certificates of Candidacy (COCs) originally set to run from September 28 until October 5.
He warned that if a restraining order is issued late, election operations would be disrupted.

A delay stretching into the second week of October would make it impossible to conduct the elections in November 2026 due to halted logistics, canceled teacher training sessions, and suspended COC filings, he said.
Meanwhile, Garcia said all election-related prohibitions and restrictions in connection to the November 2026 schedule including on public works and social assistance are no longer in effect.

On the financial impact of the postponement, Garcia clarified that the P8 billion already spent on election materials, such as printed ballots, indelible ink, ballpens, and thumbprint takers, will not be wasted.
Comelec plans to issue a resolution declaring that all printed ballots and purchased paraphernalia will be preserved and utilized for the rescheduled election in November 2028.
However, moving the election date will require significant additional funding, Garcia said.
According to Garcia, halting the polls means voter registration will have to reopen around November and run through July of next year.
This will require more precincts, additional ballots, and increased funding to hire more teachers and election personnel, he added.
Comelec’s budget has a remaining balance of around P11 billion in the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).
Garcia said that these remaining funds will be used in preparing for the 2028 polls.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Wake-up call’: Labor considers changing Australian laws after OpenAI Medicare hack
articles.summary:
Expert says Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime

The federal government could change Australian…

blocks.text: The federal government could change Australian laws if the current legal framework could not respond to the unprecedented OpenAI hack of Medicare, ministers have confirmed.

On Friday, the government said the review by spy agency, the Australian signals directorate, would consider whether legislative change was needed after the prime minister revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare’s statistics website and three other systems in June.
If current laws could not touch the tech giant, they would need updating, environment minister Murray Watt said on Friday.

“There’s now a review of this underway through that task force that we’ve appointed, and one of the things that they’ll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian federal police under current Australian law,” he told Channel Seven’s Sunrise program.
“If that is possible to happen, then that will happen. If it’s not possible, then clearly that indicates that we need to change Australian laws, and that’s what we’ll be doing.”

The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, acknowledged similar incidents would become “more and more prevalent into the future” and the government would need to be prepared.

“That’s why we’re conducting a review of the incident as well as a review of the laws to determine exactly … whether there needs to be legislative change to recognise this type of incident conducted by an AI agent rather than directly by a person or a company,” Charlton told ABC radio.
Labor has announced it would legislate an AI standard, which Charlton said would be informed by the rapid review. The government has said it wants the bill to be introduced by the end of the year.

UNSW professor Lyria Bennett Moses, an academic expert in technology and law, said Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault, such as intention or knowledge, is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime.
She said existing laws are clear if a human or corporation gains unauthorised access to restricted data, but it’s more complicated when an AI agent commits the physical element of the offence.
“The person is not the AI agent, so it’s not about what the AI agent intended. It’s about how you attribute that intention and that knowledge back to a corporation,” Bennett Moses said.

Bennett Moses said existing civil laws are more likely to deal with these sorts of incidents, that would allow a government or individual to seek compensation an AI company for harm “negligently caused by that corporation”.

“If their systems have suffered harm and there is financial loss, and that harm was caused by the negligence of a corporation, you’ve got a potential for litigation to get compensation for that harm,” she said.
“Here it seems to me much easier to hold a company liable, because if a company caused the harm, it’s not a defence to say that my bot did it.”
Anthony Albanese told the Asia Society on Thursday that the incident was a “wake-up call” about the risks of AI, and whether humans would remain in charge of the technology.
“This technology is moving very, very fast, and we need to make sure that we have a responsibility to keep on top of it,” Albanese said.
On Friday, the prime minister addressed the United Nations and called on other countries to act to “shape artificial intelligence development, rather than be passively shaped by it”.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told reporters the opposition would be open to working with the government to hold companies accountable.

“I’ve long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it … But we’ll wait and see what the government has in mind.”

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said on Thursday the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.
Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

articles.title: Gabriela: Absolute pardon for Mary Jane Veloso a result of long, relentless fight for justice
articles.summary: The granting of absolute pardon to Mary Jane Veloso is victory built on decades long of fight for freedom of justice, House Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago of Gabriela party-list said Friday.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 1:16pm
The granting of absolute pardon to Mary Jane Veloso is victory built on decades long of fight for freedom of justice, House Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago of Gabriela party-list said Friday.

Elago, who was one of those who called for absolute pardon for Veloso from the get go, issued the statement after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he already signed the papers granting absolute pardon to Veloso, who was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to death in Indonesia in 2010.

Her death sentence was commuted in 2015 following a strong appeal from then President Benigno Simeon "Noynoy" Aquino III, but it was only in December 2024 when Indonesian authorities agreed to transfer custody over Veloso to the Philippines on the appeal of President Marcos, Jr.
It was later learned that drug traffickers gave Veloso a suitcase as a gift, with Veloso unaware that the drugs were sewn and kept in the hem of the said suitcase’s zipper.

“Hindi kusang-loob na dumating ang kalayaan ni Mary Jane. Pinaglaban ito ng kanyang pamilya, mga migranteng Pilipino, taong simbahan, human rights defenders, women’s groups, lawyers, at mamamayang patuloy na nanindigan kahit ilang taon nang tila walang kasiguruhan ang kanyang paglaya,” Elago said.
(Her freedom was not given freely. Her family, migrant Filipinos church members, human rights defenders, women’s groups, lawyers, and all those who stood for her freedom. )
“Ang bawat pagkilos, protesta, petisyon, panawagan at pagtindig para kay Mary Jane ay bahagi ng tagumpay na ito,” Elago added.
(Every action, protest, petition standing up for Mary Jane’s freedom brought us to this victory.)
Moreover, Elago said that Veloso should have long been released, given that she was a victim of human trafficking.
“Her freedom is recognition of correcting the injustice done to Mary Jane,” Elago said.
Elago, however, said that the government’s job is not over with the granting of absolute pardon to Veloso.

“Mary Jane’s case is a reflection of a system that forces millions of Filipinos to work abroad due to lack of decent jobs, low wages and poverty. As long as these systems exist, our people will remain at risk of falling victims to human trafficking and other forms of abuse,” Elago said.
“Gabriela’s call for accountability for human traffickers, protection of migrant Filipino workers and end of such oppressive system stands,” Elago added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Chief Justice Gesmundo did not approve 13-vote threshold for VP Sara’s conviction
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court recently voted to change how the threshold is calculated; the issue has not been raised to the Supreme Court, though the Duterte camp said it is a possibility

blocks.text: Claim: Supreme Court (SC) Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo has declared a 13-vote threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, with 13 votes already approved.
Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video posted on September 19 by the channel “News Update Files” carried the claim.
Its thumbnail featured an image of Gesmundo holding papers stamped “Approved” with the overlaid text, “Chief Justice nagdesisyon na! Naku! VP Sara convict dahil dito! 13 votes approved na?!”
(The Chief Justice has already decided! Uh-oh! VP Sara to be convicted because of this! 13 votes already approved?!)
Its title reads, “Kapapasok lang! VP Sara [convicted] na? Supreme Court Chief Justice, nagdeklara na! 13 votes approved na.”
(Just in! VP Sara already convicted? The Supreme Court Chief Justice has already declared! 13 votes approved).
As of writing, the video has garnered over 10,500 views and 562 likes.

The facts: Gesmundo did not issue a ruling setting the conviction threshold at 13 votes. When the video was posted on September 19, the Senate impeachment court was still debating whether to keep the 16-vote threshold earlier set by trial presiding officer Senator Chiz Escudero.

The debate followed opinions from four retired Supreme Court justices invited as amici curiae. Three said the threshold could be recalculated based on the number of senator-judges able to participate in the impeachment trial, while retired Justice Adolfo Azcuna argued that all 24 senators should still be counted. None of them issued a ruling. (READ: ‘Amici curiae’: Where do invited ex-justices stand on conviction threshold debate?)

On September 23, the Senate impeachment court voted 13-1, with six senator-judges absent, to lower the voting threshold. Instead of the Senate’s full 24-member membership as the baseline for determining the two-thirds vote needed to convict Duterte, the impeachment court ruled that only senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings should be counted.
Contrary to the claim, 13 votes was not set as the new threshold. The actual number relied on how many senator-judges are eligible to participate.

Additionally, the claim that Gesmundo supposedly made a ruling on the voting threshold is baseless because the issue has not been formally raised before the High Court, although the Duterte camp has said this remains a possibility.

The impeachment trial: The voting threshold has become a significant issue in the impeachment trial, as Duterte faces allegations of misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery, and grave threats.

Discussions on lowering the voting threshold was prompted by the absence of four senator-judges: Loren Legarda, who is on her sixth medical leave extension abroad; Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, whose whereabouts are unknown amid an International Criminal Court arrest warrant; and Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada, who are detained on separate plunder charges. All four are members of the Senate minority bloc.
With 20 senator-judges counted, two-thirds vote would be 13.33, which rounds up to 14.
If convicted, Duterte would be removed from office and permanently barred from holding public office. (WATCH: What is impeachment?) – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

articles.title: Two-year NHS waiting times reveal system’s struggle with rise in ADHD and autism awareness
articles.summary:
NHS assessment bottlenecks have knock-on effects, leading to delays in medical help and lack of access to specialist support

That NHS boards have imposed

blocks.text: That NHS boards have imposed minimum two-year waiting times for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism assessments shows a health service struggling to deal with the consequences of huge changes in understanding of and social attitudes to these conditions.

Sharp rises in referrals for clinical assessments over the past six years mean nearly 1 million people in England are on ADHD waiting lists, with the average wait already over a year (64 weeks). About 295,000 await an autism assessment.

Formal diagnosis has grown in recent years, slowly from the early 2000s and rapidly since 2020. Between 2020 and 2022, annual incidence of autism diagnosis in three- to 25-year-old males rose from 185 to 580 per 100,000, and from 45 to 320 in females.

The lengthening waiting lists tell a tale not only of an NHS under financial strain and short of key staff, but also one of deepening distress for many patients and families for whom diagnosis is the key to clinical treatment and other forms of support.

The explosion in diagnosis reflects the role of the NHS as a crucial gateway for a range of social support. If assessment bottlenecks mean it cannot deliver timely clinical assessments, this has serious knock-on effects; delays not just in medical help but in access to specialist support in schools or financial support through disability benefits.

This trend has caught public services by surprise, causing alarm at the Treasury and triggering a bitter culture war that on one side derides this trend as the product of faddish and woke overdiagnosis, and on the other is hailed as the belated recognition of genuine conditions with real-life challenges for individuals.

The interim report of a government-commissioned review into these trends by Peter Fonagy, published earlier this year, did not take sides. “Unmet needs, misdiagnosis and concerns about over-medicalisation can coexist in the same system,” he wrote, with a nod to the raging culture war debates.

What was not in doubt was that more people were experiencing distress, especially younger people, he concluded, and more people were seeking help as a result. Thresholds for referral had lowered, driving more referrals into an NHS poorly equipped to deal with the rise in demand.

That increase in part reflected improved clinical understanding and greater recognition of unmet needs, especially in previously underdiagnosed groups such as girls and young women. “Some groups that were historically under-identified are now entering the services in greater numbers,” the report said.

Diagnosis was also driven by institutional demand, whether in schools or the benefit system. It operates as what Fonagy describes as the “practical mechanism through which individuals obtain access to support, adjustments or formal recognition” – or what culture warriors disdain as the “golden ticket”.

The bigger picture driving increases in referrals for diagnosis includes a variety of other factors: the impact of the pandemic, economic insecurity, greater public awareness and a decline in stigma surrounding ADHD and autism.

Fonagy is expected to deliver his final report in the next few weeks. He has shown why the NHS is under huge strain coping with the rise in referrals for autism and ADHD. His next task is harder: to recommend ways of fixing the system.

articles.title: ‘Devastating’: council rejects Frome residents’ bid for regeneration project
articles.summary:
Locals raised £1m for Mayday Saxonvale scheme involving homes and park but Somerset officials agreed deal with London-based real estate company

A bold bid by residents of a progressive town…

blocks.text: A bold bid by residents of a progressive town in the English West Country who raised almost £1m to create what could have been the UK’s largest community-led regeneration project is in tatters.
More than 1,000 residents of Frome in Somerset had clubbed together with the aim of building homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido on a brownfield area in their town centre.

But rather than selling the 5-hectare (12-acre) site to the community-led Mayday Saxonvale project, Somerset council has agreed a deal with a real estate investment company based in Soho, central London.

The announcement of the preferred bidder’s identity at a packed meeting in Frome town hall was greeted with shouts of “who?”, “shame on you” and “stitch-up”. Some of those who had worked on the Mayday project for more than five years were in tears.

blocks.caption: The Saxonvale brownfield site in Frome, Somerset. Photograph: Sam Frost/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Liberal Democrat-led council said it hoped the prospective owners would work with Frome residents but admitted the sale was unconditional.

Some local people fear that rather than providing the sort of mixed development with a generous proportion of affordable homes they envisaged, the prospective owners will be free to build expensive riverside houses and lucrative accommodation for elderly people.

“It’s devastating news,” said Sara Butler, a Frome town councillor. “So many people have worked so hard on trying to ensure this site is developed with the best interests of Frome. It’s been a town-wide mission and this is a slap in the face.”

Frome is famed for its independent, renegade spirit and the leader of the town council, Fiona Barrows, said the idea of the Mayday plan had been to create homes that local people could afford and places where they could work.

She said the town council would work with the prospective owners but criticised the transparency of the process. “Saxonvale is simply too important to Frome to be treated as an ordinary land disposal,” she said.

Susie Jenkins Temple, who had got together with friends to put money up for the Mayday project, said it had been an extraordinary effort. “Across Frome, people reached into their own pockets because they believe this place matters,” she said.
Many local people suspect Somerset council’s executive had decided who to sell the site to before it met at Frome town hall on Wednesday to hear last-minute appeals from the townsfolk.
The way the identity of the successful bidder was revealed added to residents’ suspicions that the meeting was little more than a PR exercise.

Within two minutes of Somerset council announcing the identity of the preferred bidder – Newcore Capital – at the end of an impassioned meeting, it had issued a full press release on the deal. Less than 15 minutes later, Newcore released its own press release.
after newsletter promotion
Paul Oster, an executive director of Mayday Saxonvale community benefit society, said the chance to create the UK’s largest community-led regeneration project had been lost.

The council argued it could not be sure Mayday had the full funds for the project. However, as well as the money invested by local people, Mayday had secured £1.2m from the social impact fund Resonance – the largest investment it had offered. Mayday said it had other investors interested. It is thought the agreed sale price for land was about £3m.

Jon Rolls, the head of developing communities at Resonance, said that without local ownership there was a “real danger” that Saxonvale would become another regeneration scheme done to a community, rather than by and with that community.
He said: “The people of Frome haven’t simply expressed an opinion. They organised behind this vision and invested their own money.”

Other Newcore projects include a 3.2-hectare (8-acre) site in east London, where the plan is to build a new supermarket, community health centre and childcare facilities alongside 1,047 new homes, and a care home and retirement living apartments on a brownfield site in Cambridge.

In its statement, Newcore said it was committed to working closely with the people of Frome “to understand local aspirations, discuss the opportunities and constraints and work collaboratively to develop the plans in partnership with the community”.
It added: “Emerging proposals are likely to include a range of new homes, intergenerational accommodation, community facilities including space for local artists, open space and new car parking.”

articles.title: Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
articles.summary: Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods a "warning to the world" — and questioned if the world had "really heard that warning."

image.caption: Residents carry their belongings salvaged from their damaged homes filled with mud and debris [File: August 29, 2026 ] Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's prime minister stood at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in his UNGA address Thursday.
Nepal's leader calls for cooperation to protect the Himalayas
The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

blocks.caption: Nepal's prime minister was the youngest head of government to address the UN General AssemblyImage: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Nepal paying 'colossal' price for climate change
Shah noted that his country contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he was not blaming any individual nation or continent.
"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.
Grants, not loans, necessary for flood recovery
The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of responsibility, reparation and resilience as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.
Shah said vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.
The 36-year-old Shah was the youngest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.
Nepal-Tibet floods — the deadly 'Himalayan tsunami'
On August 26, a glacier collapsed near the border between Nepal and China's ​Tibet Autonomous Region, unleashing landslides and a flash flood that ripped through downstream valleys.
In the days after the disaster, the world watched powerful images of the widespread destruction emerge from Nepal.
Entire villages were flattened. In other visuals, people trapped in hydropower tunnels deep within the Himalayas were seen crawling away a thick sludge of mud to reach rescuers.
Over 6,000 people are still reported to be missing, with search and recovery efforts still ongoing.

articles.title: Trillanes sought as witness on Duterte wealth allegations
articles.summary: They want him questioned over alleged P181.6-M transactions involving Sara Duterte and her family.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 12:19pm
Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV files another plunder complaint against former President Rodrigo Duterte and Sen. Bong Go at the Department of Justice on Aug. 7, 2024.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial has asked the Senate impeachment court to subpoena former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV to testify on allegations involving her unexplained wealth next week.
In a manifestation before the impeachment court released on Thursday, September 24, the prosecution sought Trillanes' testimony in connection with Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

Article II covers allegations involving Duterte's unexplained wealth and her alleged receipt or acquisition of funds from persons or sources identified in evidence presented before the impeachment court.
The prosecution's request comes as it presents evidence on Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth, including allegations previously raised by Trillanes.
P181.6 million alleged funds
Trillanes earlier testified before the House Committee on Justice during its impeachment proceedings against Duterte.

In April, he alleged that five members of the Duterte family, including Sara Duterte and her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, received or encashed P181.6 million in checks allegedly from Davao drug lord Samuel "Sammy" Uy between 2011 and 2013.

The former senator made the allegation in a sworn affidavit presented during the House impeachment hearing on April 22. The House panel was also shown bank transaction records that Trillanes said supported his claim.
According to Trillanes, Sara Duterte received P22.3 million in three transactions, while Rodrigo Duterte was listed at P15.6 million.
Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte was listed at P51.5 million, while former Davao City mayor and now Rep. Paolo Duterte was listed at P38.8 million.
Honeylet Avanceña, Rodrigo Duterte's common-law partner, and her daughter Veronica Duterte were listed at P53.2 million combined, according to Trillanes.
Trillanes said the transactions followed a similar pattern, with checks issued at regular intervals over about two years, often in identical or near-identical amounts.
Other witnesses
The prosecution said Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System division chief Rendell Sopeña is expected to return to the witness stand on Monday.
Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte, the younger brother of Vice President Sara Duterte, has also been subpoenaed and could be presented as a witness on Monday or Tuesday.
Baste's testimony is expected to focus on the Davao City government's transactions with GenCorp Industries Inc., which secured 19 contracts with the city worth more than P33.2 million.
The vice president declared GenCorp as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 SALNs.

Baste earlier said he and other Davao City officials were unaware of his sister's interest in GenCorp. He also said neither Sara Duterte's name nor the surname "Duterte" appeared in the company's official documents submitted for its transactions with the city.

The impeachment trial will continue to hear evidence under Article II, which covers allegations involving Duterte's wealth, SALN disclosures and alleged continued business interests while in office. — with a report from Cristina Chi

articles.title: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
articles.summary: China wanted progress on trade, technology and Taiwan - but hasn't got as much as it would have hoped for.

blocks.text: Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?
ByLaura Bicker
China correspondent
President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.
China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.
On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted.
The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January.
Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency.
This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations.
This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House

The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes.
Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year.
On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China.
The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself.
In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".
Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.
Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict.
On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.
However, Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trade is helping to prop up growth

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Trade is helping to prop up growth
The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards.

All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans.

But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax".

And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes.
There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures

blocks.text: Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures
But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics.

The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal.
Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive.

Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower.
The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

articles.title: Marcos signs law postponing 2026 barangay, SK elections
articles.summary: The newly approved law moved the elections to the first Monday of November 2028, and extended the terms of village officers from four to five years.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 11:52am
Women cast their vote at Pasong Tamo Elementary School in Quezon City during the automated mock barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) elections on August 8, 2023.
STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed the bill postponing the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) on November 2, according to Malacañang.
The approval of Republic Act No. 12326 was announced by Palace Press Office Claire Castro in a press briefing on Friday, September 25, at Batac City, Ilocos Norte.
The newly approved law moved the elections to the first Monday of November 2028 and extended the terms of village officers from four to five years.
“Nakita po ng mga mambabatas natin; nakita rin po ng Pangulo kung gaano ba kahalaga sa ngayon ang papel ng mga barangay officials,” Castro said.
(Our lawmakers and even the president saw how important the roles of our barangay officials are.)
Castro added that the president considered the roles of barangay officials in conducting programs on crime prevention and flood mitigation.
“Kailangan po natin sila ngayon. So kung magkakaroon po ng election, mahihirapan po tayong makapagpatupad ng mga ganitong klase ng programa,” Castro said.
(We need them now. So if there will be an election, we will be having difficulty implementing these programs.)
In a statement online, Marcos said his approval of the postponement extends barangay officials' duty to their constituents.
"Hindi ito dagdag na panahon sa puwesto. Dagdag itong panahon ng pananagutan sa taumbayan," Marcos said.
(This is not additional time in office. This is additional time to be accountable to people.)

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed into law a bill postponing the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE),

"Sa paglagda natin sa Republic Act No, 12326, na nagtatakda ng limang taong termino para sa mga opisyal ng barangay at Sangguniang Kabataan, malinaw ang ating inaasahan sa ating mga kasalukuyang opisyal. Gamitin ang panahong ito upang mas pagbutihin ang serbisyo, tapusin ang mga nasimulang programa at mas tutukan ang pangangailangan ng bawat komunidad, pamilya at kabataan," Marcos said in his Facebook page.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro also confirmed the signing of the bill in a press briefing on Friday.

Castro said that both the President and lawmakers were able to see why barangay officials were so important, including fighting criminality and maintaining cleanliness of the streets.
She also reasoned that longer terms allowed officials to implement long-term projects. The new measure is not there so that these officials could be lazy.

articles.title: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election
articles.summary: A TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway October’s presidential vote in favour of Lula’s far-right opponents
articles.byline: Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election.
The accusation came in a televised campaign advert that was broadcast on Thursday by Lula’s team amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote.

The TV spot claimed the US president was trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation.

“Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video.

The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement.
Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”.
“If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added.

With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.

In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington’s apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports.

blocks.caption: Workers prepare electronic voting machines during a sealing operation before being used in the first round of Brazilian elections. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Speaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US’ perceived meddling, telling delegates: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.”

Earlier this week, dozens of Democratic party congresspeople wrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration’s “apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections through what they called a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil”.
The narrator of Lula’s campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling.

They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil’s intelligence agency warning of a “critical level” of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump’s vice-president JD Vance.

Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to “alert the Brazilian people” to the ideologically-driven US campaign. “We don’t believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,” Valadares said.
“President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,” added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday.

Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil’s election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump’s behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. “They want to interfere in Brazil’s elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,” Santos claimed in a social media video.
Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.”

In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.

They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

articles.title: PH, 7 countries join drills in West Philippine Sea
articles.summary: Naval vessels from the Philippines and seven other countries sailed into the West Philippine Sea for a joint maritime exercise on Wednesday, the Philippine Navy said on Friday.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 11:32am
Naval vessels from the Philippines and seven other countries sailed into the West Philippine Sea for a joint maritime exercise on Wednesday, the Philippine Navy said on Friday.

In a statement, the Philippine Navy said the activity was part of the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus Experts’ Working Group on Maritime Security Joint Cooperative Activity and Future Leaders' Program.
Led by the Philippines, the exercises involved participating forces from the United States, Japan, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and Brunei.
The Philippine Navy frigate BRP Jose Rizal (FFG14) led the column formation as other warships performed coordinated maneuvering and navigation at sea.
Other participating vessels were the following:

items: Philippines: Landing dock BRP Tarlac (LD601)
United States: US Navy littoral combat ship
Australia: Royal Australian Navy frigate
Japan: Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) helicopter destroyer
New Zealand: Royal New Zealand Navy frigate and sustainment vessel
India: Indian Navy frigate and corvette
Singapore: Republic of Singapore Navy littoral ship
Brunei: Royal Brunei Navy patrol ship

blocks.caption: Participants take action during the drills as part of the At-Sea Phase of the ADMM-Plus EWG on MS JCA and FLP in the West Philippine Sea, September 23, 2026.

blocks.text: Participants take action during the drills as part of the At-Sea Phase of the ADMM-Plus EWG on MS JCA and FLP in the West Philippine Sea, September 23, 2026. Photo from PH Navy
As part of the joint operations, the Philippine Navy deployed an AW159 Wildcat helicopter to carry out a simulated medical evacuation (MEDEVAC).
During the simulation, the helicopter airlifted a mock casualty from Japan’s JS Ise and transported the patient to BRP Jose Rizal for immediate medical evaluation and treatment.
The Philippine Navy said the joint activity aims to strengthen operational interoperability, improve practical cooperation, and facilitate knowledge sharing among the forces.

“Through the activity, the Philippine Navy continues to strengthen interoperability and cooperation with regional and international partners in support of a secure, peaceful, and resilient maritime region,” the Philippine Navy said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos grants absolute pardon to Mary Jane Veloso
articles.summary: This is after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed an executive clemency for Veloso, giving her a clean slate.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 11:28am
Mary Jane Veloso on Dec. 18, 2024.
Bureau of Corrections / Released
MANILA, Philippines — After more than a year in a Philippine prison without charges, Mary Jane Veloso, who was previously put on death row in Indonesia, will finally be free.
This is after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed an executive clemency for Veloso, giving her a clean slate.
“Pinirmahan ko na ‘yung pardon niya kahapon,” Marcos said in an ambush interview with reporters on Friday, September 25.
(I signed her pardon yesterday.)
Veloso is currently detained at the Correctional Institute for Women in Mandaluyong City after she returned to the Philippines on Dec. 18, 2024, from Indonesia.

Veloso was arrested in 2010 on drug trafficking charges. In 2015, following the surrender of her illegal recruiter in the Philippines, then-President Benigno Aquino III made a last-minute plea to Indonesian authorities to spare her life.
Granted a reprieve just hours before her scheduled execution by firing squad on April 29, 2015, the decision came so late that several print outlets mistakenly reported her death.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts wave of Houthi missiles as oil climbs to one-week high
articles.summary:
The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, the main alternative route for Saudi oil

Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, with the latest attacks pushing oil prices ⁠to a one-week high over fears of spiralling supply disruptions.

The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif in western Saudi ​Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, with the Houthis claiming their attacks were aimed at “a sensitive target” in the capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Tanbu.
Oil prices climbed about 3%, but trade was volatile and prices came off session highs after reports the US and Iran discussed reopening the strait of Hormuz.

The escalating attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s ⁠ability to export oil through the Red Sea at a time when the strait of Hormuz is disrupted and the kingdom’s east-west pipeline is only now resuming operations after drone strikes earlier ​this month. The Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, opening a ‌second theatre in the US-Iran war.
It was ‌not clear whether there was any damage or casualties in either Taif or Yanbu, the main alternative route for Saudi oil.
The Houthis seized the whole Yemeni western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab el-Mandeb waterway.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government pressed world leaders on Thursday for help defeating the militants, saying that their new perch along one of the world’s busiest waterways presents an international economic risk.
While claiming that their blockade only applies to Saudi shipping and there remains no threat to commercial shipping on the Red Sea, the Houths have also warned other nations not to get involved.

But the vice-president of the internationally recognised government council urged world leaders at the UN general assembly not to trust the Houthis’ assurances – and to see a bigger picture in the crisis around the strait.

“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” said vice-president, Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer.

Arguing that protecting the strait “is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation,” he urged the international community to keep weapons and technology from getting into the rebels’ hands.

The Saudi-backed government’s forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen’s third-biggest city Taiz from the southern port city of Aden where the internationally recognised administration is based, government sources said.

The Houthis ⁠have kept up pressure along a steep, winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for government forces and the ​only route for goods and residents to reach Taiz and travel ​abroad. Seizing parts of the road could allow the Houthis to ​tighten their grip around the city and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast.

Riyadh’s foreign ministry said on Friday that Saudi ⁠Arabia, Turkey and ⁠Pakistan would ⁠hold ​an urgent ⁠meeting of their chiefs ⁠of ​staff ‌to ‌discuss ways to ‌support repel the Houthi attacks under their joint ‌defence agreement. Under the defence pact, all three countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three.
Officials in Pakistan are said to be deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East.
With Reuters and the Associated Press

articles.title: DOE sees P8 diesel price rollback by end-September
articles.summary: The P8 per liter rollback on diesel, P6 on kerosene and P0.90 in gasoline, are expected next week.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 10:53am
Motorists queue at a gas station in Paco, Manila on Monday to refuel ahead of an expected fuel price rollback on April 14, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — After three consecutive weeks of steep price hikes, diesel prices are expected to see a rollback of as much as P8 per liter by the end of September, the Department of Energy (DOE) said on Friday, September 25.
Kerosene is also expected to go down by P6 per liter, while the P0.90 per liter cut on gasoline is not yet certain.
DOE’s Oil Industry Management Bureau Director Rino Abad said the estimated price adjustments are based on the movements of global oil prices in the first four trading days.

“Mataas pa rin ang tyansa ho talaga natin na rollback tayo sa diesel and kerosene. Sa gasolina, hindi ho tayo pa sigurado. Hintayin ho natin ‘yung Friday trading,” Abad said in an interview with dzMM.
(Chances of having a rollback on diesel and kerosene remain high. On gasoline, we’re not yet sure. Let us wait for the Friday trading.)
Easing global prices

In a separate interview with dzBB on Friday, Abad said the potential decrease on local pump prices is brought by the easing movement in the global market as Saudi Arabia announced partial resumption of their oil export operations.

“This week, announced by Saudi, na makakabalik na ‘yung 40% ng kanilang resumption of the export,” Abad said. “Kumalma ‘yung market dahil nabalik ulit ang export galing ng Persian Gulf. At alam naman natin na ang kliyente ng Saudi is Asia Pacific.”
(This week, Saudi Arabia announced that 40% of its operations will resume. The market eased because exports from the Persian Gulf were brought back. And we know that Saudi’s client is Asia Pacific.)

In the last three weeks, local oil and fuel prices went up after the escalation of tensions in the Red Sea, and the reported damages on Saudi Arabia’s 1,200-kilometer pipeline that led to its temporary shutdown.

The damage affected the transport of crude oil in Yanbu on the Red Sea, which gives Saudi Arabia an alternative route to export oil without going through the Strait of Hormuz. Without this route, Saudi Arabia has fewer options to send crude to the international markets.
The Hormuz Strait remains heavily affected by the ongoing conflict between the United States-Israel and Iran.
PH bears ME conflict impacts
The Philippines, meanwhile, bears the impact of tensions as it imports 98% of its oil supply from the Middle East.
This week, the transport sector has renewed its calls for implementing a fare increase, but the government says it is considered a ‘last resort’ to avoid passing on the burden to commuters.

The Department of Finance, meanwhile, has signed a resolution recommending the excise tax relief on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene, but left out diesel and gasoline over concerns of losing P12 billion per month in government revenues.
The excise tax suspension is yet to reach President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who can either approve or disapprove the recommendation.

articles.title: NBI sees 6 potential ghost flood control projects in Davao City
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Friday flagged six flood control projects in Davao City as strong candidates for being ghost projects. Interviewed on Super Radyo dzBB, NBI director…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 10:42am
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Friday flagged six flood control projects in Davao City as strong candidates for being ghost projects.
Interviewed on Super Radyo dzBB, NBI director Melvin Matibag said that out of 100 flood control projects inspected, 51 have been red-flagged for potential irregularities.
“Meron na pong nagpunta at based doon po sa 100 projects na tinignan, 51 po na red flag na po natin. At doon po sa 51 na yan, merong anim nasa strongly candidate na ghost project,” he said.

(Some personnel have inspected it and based on that, out of the 100 projects that were checked, we have already red flagged 51. And out of those 51, there are six that are strongly candidate ghost projects.)

According to the NBI chief, investigators also discovered suspicious funding patterns, including a single geographic coordinate that received national allocation five times within a single General Appropriations Act (GAA) budget year under different project titles.
"Dalawang beses po pinondohan ng P21 million at tatlong beses na P22 million po," Matibag said.
(It was funded twice with P21 million and three times with P22 million.)
Further investigation
A single contractor, Genesis 88, allegedly secured around P7 billion worth of DPWH-implemented flood control projects between 2018 and 2024.
According to Matibag, the owner of the company was allegedly close to Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte.

Responding to allegations of political targeting, Matibag said that the NBI said it is also actively probing flood control projects in multiple provinces nationwide like Bulacan, Mindoro, Cebu, Quezon, Tarlac, and La Union.
If evidence confirms criminal acts, the NBI will forward its recommendations to the Department of Justice or the Office of the Ombudsman for prosecution.
“We will recommend it for further investigation by the Department of Justice or kung pwede na pong idiretso sa Ombudsman, dadalhin po natin sa Ombudsman,” Matibag said.
(We will recommend it for further investigation by the Department of Justice or if it can be taken directly to the Ombudsman, we will take it to the Ombudsman.)
Welcomes probe
Duterte earlier welcomed the probe but called for more investigation in other provinces, including in the district of Matibag’s wife, Laguna First District Representative Ann Matibag.

"We welcome Melvin Matibag’s statement on the flood control projects in Davao City’s First District... Pero sana lang kung seryoso tayo sa imbestigasyon, dapat pare-pareho ang standards sa lahat ng lugar,” Duterte said.

(We welcome Melvin Matibag's statement on the flood control projects in Davao City's First District... But I hope if we are serious about the investigation, the standards should be the same everywhere.)
“May hawak kami na videos sa projects sa distrito ni Ann Matibag at ng mga Discaya. Kung may ghost o substandard projects, imbestigahan lahat—Davao man o saan mang bahagi ng bansa," he added.

(We have videos of the projects in Ann Matibag's district and the Discayas'. If there are ghost or substandard projects, we should investigate them all—whether in Davao or anywhere else in the country.)

In response to Duterte, Ann Matibag said, "If Congressman Duterte has documents or videos showing possible irregularities in projects in my district, he should submit them, together with the specific project details, to the proper authorities. My office will cooperate fully in securing the records and in any lawful inquiry.” —Joviland Rita/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Carney's comments over possibility of U.S. invasion reveal how contingency plans are always in place

image.caption: Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at a working luncheon during the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, on Tuesday, June 16, 2026. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Analysis

An American invasion of Canada? A top U.S. commander calls the idea preposterous. Prime Minister Mark Carney isn’t laughing. Donald Trump’s threats and talk of a 51st state have pushed Ottawa to revisit contingency plans for the unthinkable — including scenarios whose roots stretch back more than a century.
Former army commander says defence plans would have been amended in light of Trump's threats to sovereignty
A senior U.S. military commander recently dismissed a journalist's hypothetical question about a feared American invasion of Canada as "absolutely and utterly preposterous."
The head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Samuel Paparo, added: "Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?"

It seems, however, it hasn't been such a far-fetched notion for Prime Minister Mark Carney, nor his senior defence officials who have dusted off various long-established — in some cases decades old — contingency plans and worst case scenarios.
In an interview with the New York Times on Wednesday, Carney said he had prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the Trump administration might order military action against Canada.
That's his way of saying there's a really, really low probability of this happening, but the risk is not zero.

items: Carney tells NYT he studied risk of U.S.-led military action in Canada

blocks.text: The Times reported that the prime minister, after being pressed on whether he took U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state seriously, "suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of a U.S.-led military invasion," but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.
"All militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios," Defence Minister David McGuinty said Thursday. "Canadians should take it as described to the prime minister: a tail risk."
McGuinty also refused to discuss details of the contingency planning.
Defence minister says preparations for possible U.S.-led military action are 'normal'
Vault full of contingency plans

While the default vision of the phrase "American military action" for many is one of heavily armoured tanks, jets and drones roaring across the Canadian border, an overwhelming number of experts agree such a scenario is unlikely given the vastness of Canada and the difficulty in securing the whole country.
It's generally agreed that in a conventional conflict the Canadian military would be quickly overwhelmed and resistance would take the form of a guerilla campaign.

There are, however, a number of other different scenarios. They range from the kind of rapid regime change that took place when former Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro was captured by U.S. commandos, to the limited air campaign that's been fought over Iran.
As for contingency plans, the Department of National Defence, like militaries across the world, has a vault full of them — some dating back decades.

items: As Canada deepens ties with Europe, could it leave U.S. banks and dollars behind?

blocks.text: Retired Lt.-Gen. Andrew Leslie headed the section at the defence department that writes and updates the plans.
He said they are amended as world circumstances dictate, often when a new leader takes power in a country where Canada has an interest.
"You make judgment calls on what is likely to happen, what is unlikely to happen," Leslie said in an interview with CBC News.
"You consult with other departments, with other experts, and then you put it away again."
'Heightened focus' in light of Trump's threats

The planning, Leslie said, would have been updated after Trump's re-election in 2024 and would have been pulled out regularly, especially in light of the Trump administration's threats in January to seize Greenland by force.

"In the context of the threats that the White House has issued against Canada … those would have probably resulted in a heightened focus," Leslie said, citing talk of a 51st state and maps showing Canada as part of the U.S.
Over a year ago, Trump ruled out military action against Canada, saying he'd use economic coercion instead to force the country into the Union.
Given everything that's been said, it would have been natural for Carney to call for defence plans to be revised, Leslie said.

"What a lot of people sometimes forget is that a political leader's first remit at the national level is the safety, security of Canadians," said Leslie, who also served as commander of the Canadian Army.

"So it would be his duty to ensure that all due diligence and prudent steps have been taken to see what might have changed from the way that the old plans were written or updated. And it would be the duty of the Chief of the Defence Staff [Gen. Jennie Carignan] to advise them accordingly, which I'm absolutely sure she did."
Carney considering U.S. invasion of Canada shows 'profound change' in relations: NDP MP
Impact of Trump's threats go unnoticed in U.S.
The notion of U.S. military action is a hot-button issue for many.

"I think every Canadian worries about it," New Democrat MP Gord Johns said going into the House of Commons on Thursday. Canadians are paying attention when Trump calls the country the 51st state or refers to Carney as the governor of Canada, Johns added.
There is, however, an increasingly puzzled reaction among some Americans who have grown accustomed to Trump's threats, taunts and trolling.

Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and a former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, said many Americans, including himself, are unaware of how Trump's words affect people in other nations.

"I don't think I have a visceral sense of what Canadians are feeling about the United States," Schmidt said. "We really don't have a sense of the impact of what the president is saying has on other places."

items: Trump says Canada is 'destroying itself' with immigration. Ministers say that's bogus

blocks.text: He dismissed the notion of the U.S. military taking action against Canada, but said Carney has taken the prudent, responsible course of a leader and measured the risk.
Schmidt said he also wonders whether the prime minister's reference was intended as more of a political signal to not only the Canadian public, but Americans and others.
"When Mark Carney stands up and says that, it just highlights the absurdity of what the American president said. Right? It's a way to emphasize that absurdity," Schmidt said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

Email to members says One Nation has loaned funds to a company linked to the party in order to build the structure and establish a micro distillery

One Nation has admitted using party funds…

blocks.text: One Nation has admitted using party funds to build a $56,000 shed on James Ashby’s private property.

Guardian Australia revealed on Monday that a company linked to One Nation – Small Batch Brewing Pty Ltd – was the purchaser of the shed on Ashby’s property despite having no revenue stream and not being licensed to make or sell alcohol.
Ashby is living in the shed on his Yeppoon property while he undertakes renovations.
In an email sent to members on Thursday night, the party’s general manager, Kelvin Morton, said party funds had been used to build the shed.
He said the party’s national executive – on which Ashby sits as a member – had approved a “reinvestment package” into Small Batch Brewing to establish a micro distillery.
He told members that the party hoped to make money out of the “unconventional” business venture as early as next year.

“In an effort to minimise costs, including commercial rent and outgoings, it was unanimously agreed that One Nation would loan Small Batch Brewing the establishment costs for a shed and distilling equipment, which could be placed on land owned by a member of the executive,” the email from Morton to members said.
It is unclear how much money has been lent to the entity for brewing equipment.
“While Small Batch Brewing may appear on the surface as unconventional, One Nation are not alone in our investment decisions,” Morton said.
He pointed to the Labor party’s interests in licensed clubs and the Liberal party’s software company Parakeelia as similar ventures.

But, unlike these arrangements, Asic documents show that Small Batch Brewing Pty Ltd is not owned by the party or party-controlled trusts. Instead, the company is privately owned by Ashby, Hanson and the party’s former treasurer Alex Jones, who are equal shareholders.

Morton said the party anticipated making licensing revenue of between $400,000 and $500,000 a year based on projected sales, which was a “significant increase” in alcohol revenue from its current average of $105,796.00 each year.
The party now uses the contract brewer CAVU based on the Sunshine Coast to make its line of alcohol products.
“We are confident that our members will see the business opportunity that will drive stronger revenue and assist in the funding of future campaigns,” Morton said.
“Small Batch Brewing has engaged liquor licensing consultants to finalise licensing and ATO requirements before commencing production in 2027 …
“We look forward to providing you further updates on the progress of Small Batch Brewing and anticipate a special joint partner spirit ahead of Christmas.”
Ashby previously told Guardian Australia that Small Batch Brewing was “currently a non-trading entity”.
“The business will go through the necessary licensing application and approval process when the time is right,” he said.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon used friend to help fake cancer diagnosis before alleged double murder, court told
articles.summary: Former NSW police officer, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington terrace in early 2024

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon “guilt-tripped” a friend into helping him fake a cancer diagnosis in the hope of explaining his erratic behaviour, months before the police officer allegedly murdered Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a Sydney court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Baird, 26, and his partner, Davies, 29, with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
A close friend of Lamarre-Condon told the NSW supreme court on Friday that the policeman had become “infatuated” with Baird during a brief relationship.
Baird ended the relationship in November 2023 after the accused went through his phone and deleted messages from other men, which made Lamarre-Condon “really upset”, Shae Davison told the jury.
Lamarre-Condon then asked to stay at her house because he did not want to be alone, Davison said.
The police officer arrived at her home with a backpack the next day and asked to send a message from her Instagram to Baird as “one last try to win Jesse back”, she told the court.
But Lamarre-Condon did not want her to read the message, claiming there were medical details he did not want her to know.
She didn’t want to do it initially but said: “He put a lot of pressure on me, he said he never asked anything of me, he’s so upset, can I help.”
“He wore me down,” Davison said on Friday. “It felt like guilt-tripping to me and using my friendship to get what he wanted.”
She agreed, on the condition Lamarre-Condon read out the text to her, while leaving out the medical details.
When he read out the message, she asked him to delete parts that weren’t true, and it looked like he was typing and actioning her edits, she told the court.

He then sent the note in a series of messages, and told her she was allowed to read it after 4 December 2023, when he told her he was set to undergo surgery. He left her home about an hour after he arrived.
The 1,600-word Instagram note claimed Davison had gone to Westmead hospital with Lamarre-Condon.
“He was told he had a cancerous tumour growing in his left shoulder joint/ligament area,” the text read out in court stated.
“Worst-case scenario, it could result in … possibly having his arm amputated.

“He was then immediately subscribed [sic] numerous medications … everyone knows these medications are some of the strongest you can be subscribed, which throw off your hormones massively, which throws off how a person can act in their day to day life.”
after newsletter promotion
The friend told the jury she had not attended the hospital with Lamarre-Condon, nor did he clear this part of the text with her.
The messages tried to justify the officer going through Baird’s phone and stated “this is very out of character for him”.
“There is real love there, trust can be built back on that,” the note purportedly from Davison stated. “Even if you guys never hang out again, I know Beau wants to make things right.”

blocks.caption: Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird. Composite: Supplied by NSW supreme court

blocks.text: The friend was unsure if Baird read the messages but said it was possible he had seen them through Instagram’s preview function. Lamarre-Condon later asked her to unsend the messages.
She obliged and tried to ask him about the content of the messages but he did not want to talk about them.
“He was quite annoyed, I could tell in his voice he was frustrated that I had [read them],” she said.
It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.
The defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.
The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: NSW police officer killed ‘instantly’ after car she was travelling in crashed into tree in Redfern
articles.summary: The marked police car was travelling with its sirens on when it hit a tree in inner-city Sydney about 1.30am on Friday

blocks.text: A police officer has been killed on duty when the car she was travelling in crashed into a tree.

NSW Police said the marked police car was travelling under lights and sirens along Gibbons Street in Redfern, Sydney, when it crashed about 1.30am on Friday. The officers were responding to a reported vehicle theft at Glebe, driving with lights and sirens activated.
The passenger in the car, Mia Lay, a female constable aged 20 had been with the force for 16 months. She died instantly in the crash.
Mal Lanyon, the police commissioner, said thanked Mia for her courage and for choosing the police for her career. “You will not be forgotten”, he said.
Paramedics treated the 24-year-old male constable who was driving before he was taken to hospital in a stable condition.
A crime scene has been established, and police have declared a critical incident.
The NSW Police watchdog said it would monitor the force’s investigation into the crash to “ensure public confidence”.
The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission said it could not independently investigate the incident until NSW police finishes its probe, and any coronial or criminal proceedings are over.
The premier, Chris Minns, and the police minister, Yasmin Catley, said their thoughts were with the loved ones of the officer who died.
“Our police officers dedicate themselves to looking after others, and today the NSW Police family is mourning one of its own,” Catley said.
Minns said he was also thinking of the officer injured in the crash and those who responded at the scene.
The NSW opposition leader, Kelly Sloane, said she was “heartbroken” by the news.
“(The officer) was out working while most of us were asleep, protecting the community,” she said.
Nearby Regent Street remains closed in both directions between Lawson and Cleveland streets.
Motorists have been advised to avoid the area, with several bus routes being diverted.

articles.title: New Jersey governor calls on lieutenant governor to resign after ethics investigation
articles.summary:
Mikie Sherrill says Dale Caldwell ‘engaged in serious, repeated violations’ involving staffers and gifts

New Jersey’s governor on Thursday called on the state’s lieutenant governor, Dale…

blocks.text: New Jersey’s governor on Thursday called on the state’s lieutenant governor, Dale Caldwell, to resign by Friday after a law firm hired by her office concluded he violated the state’s ethics and discrimination rules.

The report published Wednesday found that Caldwell violated the state’s policy prohibiting discrimination in the workplace. It said he made an advance toward a staffer’s friend and when he was rebuffed, he told the staffer: “You young women are looking for young sperm.”

“The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office,” Mikie Sherrill, the governor, said in a statement.
Caldwell’s lawyer, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the allegations, calling the investigation a one-sided operation that did not include necessary due process.
“The Lieutenant Governor was not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations,” he said in a statement.

The report also accused Caldwell of breaking the state’s ethics rules by trying to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating and by bringing his personal guests to ticketed events without paying for them.
“Where a sponsor waives admission to an event for an official’s family member, friend, or date, the value of that admission is an impermissible benefit to the official,” the report said.
Sherrill, a Democrat, said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses” continued even with multiple warnings and trainings. She called his resignation “in the best interest of New Jersey residents”.
“These violations substantiated in the investigation reflect a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this Administration,” she said.
