articles.title: SWS: 30% of Filipinos disagree that they are unable to reduce corruption
articles.summary: Only 30% of adult Filipinos disagree with the statement, “A person like me cannot do anything to reduce corruption in the government," according to the Social Weather Survey (SWS) on personal…

blocks.text: Only 30% of adult Filipinos disagree with the statement, “A person like me cannot do anything to reduce corruption in the government," according to the Social Weather Survey (SWS) on personal efficacy against corruption conducted in June 2026.

In the most recent quarterly national survey, conducted from June 20 to 29, 2026, the respondents were asked whether they agree of disagree with the statement “Ang isang taong katulad ko ay walang magagawa upang mabawasan ang korupsyon sa gobyerno (A person like me cannot do anything to reduce corruption in the government”).
At least 17% are undecided and a majority or 52% agree with the phrase.
The resulting net disagreement score (% disagree minus % agree, correctly rounded) was –22, classified by SWS as moderately weak (–10 to –29).

The result of the latest survey is close to -23 score from the one conducted in March 2026, which indicates, according to SWS, "no meaningful shift in personal efficacy against corruption during 2026 itself."

Before March 2026, the question on personal efficacy against corruption had been fielded nationally in November 2006 (moderately weak –11), March 2008 (neutral –9), and December 2009 (neutral net zero).
It was also asked in the October 19–22, 2025 SWS Mega Manila Survey (neutral –3), ahead of its return to the national quarterly survey in March 2026.
"With net disagreement twice as negative as in any earlier reading, 2026 continues to be the worst year for personal efficacy against corruption in the whole series," the SWS showed.

The non-commissioned Second Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey used face-to-face interviews of 1,200 adults (18 years old and above) nationwide with 300 each in Metro Manila, Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila), the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages and ±6% each for Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
Net disagreement is highest in the Visayas

As of June 2026, net disagreement that a person cannot do anything to reduce corruption was highest in the Visayas (moderately weak –10), followed by Mindanao (moderately weak –21), Balance Luzon (moderately weak –23), and Metro Manila (very weak –37).

Compared to March 2026, net disagreement rose from very weak to moderately weak in Mindanao, up by 10 points from –31. It stayed moderately weak but edged up slightly in Balance Luzon, up by 3 points from –26.
However, net disagreement fell from neutral to moderately weak in the Visayas, down by 10 points from net zero. It fell but stayed very weak in Metro Manila, down by 6 points from –31.
Net disagreement based on education

As of June 2026, net disagreement was highest among those who either had no formal education or some elementary education (or non-elementary graduates) (neutral –2), followed by those who are college graduates or post-graduates (or college graduates) (moderately weak –14).

The survey also showed moderately weak (–20) for those who either finished elementary or had some high school education (or elementary graduates), and moderately weak (-29) for those who either finished junior high school, had some vocational schooling, had some senior high school, finished senior high school, completed vocational school, or attended some college (or junior high school graduates).

Compared to March 2026, net disagreement rose from moderately weak to neutral among non-elementary graduates, up by 17 points from –19. It edged up but stayed moderately weak among elementary graduates, up by 3 points from –23.

However, net disagreement fell sharply from neutral to moderately weak among college graduates, down by 17 points from +3. It fell slightly but stayed moderately weak among junior high school graduates, down by 2 points from –27.
The SWS also showed that personal efficacy against corruption also varies by how adult Filipinos rate the National Administration’s own performance in eradicating graft and corruption in government.

The June 2026 survey found 36% of adults satisfied, 13% neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, and 50% dissatisfied with the performance of the current National Administration in eradicating graft and corruption in the government.

Those who said they were dissatisfied with the National Administration in fighting corruption posted a net disagreement of moderately weak –13 that “a person like me cannot do anything to reduce corruption in the government,” and moderately weak –14 among those who were undecided, compared with very weak –37 among those who were satisfied.

The same pattern held in March 2026: net disagreement was moderately weak –13 among those dissatisfied with the government’s anti-corruption performance, moderately weak –27 among those undecided, and very weak –34 among those satisfied.

"In other words, adult Filipinos who are dissatisfied with the government’s performance are somewhat more likely to feel they can still make a difference, while those who already think the government is doing well against corruption are, if anything, somewhat more likely to feel personally powerless to reduce it," the survey showed. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Hypothetical tandem of Sara Duterte-Robin Padilla leads over Leni Robredo-Bam Aquino, says OCTA Research
articles.summary: The hypothetical tandem of Vice President Sara Duterte and Senator Robin Padilla would take the lead over Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo and Senator Bam Aquino but with a smaller margin, according to…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 6:47am

The hypothetical tandem of Vice President Sara Duterte and Senator Robin Padilla would take the lead over Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo and Senator Bam Aquino but with a smaller margin, according to key findings from the Tugon ng Masa (TNM) nationwide survey.

The non-commissioned, independent and non-partisan poll conducted regularly by OCTA Research showed that the Duterte–Padilla team leads with 48% over the Robredo-Aquino tandem with 36% nationally by 12 points, with 16% still undecided.
This is the narrowest gap recorded between the two tandems to date, according to the survey.

"In previous commissioned surveys conducted in 2025, the gap between the tandem of VP Sara Duterte–Sen. Robin Padilla and the tandem of VP Leni Robredo Sen. Bam Aquino had ranged from approximately 20 to 25 points, indicating a narrowing trend heading into 2028," it added.

The survey fieldwork was conducted from July 4 to 11, 2026, using face-to-face interviews with 1,200 male and female probability respondents aged 18 and above were interviewed for the study. This survey has a margin of error of ±3% at a 95% confidence level nationally.
"Subnational estimates have a margin of error of ±6% at a 95% confidence level for Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao," OCTA Research said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Fanfare surrounds Trump-Xi summit at White House, but no breakthroughs expected
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a lavish state summit that was heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with no sign that a…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife Melania Trump attend a ceremony at the White House, alongside the visiting Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan, on Thursday. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a lavish state summit that was heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with no sign that a closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran.
Summit marks Xi Jinping's first visit to Washington in more than a decade

During a bilateral discussion in the afternoon, Xi urged the U.S. to oppose "Taiwan independence," according to a readout from the ‌official Chinese news agency Xinhua shortly after it concluded. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary of the talks.

Xi had been expected to press Trump this week to halt arms sales to Taiwan. Following his visit to China in May, Trump said he was holding in abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth some $14 billion US and called it a "very good negotiating chip."

That move left some U.S. allies in Asia and even some of Trump's fellow Republicans concerned that he may be tempted to soften Washington's support for Taipei in exchange for economic wins. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain ​control over the island.
Trump welcomes Chinese president to White House for state visit
The summit between the two leaders came shortly after Trump forcefully defended his use of military power in a speech ​at the UN earlier this week, suggesting he could "annihilate" Iran.
Trump took a strikingly different tone with Xi on Thursday, reflecting a power balance that has shifted toward the Chinese leader after a trade war that ended with a U.S. climbdown on tariffs.
Trump touts 'truly great friendship'

In remarks after Xi's arrival on Thursday, Trump emphasized his "truly great friendship" with Xi, rather than focusing on policy differences, and said the two powers had made strides on trade ​since his trip to China in May.
"During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology and 'super intelligence,'" Trump said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence.

In somewhat more pointed remarks, Xi ⁠said the two countries' interests were deeply intertwined and that competition ⁠between them should be a "healthy one." U.S. companies were welcome in China, he said, adding that he hopes "Chinese companies are treated fairly here in ‌the United States."
Xi also said both militaries should maintain regular dialogue to improve crisis prevention.

items: U.S.-China summit highlights the 'hypocrisy' of American trade policy, experts say
Trump greets Xi on tarmac as Chinese leader arrives for state visit

blocks.text: Edgard Kagan, a former senior White House official for East Asia, said the contrasting rhetoric demonstrates the different strategy of each leader.

"The president is casting it very much as about his personal relationship with Xi," said Kagan, now with the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "What I found interesting was Xi is being much more cautious and suggesting that it's less about the personal relationship than the national relationship."
The summit, Xi's first visit to Washington in more than a decade, is the second meeting this year between the leaders of the world's two biggest economies.
Remarks not shown live on U.S. TV networks
For Trump, who ⁠relishes ceremony and prizes his ties with powerful leaders, the visit is as much a matter of national prestige as an opportunity for high-stakes diplomacy.
Some reporters return to White House after judge blocks Trump's media ban
But Trump and Xi's remarks were not carried live by any U.S. television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House's ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico.

Following their remarks on Thursday, the two leaders observed a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden. After their closed-door meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House's South Lawn.
"He loves good granite," Trump told reporters, adding that the two men had a "great meeting" without elaborating.

Trump's embrace of Xi could complicate his campaign message at home ahead of November's midterm elections, when Republicans' narrow congressional majorities are at stake as voters fret about inflation and the war on Iran.

The president for months has labelled Democrats "communists" in an effort to paint them as too extreme, but he welcomed Xi, the head of the ​Chinese Communist Party, as a dear personal friend, with Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside U.S. flags.
Discussion of AI
Despite the fanfare, major breakthroughs appeared unlikely, analysts said.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng that they had agreed to extend until Jan. 10 an agreement pausing their trade war.

items: 'Nuclear' threat or market boom? Either way, AI race looms over Trump-Xi talks
Trump decries critics of AI, saying they're 'negative forces' with exaggerated concerns

blocks.text: Trump ⁠wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that the two leaders would discuss "super intelligence" but again indicated little interest in new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big ⁠topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is," Trump wrote. "That is China's position also."
During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries must "ensure that the development of AI is always under human control."
Analysts say intense competition ⁠between the two powers ⁠in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements.

People familiar ​with the plans say the talks could also yield deals to lower some tariffs, combat drug trafficking and expand military-to-military dialogue, while Trump is expected to seek the release of Americans and others detained in China.
Xi in strong position
Xi appears to be in a stronger position, having ​overseen a surge in China's trade and firmly in control of supplies of ⁠rare earth minerals that give him powerful leverage.
Both leaders see advantages in keeping relations stable, with Trump mired in the unpopular Iran war and Xi grappling with domestic economic challenges.
But beneath the surface are challenges that could reignite tensions, including disputes over Taiwan, export controls, AI and the war with Iran, a Chinese ally.

There has been little sign Beijing is willing to exert pressure on Iran to yield to U.S. demands. During Thursday's meeting, Xi expressed support for the U.S. and Iran to return to a ceasefire and eventually negotiate a peace deal, Xinhua reported.

articles.title: Man shot and wounded during Trump assassination attempt dies in Pennsylvania
articles.summary:
James Copenhaver, 76, was left with lingering injuries after gunman opened fire from rooftop at Butler rally

James Copenhaver, one of three campaign rally attendees shot in 2024 during an…

blocks.text: James Copenhaver, one of three campaign rally attendees shot in 2024 during an assassination attempt on then candidate Donald Trump, has died in Pittsburgh, his lawyer said Thursday. He was 76.

Copenhaver was in the bleachers during the event in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop, grazing Trump’s right ear with one bullet. Copenhaver was struck in the arm and in the abdomen, wounds that left him with lingering injuries and walking with a cane.
Two other attendees were also shot – David Dutch, who survived, and Corey Comperatore, who shielded his family from gunfire before he was killed.
Copenhaver died Wednesday at Allegheny Health Network’s West Penn hospital in Pittsburgh, according to a statement from the Allegheny county medical examiner cited in local media accounts.

Copenhaver’s lawyer, Joseph Feldman, said in a statement issued on behalf of the family that he died surrounded by loved ones. The statement did not specify if his death was directly related to the injuries he suffered at the rally.

Copenhaver and his wife, Marianne Copenhaver, sued the federal government in June, alleging that the Secret Service and Department of Homeland Security had “utterly failed” to provide appropriate security at the rally.

Copenhaver’s injuries required multiple surgeries, including a transection of his colon, and he had lingering kidney and other damage, including a loss of feeling in his leg. The lawsuit described the wounds as “debilitating, grievous, permanent and life altering”.
The White House did not immediately comment on Copenhaver’s death.

articles.title: Alberta separation group releases report touting affordable transition to independence
articles.summary: An independence organization is the latest group to try to price out what it might cost should Alberta decide to become a sovereign nation, although critics say the new report omits major expenses…

image.caption: Keith Wilson speaks at the launch of Alberta independence organization "Let Alberta Decide" in Calgary on June 19. Wilson is also behind the Alberta Transition Council, which released a budget and costing plan this week in the event Alberta separates from Canada. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

An independence organization is the latest group to try to price out what it might cost should Alberta decide to become a sovereign nation, although critics say the new report omits major expenses such as military spending, Indigenous supports, and Alberta's share of the federal debt.
Former Alberta Treasury Board senior manager calls plan 'magic' by omitting major expenses
An independence organization is the latest group to try to price out what it might cost should Alberta decide in the future to become a sovereign nation.

The Alberta Transition Council (ATC) released a budget and costing plan this week which estimates about $5 billion in one-time expenses, while predicting that an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of between $22.2 to $32.1 billion each year.

“This is affordable, this is doable and actually well within the means that Alberta has today. So our view is we can become independent, we can operate as an independent country and we can be successful financially,” said Dennis Kalma, the principal author of the ATC financial reports, in an interview with CBC News.

Having between $22 billion to $32 billion left over every year is money that could be used for different priorities, Kalma said, such as lowering taxes, paying down debt, building savings, or service and infrastructure improvements.
“Canada is a bigger organization. It's not known for its efficiency and a smaller country could do some simplification,” said Kalma.
ATC's figures vary drastically from a similar report by academics at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy.

A former treasury board senior manager called the ATC financials “magic” for ignoring hundreds of billions of dollars in costs, while also not detailing potential cuts in financial supports to seniors, low-income Albertans, and parents.
The ATC is the same group that previously released a 214-page “transition plan,” laying out a range of regulations and institutions that would need to transition to Alberta’s control from Ottawa.
Lawyer Keith Wilson, who leads the Alberta Transition Council and is also a leader with the independence group Let Alberta Decide, said the important point is not simply whether the books balance.
“It is whether there could be meaningful financial room left after Alberta pays for the services and responsibilities of a country,” Wilson said in a news release.
‘Magic a prevailing theme’
This is the latest in a long line of reports trying to envision what would need to happen and what it would cost if Alberta residents decide to leave Canada.

Last week, the University of Calgary School of Public Policy estimated that the cost of establishing a new country would range between $50 billion and $170 billion over a five-year period and would be highly unpredictable over the long-term.

Former Treasury Board senior manager Lennie Kaplan also contributed a projection to a report from the Canada West Foundation, a Calgary-based think-tank. Kaplan estimated setting up an independent Alberta would cost more than $200 billion, with ongoing costs of more than $50 billion annually.

After reviewing the ATC’s reports, Kaplan described “magic as a prevailing theme,” since it should not be assumed that by virtue of Alberta becoming independent it can grow its way out of deficit and debt.

“Uncertainties and risks are treated as things to negotiate later on after separation,” said Kaplan in an email. The ATC “does not model output, employment or trade, and it makes no claim about the size of the economy in any future year.”
In addition, the reports do not cost continued access to trade agreements, among other issues, said Kaplan, which will “need to be reconciled by the ATC.”

items: Establishing independent Alberta could cost up to $170B over 5 years: report

blocks.text: Debt, service cuts and military
The biggest omission, experts say, is the ATC anticipating that an independent Alberta would not inherit its share of the federal debt.

In contrast, the U of C report forecast Alberta's debt would balloon as it takes on a portion of Canada's federal debt, rising to between $324 billion and $442.3 billion — requiring the province to spend billions more than it currently does on paying that debt's interest.
The ATC explained the federal debt was omitted since no settlement has been negotiated and the outcome cannot be known in advance.

For Trevor Tombe, an economics professor and contributor to the U of C’s report, the ATC’s decision to not account for any debt whatsoever being taken on by an independent Alberta, is “not a realistic scenario to contemplate.”
In addition, the ATC does not adhere to military spending to align Alberta with the international commitment of two per cent of GDP and does not include spending on First Nations and Métis programs.

The ATC also lists considerable savings "after replacing everything Canada does” currently for Alberta, however Tombe said those figures envision “a scale of services that are far lower than what currently exists,” and there is only leftover cash because of cuts.

For instance, the federal government provides individual benefits to seniors and low income individuals. There are other supports such as the Canada Child Benefit and grants to individuals and businesses.

The ATC proposes paying for the existing federal Old Age Security program by including it in a new Alberta Pension Plan, as opposed to covering the cost in an annual budget, as the federal government currently does.
“That's an unsustainable strategy,” said Tombe, unless taxes or worker contribution rates were increased.
“Those are big ticket items and largely accounts for the gap between their numbers and what we had from the School of Public Policy,” he said.
With files from Joel Dryden

articles.title: Fat Bear Week is back. And this year, it's all about the mamas
articles.summary: For the first time ever, Fat Bear Week includes big, beautiful mommas and their big, beautiful babies.

image.caption: Bear 901 and her sole surviving cub are one of five brown bear families competing in this year's annual Fat Bear Week contest against 11 solo competitors. (C. Loberg/Fat Bear Week)

blocks.text: As It Happens
For the first time ever, Fat Bear Week includes big, beautiful mommas and their big, beautiful babies.
For the 1st time, the Alaska contest features mother bears and their cubs
LISTEN | Interview with naturalist Mike Fitz:
As It Happens6:21Mamas and their cubs join Fat Bear Week contest for 1st time
For the first time, Fat Bear Week includes big, beautiful mommas and their big, beautiful babies.

The annual brackets-style contest, run by Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve, is a celebration of the park's beefiest brown bears, who gorge on salmon from the Brooks River in order to pack on as many pounds as possible ahead of their winter hibernation.
"This year, we saw more bear families at the river than ever before," Alaska naturalist Mike Fitz told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"So this year we are featuring five mother bears and their cubs in Fat Bear Week to try to tell some of those stories, because the health and size of a cub is a direct reflection of a mother's effort."
Fat Bear Week started in 2014 and has since surged in popularity, inspiring similar initiatives, like Fat Marmot Week in Colorado.

More than 1.7 million votes were cast last year and the team expects to exceed that number this year, says Fitz, a former Katmai National Park ranger who now works as the resident naturalist for Explore.org, which helps run the contest.
The contest features 16 bears or bear families facing off in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament.
And thanks to a particularly plentiful salmon run, the competition is fierce.
Chunk defends his crown
The bear to beat is Chunk, a.k.a. Bear 32, a crowd favourite with several victories under his belt. He won last year's competition after reaching a whopping 1,200s pounds while nursing a broken jaw.
But Fitz says there are a few up-and-comers to watch this year, including Bear 151, a.k.a. Walker.
"He's never won, but he's just a light bulb of a bear," Fitz said. "Every year, he just gets super pudgy. If I was to use another adjective for him, I would call him a pear-shaped."
There's also Bear 89, a.k.a., Backpack, who survived a severe limp during his adolescence to become the brawny beast he is today.
"He was the first bear that taught me how tough and resilient bears are, even at a young age," Fitz said.
Meet the mamas
But enough about the boys.
The fatter a bear gets during the summer and fall, the better their chance of surviving the long, cold winter. That's doubly important for females, says Fitz.
"A mother bear goes into the den with fat reserves not only to survive that hibernation period for herself, but also for her cubs," he said.
A female bear may mate in early summer, but the fertilized embryos don't implant until she's hibernating in her den come November.

"If you don't go into the den with enough body fat reserves, then the mother is not going to give birth," he said. "So the fact that we saw so many cubs return to Brooks River this year means that a lot of female bears in 2025 went into the den healthy."
To celebrate that success, this year's bracket features five mother bears and their cubs.
There's Bear 132 and her three cubs, one of whom became lost for several frantic days in June, only to be reunited with its family.

There's also Bear 284, a.k.a. Electra, a mother of two who, according to her online bio, is known for her "curious and bold" personality, and Bear 610, described as "a small statured bear with a disproportionately large ability to overcome hardship."

Bear 806 is repping blended families with her biological cub and her adopted son, Biggie. Despite being generous enough to take in another bear's lost baby, she also killed and partially ate another bear cub in July who swam too close to her family.
Last, but not least, is Bear 901, who "readily achieves a level of fatness above that of many other bears," along with her sole surviving baby, one of the biggest cubs on the river.
Protecting salmon = protecting bears

Fitz says the Katmai bears' success is the product of Alaskans' dedication to protecting sockeye salmon, especially in the pristine waters of Bristol Bay, which is home to what he calls "one of the last great salmon runs on Earth."
But while Bristol Bay has seen record salmon runs over the last decade, he says the same is not true for all Alaska salmon.

"Many are struggling, likely due to the effects of climate change and how it is impacting ocean food webs. Even though sockeye in Bristol Bay are doing well, we can't assume that will be the case in the future, especially if we continue to burn fossil fuels and force the climate to warm further or allow mining to happen," he said.
"Fat Bear Week offers us an opportunity to see the benefits that large, healthy salmon runs bring to ecosystems."
Fat bear enthusiasts can vote online all week, and a winner will be declared Sept. 29.
Interview with Mike Fitz produced by Emma Marshall

articles.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
articles.summary: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp's first Germany game ended in a Nations League drawImage: Malte Ossowski/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: It looked, until the final moments, as though Germany would somehow hold on and grant Jürgen Klopp a victory in his first game as Germany coach.

"It felt mostly good," Klopp told German broadcaster RTL after the match, with his voice strained after a typically energetic display on the sidelines. "That was really exhausting for both teams today." He added that he naturally wanted a win but that he can "live with the point, too."

In the end, an injury time Cody Gakpo goal meant Klopp and his team had to settle for a 1-1 draw in their Nations League opener against the Netherlands. While the timing of the equalizer will sting, Germany was second best for much of the contest, which turned a ill-tempered at times. Nevertheless, Klopp was upbeat.
"I was very, very, very satisfied with many of the individual performances," he said, before admitting that "we can play better football and create more chances — that's for sure."

Gakpo plays his club football for Liverpool, where Klopp coached for more than eight years. So too does Dutch captain Virgil van Dijk, who thought he'd opened the scoring for the hosts early on, only to see his headed goal ruled out. A close-range finish from Lukas Nmecha then gave Germany the lead but not control of the game.
New faces, new coach, not yet new Germany

While there were a few patches of attacking play that resembled the kind of high-intensity, exhilarating football that Klopp produced at Liverpool and, before that, at Borussia Dortmund, Germany looked shaky at the back and were thankful for some wasteful Dutch finishing.

It is, though, difficult to judge much at this early stage. Klopp replaced Julian Nagelsmann after another poor World Cup showing from Germany and, after naming two different squads for the four Nations Leagues games in an extended international period, is still assessing how to make the most of what he has. Three players — Younes Ebnoutalib, Yannik Engelhardt and Philipp Treu — made debuts on Thursday, and more are likely follow over the next three games.

"I won't promise anything [in terms of trophies]. What I can promise is that we will definitely give it a try," he told reporters ahead of the game. "There's an impression that we have less quality than other countries. When things aren't working, you take a closer look and try to bring about changes. That's what we're working on now."

After Germany lost Kai Havertz to injury in the first half, having already had to change to starting XI after Jamal Musiala pulled out of the match in the warmup, the team was left without much of their attacking experience and class.
Klopp's record should buy him time
But Klopp won't panic. His methods, both tactically and emotionally, will take time to bear fruit. At Liverpool, it took nearly five years to win a trophy; at Dortmund, it took three.

"When the system isn't yet in place and the processes aren't yet established, then something like this happens," he said about Wednesday's performance. "I was very pleased with the passion, the intensity, but we can definitely play better."

Usually, waiting for success would not be acceptable for German national team fans. But after repeated recent failures, and with Klopp a popular figure, he has more credit in that bank than his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. The last coach to win a World Cup for Germany, Joachim Löw, said he will need it.

blocks.caption: Jürgen Klopp has combined experienced internationals and newcomers in his first squadsImage: Christian Schulze/nordphoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It is crucial now to give him the necessary time and space to implement his ideas," he told the Münchner Merkur/tz newspaper. "Jürgen stands for energy, intensity and a strong bond between the team and the fans. But even for him, not everything will work from one day to the next. After a disappointing World Cup, it takes trust, patience and a team that once again plays for Germany with great conviction."
Klopp calls for German unity, seeks Greece win

Klopp has already tried to unite the country behind the team. On the touchline in Amsterdam, he ran through his familiar repertoire of fist bumps, beaming smiles and growls at officials in a cap emblazoned with the words "one of 83 million" on it.

The headgear has already become a familiar sight. It's a reference to Germany's population and the 59-year-old has also referenced the importance of his team, and their flag, as a symbol of nationhood at a time when the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) are making substantial electoral gains.

"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said. "I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?' But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."

While Klopp's charisma makes such a lofty ambition seem somewhat feasible, he's also pragmatic enough to know that for the German national team to be universally loved, it needs to win. Augsburg on Saturday, against Greece in the Nations League, would be a good place to start.

articles.title: ‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammer
articles.summary:
Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animators

Wallace’s reaction as the auction got into full swing might have been a…

blocks.text: Wallace’s reaction as the auction got into full swing might have been a trademark “good grief!” – and the enthusiasm of some of the bidding could have caused even the phlegmatic Gromit to show surprise.

Fans of Wallace and Gromit and other beloved creations of Aardman Animations seized the chance to grab souvenirs when more than 200 pieces – including Wallace, Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run puppets from Aardman productions – went under the hammer on Thursday.
Sought-after items included Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models from the Bristol studio’s hugely popular 2024 film Vengeance Most Fowl.

Lot 216, for example, was Wallace in his traditional outfit of a knitted green tank top, red tie and brown trousers. The catalogue said he was in “smashing condition”, and gave details of his construction: “Wallace’s head is moulded from clay; while his body is made of silicone to facilitate smooth repositioning by the animators.

“He has a skeleton, just like every salt-of-the-earth lad, it’s just that his happens to be made of metal. His teeth, shirt collar, tie, pen, and pencil are fast-cast resin and his eyes are plastic.” It sold for an eye-popping £50,400.
A puppet of Gromit on all fours from the same film was “crafted over a fully jointed internal metal armature, allowing him to be held in his most natural pose”. It fetched £31,500.

The catalogue made it clear these were not toys but pieces of art needing special packaging, shipping and careful handling. “Please also be aware that exposure to extreme temperatures may cause damage,” it said.

blocks.caption: Feathers McGraw alongside CI Mackintosh. A Feathers puppet, with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise, sold for almost £57,000. Photograph: Richard Gardner/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Another eye-catching lot was number 219 – Wallace and Gromit’s nemesis, Feathers McGraw, disguised as a nun. The catalogue reminded bidders of one of the best Wallace and Gromit lines: “Feathers McGraw? Don’t be ridiculous. That’s just an innocent nun, out for a pleasure cruise.”

It went for more than £30,000 while a second Feathers puppet – with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise to make out he was a chicken rather than a sinister penguin – did even better, selling for almost £57,000. Crime, it appears, does pay.
It was not only Wallace, Gromit and Feathers that proved popular. Aardman aficionados snapped up pieces related to the studio’s early days, including clay puppets of Morph and his pal Chas.
Every lot started at £100 but as bidding got under way at teatime in London, it was clear they were not going to stay low for long.
The Morph and Chas puppets, made from plasticine by Aardman co-founder Peter Lord and accompanied by handwritten care instructions, one of the first lots to be auctioned, sold for £3,780.

blocks.caption: Chas (left) and Morph sold for £3,780. Photograph: Propstore

blocks.text: Mischievous Morph first appeared in 1977 as part of Take Hart, before starring in his own series of adventures. Another lot – lunch for six with Lord in Bristol – was bought by someone for more than £11,000. A stop-motion masterclass with an Aardman animator sold for just over £20,000.

Storyboards from Wallace & Gromit: the Wrong Trousers signed by another Aardman grandee, Nick Park, went for almost £4,000. A 9cm-tall clay rabbit that appeared in The Curse of the Were-Rabbit cost almost £10,000.

Bidders whose budget could not stretch to a Wallace or Gromit puppet could buy more modest souvenirs such as lot 89 – dry stone walls and gate from the Shaun the Sheep TV series. That came with “adhesive remnants from where the pieces were secured to the set”. It sold for a more affordable £567.
The sale, run by the memorabilia auction house Propstore, marked the 50th anniversary of the studio, with the profits to be used to train new generations of animators.
Ngaio Harding-Hill, the director of attractions and live experiences and archive at Aardman, described it as an “unprecedented opportunity” to own a part of the studio’s 50-year history.
Harding-Hill said the collection had been carefully curated by the Aardman team to make sure the studio’s five decades were reflected in the auction.

She said: “Proceeds from the auction will be invested in talent development initiatives across Aardman, including bursaries at our world-class training facility, the Aardman Academy, meaning every sale is contributing to nurturing the next generation of animation talent.”

articles.title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military actions in Middle East in UN speech
articles.summary: Dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took the podium, with the Israeli leader labelling them "moral cowards".

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly.
After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice."
In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now."
The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland".
He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians.
Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military.
The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because had been denied a US entry visa.
Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him.
"They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said.
He went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity".
New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader.
"Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said.
In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians".
Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February.
"Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.
A number of people protesting against Netanyahu's visit were detained in New York City. Among them were the Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Emmy-winning actress Hannah Einbinder.
The Israeli military launched a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack against Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostages.
During the Israeli military campaign more than 73,920 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.
Last year, the world's leading association of genocide scholars declared that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
A resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) stated that Israel's conduct meets the legal definition as laid out in the UN convention on genocide.
Israel has regularly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence.
On 28 February, Israel and the US started launching massive air strikes on Iran, suspecting it of secretly building a nuclear weapon - a claim denied by Tehran.
Iran retaliated by carrying out missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.

articles.title: NHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments
articles.summary:
Patient groups decry ‘scandalous’ delays as four integrated care boards take step due to soaring demand for diagnoses

NHS bodies are forcing people with suspected attention deficit…

blocks.text: NHS bodies are forcing people with suspected attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism to wait at least two years before they can be assessed as they struggle to meet surging demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity.
Four NHS integrated care boards (ICBs) covering large regions of England have adopted the approach because they cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments that people are seeking.

Patient groups are warning that the “scandalous” delays such policies involve may damage children’s chances of succeeding at school, deny people the help they need to manage their lives, and increase the risk of suicide. The charity ADHD UK denounced minimum waits as “heartless and dangerous”.

In all, 15 ICBs, which between them cover 19 million people, have brought in various ways of rationing assessments for ADHD and autism to try to balance their books. These include limiting the number of assessments the ICBs will pay for in any given year and using “clinical prioritisation” criteria to restrict assessment to those with the most serious signs of neurodiversity.

Disclosure of the NHS’s widespread efforts to delay and deny access to assessments comes before the publication of a major government-commissioned review of the colossal increases in diagnoses of mental illness, as well as ADHD and autism, in recent years. It was ordered last year by Wes Streeting, the then health secretary, amid concern that the weight of requests for assessment, diagnosis and care was overwhelming the health service’s ability to meet demand.
The 700-page report of the review, led by Prof Peter Fonagy, was due to be published on Thursday but was unexpectedly postponed until early next month.

Sources familiar with the document told the Guardian that it painted a detailed picture of how the fast-rising demand for help with mental illness conditions, ADHD and autism has left those affected struggling to get rapid access to NHS care and increasingly reliant on private providers.

Fonagy’s report raises serious concerns about the sector, especially about the consistency and quality of the assessments it provides and the fact that there are “financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.

It also lays bare the scale of the challenge that the increasing number of diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism pose for the NHS, as well as schools, employers and families, by highlighting up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.

It reveals that the percentage of seven- to 18-year-old boys with autism rose from 0.2% in 2000 to 4.7% in 2025. Prevalence among boys aged six to 11 rose from 0.4% to 6.3% over the same period – a 16-fold jump.

Similarly, the percentage of seven to 18-year-old boys diagnosed with ADHD rose from 0.4% to 5.1% between 2000 and 2025 – an almost 13-fold leap – and from 0.7% to 3.8% – up five-fold – among boys aged six to 11, according to figures provided by the Clinical Practice Research Datalink.

“Minimum waits” after referral by a GP mean people in the areas affected cannot seek an assessment by a private sector provider. That is even though private clinics now undertake half of NHS-funded assessments of ADHD and a third of those for autism, because many patients exercise their legal right to choose non-NHS care, given the NHS’s own limited capacity to do the assessments.

Such curbs by the NHS are likely to force those who can afford it to pay a private provider for an assessment for themselves or their child, which can cost several thousand pounds. They are being implemented at a time when there are 960,000 people in England waiting for an ADHD assessment and another 295,000 awaiting one for autism.

West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board has introduced a minimum waiting time of two years from referral for anyone seeking an ADHD or autism assessment with an independent provider. That was in response to its bill for such assessments soaring from £7m in 2023-24 to £21m last year, it said.

The West Yorkshire ICB’s decision applies to the 2.4 million people for whom it commissions and pays for care in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield. Its area includes the constituency of Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley – the parliamentary seat of the health secretary Yvette Cooper.
Private providers that the North East and North Cumbria ICB funds to assess people “are working to an approximately 78-week minimum waiting time for an initial assessment”, it says.
Somerset ICB is operating a minimum wait of 52 weeks, while the equivalent in Devon is a lot lower, at 14 weeks. Kent and Medway ICB has also decided to impose a minimum wait.
This month, in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, assessment for ADHD and autism has been restricted to those patients who meet the ICB’s priority criteria.
“It’s scandalous that any NHS body should impose a two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments,” said Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK.

“This is the health service denying people care they need, and care that is available, and slamming the door shut on people who need an assessment of their symptoms to give them a diagnosis and unlock essential care that helps people hold down jobs, stay in education and stay out of crisis services.
after newsletter promotion
“A minimum wait is heartless and dangerous. It is institutionalised cruelty.’
A spokesperson for Finally Seen, which tracks NHS restrictions on the right to choose, said: “A two-year minimum wait is not a waiting list. It is a locked door with a date on it.
“The right to choose still exists on paper. In practice it is being rationed by the calendar, which is a blunt and bleak way to treat a legal right.”

The British Medical Journal recently revealed that 17 of the 36 ICBs had introduced minimum waits of 12 to 16 weeks before patients could have a new hip or knee fitted or cataract removed, even though the NHS is meant to give 92% of patients planned hospital care within 18 weeks.

Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Restricting access to autism assessments denies people support because, while it shouldn’t be the case, a diagnosis is needed to get help. For children, this can mean years of wasted school while they wait for an assessment and further waits to get a plan for support and adjustments to be put into place.

“A diagnosis doesn’t only confirm if people are autistic or not, but also their needs and what adjustments could make a massive difference to being able to participate and enjoy life. Longer waiting times and restricting access to assessments will only worsen challenges for autistic people, pushing them into crisis and increasing the number of people with urgent needs.”
The Independent Healthcare Providers Network, which represents many independent assessment services, urged the NHS to let private clinics offer as many appointments as were available.

Sean Phillips, its head of policy, said: “For someone struggling with suspected ADHD or autism, those extra months or years without diagnosis and support can have a profound impact on their mental health, education, work and family life.

“With more than a million people already waiting, we should be using all available capacity to get people the support and treatment they need as well as ensuring that their legal right to choose the best provider for them is being upheld.”

Rebecca Gray, the director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said local NHS leaders were “keenly aware of the deep frustration caused by long delays and are doing all they can to address them.
“But the need to balance budgets and the pressures of soaring demand have – in some places – led to ‘minimum waits’ or even the closure of some waiting lists.
“The current situation is unsustainable and delivers a bad deal for patients and taxpayers.”

articles.title: Australia news live: Paterson says PM’s AI hack timing not a coincidence; Gen Z going without for a house
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live.

  • Get our breaking news email, free…

blocks.text: Australia’s Gen Z are the generation most willing to cut their spending way back to afford a home, according to Cotality data reported by AAP.

The figures show more than 75% of all Australians were curbing their outgoings in pursuit of property, meaning we are more likely to do so than our Canadian, US and UK peers (for whom the figures sat below 70%).
Levels of discretionary spending, like eating out, owning a car, and even moving from the family home into a sharehouse, have dropped among young adults in recent years.

But it wasn’t just first-time buyers making significant financial sacrifices to climb the ladder. Millennials – the largest buyer cohort in the world – are readily forgoing small luxuries to afford homes large enough for their families.
Prospective buyers were selling their second car or putting off holidays while their children were young, Capital Buyers Agency owner Claire Corby said.
double quotation markFor many, it’s around delaying things like going away, or reducing things like dinners out. People are leaving where they want to live and buying in cheaper markets.
Most Australians would not be persuaded to participate in the housing market until mortgage interest rates hit a 4.9% average, the data revealed.
The average rate for an owner-occupier in August 2026 was 6.3%, meaning the market is likely to stay quiet for some time and allowing bold buyers to swoop in.
double quotation markPeople are being conservative and cautious.

blocks.caption: Catie McLeod

blocks.text: Catie McLeod
The opposition’s defence spokesperson, James Paterson, has questioned the timing of the prime minister’s announcement that an AI agent hacked Medicare.

Paterson made the claim on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night after Anthony Albanese publicly disclosed that an AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and that the tech giant only notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.
Paterson told 7.30 he believed Albanese had chosen to make the announcement at the UN summit in New York, as part of his effort to stand up to “big tech” on AI.
The senator said:

double quotation markThe government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did. But in terms of the nature of the potential of actual security breach this is the bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness. I don’t think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City.

Paterson said he didn’t consider the breach to be overly serious because the data the AI agent accessed was made freely available to researchers and academics studying the health system, and was not personal or private in nature.
He said the breach was cause for “being alert but not alarmed”.
Nevertheless, he said Australians were “entitled to demand explanations and contrition” and to want high levels of confidence when entering into agreements with big tech companies such as OpenAI.
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Was this award-winning book written by AI? Scandal deepens skepticism in literary world
articles.summary: A Quebec-based author is at the centre of an artificial intelligence scandal shaking the French literary world and raising questions around how the industry should be using AI — and its detection…

image.caption: Canadian-Haitian novelist Thélyson Orélien, middle, takes part in the literature festival in Manosque, France, on Sept.24, 2026. (Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: A Quebec-based author is at the centre of an artificial intelligence scandal shaking the French literary world and raising questions around how the industry should be using AI — and its detection tools.

Breakthrough star Thélyson Orélien, a Canadian-Haitian poet and author, has been accused of writing his debut novel using generative AI, which he vehemently denies. The scandal comes as C’était ça ou mourir is being considered for various prestigious awards.
The allegation first surfaced Monday – the same day Orélien won the Prix du roman Fnac – on the anonymous X account "Balance ton Claude," which claims to expose AI slop.
The account claims to have analyzed several excerpts from the book using the AI-detector tool Pangram, which found the text was “100 per cent” AI.
CBC News replicated the Pangram experiment with different excerpts of the book, which led to the same result.

Speaking to franceinfo Wednesday, the president of the Académie Goncourt, which shortlisted Orélien for an award, said the latter wouldn’t be disqualified unless “irrefutable evidence” were to surface.

“The academy is taking the time to consider the various factors involved in this case before making a decision that will preserve both the integrity of the prize it awards and that of its work,” Claudel Philippe told CBC in a statement Thursday.

items: A novelist was accused of using AI. Why the literary world is still grappling with guardrails

blocks.text: The executive director of Writers’ Trust of Canada, David Leonard, says the question of how trustworthy these AI-detection tools are is an issue the entire industry is grappling with. For now, the organization, which recognizes local writers, relies on self-declarations made by the authors.
But it’s exploring its options, he says.

“It's a very fast-moving issue,” Leonard said. “We don't want to be in a situation where we're getting false positives, nor do we want to be in a situation where we're using a tool that is not effective.”

On Thursday afternoon, Orélien's Montreal-based publishing house, Éditions du Boréal, announced it was suspending its press tour for the author, who is currently in France gearing up for award season.
"We unreservedly condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days and call on everyone to exercise restraint," it wrote in a statement.
It adds that its decision is to preserve Orélien's well-being and that the book, which was published in the spring, remains available.
What happened?
C'était ça ou mourir, which translates to "It was either that or die" tells the story of a man who undertakes a perilous journey across the Americas to escape gang violence in Haiti’s Port-au-Prince.
Orélien has previously said his own experience of leaving Haiti following the 2010 earthquake and stories of other migrants he met in Montreal helped shape the novel.

In a statement Tuesday evening, he attempted to soothe the scrutiny of his heavy use of metaphors and similes in the book, which many have pointed to as tells that AI was involved in the writing process.

"I come from a Haitian and Caribbean literary tradition in which poetry, imagery, repetition, and rhythm carry a living voice," Orélien said in the statement written in French and released by Éditions du Boréal.
"One might debate my style, but treating its techniques as evidence of artificial intelligence has nothing to do with literary criticism," he said.
In the same statement, Éditions du Boréal affirmed its support for the author, saying Orélien's manuscript was drafted several years ago and evolved over multiple exchanges with his editor.
However, new allegations have cast doubt on Orélien's credibility beyond the fiction-writing sphere.
Allegations of plagiarism

On Wednesday, the Quebec newspaper La Presse uncovered multiple instances of possible plagiarism in Orélion’s columns across different publications dating back to 2012. Radio-Canada's Décrypteurs has since verified those findings.
Orélien has not addressed the compounding scandal.

Speaking to Radio-Canada’s Tout un matin Thursday morning, La Presse’s vice-president of information, François Cardinal said he read the book – stopping short of calling it “incredible” – and at no point suspected the involvement of AI.
“We’ll never have a definitive answer on AI one way or the other. We can’t prove beyond all doubt that AI was used. And we can’t prove that AI wasn’t used,” he said.
But given the plagiarism allegations, he said the publication will likely not consider Orélien for future columns.
In an update Thursday morning, Éditions du Boréal said it was taking stock of the newest and "very serious" plagiarism allegations.
Thursday afternoon, the literary festival Salon du livre in the Eastern Townships announced it was dropping Orélien as its guest of honour.
A few hours later, Éditions du Boréal announced its suspension of Orélien's press tour.

In its latest statement, it continued to defend its editorial process, adding that despite its best efforts to produce a "definitive answer" as to whether the book was written by AI, the publishing house says it is simply "impossible at this stage to confirm or deny the allegations."

"The fact remains that the novel has reached tens of thousands of readers across the French-speaking world, as well as numerous international publishers," reads the statement. "In the absence of serious, tangible evidence, it is not for us to decide whether it has the right to exist."
Tools detect AI, not ideas

For Florent Michelot, a Concordia professor who researches AI in education, Orélien’s ordeal raises a key question: Have we entered an era where the final product is no longer enough when judging someone’s work?

“I didn’t read the book, but maybe [Orélien] developed very complex personalities for his characters, maybe he developed a wonderful atmosphere … and the AI only helped to write the sentences,” he said.
Michelot says he's personally tested Pangram, the AI-detector tool, and like many other experts who have spoken out since the controversy broke, he says the tool is "amazing."

Basically, the tool identifies patterns based on probability, he explains. If every word in an excerpt is statistically the most likely word to follow the one before it, then AI was most likely involved in the writing, according to the tool.
So, as more people lean on AI for things like research, spellcheck and translations, Michelot wonders if the creative process will begin to gain more value over the finished product.
Humans reading humans

For French literature professor Emeline Pierre, who teaches at the Université de Montréal, the controversy has created a sense of unease, she says. The questions of why Orélien was targeted and why now are central to how she's digesting the situation.
Regardless, she puts in doubt the reliability of AI-detecting tools. As for the repetitions and metaphors in Orélien's text, she says they are characteristic of writing styles in the Caribbean.

"Once again, we see the journey of a Black person who makes their mark. And when that person perhaps goes too far — garners too much recognition — it seems to me that they eventually become a source of discomfort," she said.

She says the attention the controversy has garnered harkens back to the case of Jason Arday, a Cambridge professor who gained prominence after becoming the university's youngest professor in 2023 at age 37.
He was found dead inside his apartment after becoming the focus of a plagiarism scandal.

Pierre worries about the effect the Orélien story will have on emerging young Black writers, adding that the speed with which scandals seem to close in on their subject when they’re Black is worrisome.

The executive director of the Writers' Trust of Canada says despite the controversy and AI’s seemingly growing writing proficiency, it’s not the future of literature itself he’s worried about, but the viability of writing as a career.
He says many authors support themselves by taking on other types of writing jobs and those are being eliminated by AI.
“So these tools are making it much more difficult for writers to make a living,” he said.
“We'll continue to write literature, and people wanting to read human-authored works will continue to want to read human-authored works.”

articles.title: RCMP says no sign of interrupted investigations following FBI's outcry over CBC
articles.summary: The head of the RCMP says there's no evidence to suggest investigations were impacted following a report last week that FBI Director Kash Patel temporarily halted co-operation with the Mounties in…

image.caption: RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme says that there is no evidence that investigations were impacted after a report that the FBI was directed to temporarily halt co-operating. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The head of the RCMP says there's no evidence to suggest investigations were impacted following a report last week that FBI Director Kash Patel temporarily halted co-operation with the Mounties in retaliation for an internal CBC memo.
New York Times reported attempt to temporarily halt FBI co-operation with Mounties

The head of the RCMP says there's no evidence to suggest investigations were impacted following a report that FBI Director Kash Patel temporarily halted co-operation with the Mounties in retaliation for an internal CBC memo.

According to a New York Times story published last week, an irate Patel sought to punish the Canadian national law enforcement agency in the wake of a leaked internal memo from the public broadcaster instructing reporters to not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks ahead of the 25th anniversary. The policy was amended following international outcry.
RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said he received no formal notification that the FBI would stop co-operation.
"My concern was the perception of the Canadian public with regards to 'did this really happen?'" he told reporters after appearing before a parliamentary committee on Thursday.
"So we did do a little bit of research throughout the country and there's nothing that was reported that any of our investigations have stopped."

Following the memo from CBC — which is editorially independent from the RCMP and the government at large — Patel put out a statement on X that "any agency in Canada that doesn't publicly reject this bastardization of history, and an insult to the souls lost during our largest terrorist attack in U.S. history will no longer have friend in this FBI."
According to the New York Times's sources, Patel sought to punish Canada and FBI officials cancelled meetings with their Canadian counterparts — telling them they would be out of touch for some time.

Duheme said he also heard Patel "told people not to go into the embassy those certain days, but there's no way for me to prove it," while stressing the RCMP's relationship with the FBI "remains very strong. "
U.S. intelligence-sharing to continue

Any kind of meaningful falling out with the FBI could be devastating for Canada. It's largely a net importer of intelligence and leans heavily on partnerships like the Fives Eyes — which includes the United States, United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand — to pass on information.
The RCMP and FBI have a longstanding partnership and collaborate on a range of issues from the shared border to terrorism and cybersecurity.

Still, the two countries' intelligence and security alliance has been called into question since the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump who has repeatedly goaded Canada with annexation rhetoric and started a trade war with his northern neighbour.

items: ShinyHunters hackers say they breached FBI, stole employee data
RCMP says relationships with allies 'strong' after NYT report

blocks.text: From the RCMP's perspective, Duheme said there's no thought to reduce co-operation.
"How would it be perceived if you're withholding information and an incident actually happened?" he said.

"We're all aware of the political environment we're operating in," Duheme said. But he said the agencies share a common purpose: "Protecting the Americans, protecting Canadians, working together. And I think that's what people would expect."
The FBI has declined to comment on the New York Times report.

Asked about the report, a spokesperson for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) said last week that it maintains "longstanding and mutually beneficial relationships with numerous agencies in the U.S. intelligence community.
"When it comes to security and intelligence, the FBI remains an important partner, and it is in our shared interest to continue working together."
CBC has a longstanding policy to generally avoid labelling specific acts as terrorism without attribution.

Following the outcry, Basem Boshra, CBC's senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, issued a clarification on Aug. 28 saying "direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism."
When reached for comment, CBC spokesperson Chuck Thompson said "it's not our place to comment on matters between the FBI and the RCMP."

articles.title: Actors Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder detained at protest outside Netanyahu's UN speech
articles.summary: Actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were detained in New York City on Thursday as a crowd protested Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech to the United Nations General Assembly.

image.caption: Actor Susan Sarandon, left, is detained during a protest ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address to the United Nations 81st General Assembly in New York City on Thursday. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were detained in New York City on Thursday as a crowd protested Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech to the United Nations General Assembly.
Photos show Sarandon in handcuffs with New York police

Actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were among the protestors detained in New York City on Thursday as Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a speech to the United Nations General Assembly.
Photos showed Sarandon, 79, and Einbinder, 31, in handcuffs with members of the New York Police Department, with the former wearing a shirt that said "fund people not bombs."
CBC News has contacted both actors' representatives for comment.

Several hundred anti-Israel protesters gathered near the United Nations before Netanyahu's speech, with dozens blocking traffic and chanting: "Stop arming Israel, let Gaza live" and "Stop arming Israel, let Iran live."

Dozens of delegates stood up and walked out of the UN hall when Netanyahu began his speech to the meeting of world leaders. His supporters in the gallery chanted in Hebrew: "The people of Israel live."
Describing those members as "moral cowards," Netanyahu asked anyone else who felt the same way to leave the room before he started to speak.

Netanyahu faces an election next month widely seen as a referendum on his responsibility for the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023 and his ability to defend Israel's reputation on the world stage.
Day after day this week, as other heads of state have stepped to the UN podium, many have harshly criticized Israel's actions, particularly in Gaza.

items: Palestinian president, denied visa to speak at UN, addresses leaders in pre-recorded video

blocks.text: Ahead of his visit, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the U.S. should honour a warrant for Netanyahu's arrest issued by the International Criminal Court. The prime minister is wanted for war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed in Gaza, though the U.S. is not a member of the court and New York City lacks the authority to make an arrest.

Earlier on Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the assembly through pre-recorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied him and other top Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.
"The Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times in its history," Abbas said, citing long-term military occupation in the West Bank and the war in Gaza.
Israel, he said, "has targeted all of the basic necessities of life."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.
