articles.title: Police arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas after ‘dinghy slashed in Channel’
articles.summary:
Thirty-seven-year-old in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life

The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been…

blocks.text: The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was onboard.

The arrest came as the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year. Responding to the figures, the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man of no fixed abode had been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder onboard was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.

He was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”. Police said he remained in custody on Thursday.

The force had earlier said it was looking at footage livestreamed by Thomas, in which he could reportedly be seen using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after asylum seekers had been helped to safety but a French rescue worker had just got onboard.

Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of the dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on to the larger boat.

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.

blocks.caption: The far-right activist Daniel Thomas in London this month. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty

blocks.text: A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform.

The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.
Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small boat arrivals in the UK. A government spokesperson said: “Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42% and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020. But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.”

Wednesday’s arrivals take the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565. Home Office data indicates this is down 42% on this time last year (32,188) and 26% below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).

This week ministers have also been concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days. Most small boats carrying asylum seekers to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time,” after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”
On Thursday a 42-year-old man was jailed after throwing a plastic bottle at a police line and swearing at officers during an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Del Somerville, of Paulsgrove, was sentenced at Portsmouth crown court to two years in prison having previously pleaded guilty to the charge of violent disorder. He is the first to be sentenced over violence that erupted after the arrival of a small boat in the Hampshire city on 6 September.

Judge Daniel Sawyer told him his sentence would act as a deterrent to others after subsequent protests in the area. Describing Somerville as a “thug”, he told the defendant: “Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them.”

articles.title: Greek PM urges UK PM to return Elgin Marbles permanently
articles.summary: Andy Burnham said in 2023 the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

blocks.text: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".
The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.
The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external.
"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.
Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.
This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".
Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".
British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.
They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.
After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.
The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.
The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.
Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.
Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.
Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.
The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.
Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

articles.title: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of $7B St. Thomas, Ont., battery plant to 2029
articles.summary: PowerCo, the Volkswagen subsidiary building a $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than…

image.caption: This aerial drone photo shows construction underway at the site of the future PowerCo plant in St. Thomas, Ont. Its opening has been delayed until 2029, Volkswagen says. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: London

PowerCo, the Volkswagen subsidiary building a $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
Conservative MP raises concerns about delay, citing federal subsidies and job promises

The Volkswagen subsidiary building an electric vehicle (EV) battery "gigafactory" in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
PowerCo Canada made the announcement in a news release about hiring Mississauga, Ont.-based EllisDon Corporation as the general contractor for construction of the factory.

"St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve," said a news release.
PowerCo declined to make a spokesperson available for an interview with CBC News about the delay.

items: Volkswagen to open its first North American EV battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont.

blocks.text: Originally scheduled for a 2027 opening, the $7-billion factory — with a promise of up to $13 billion in subsidies from the federal government — was first announced in 2023. It was estimated it would result in the creation of 3,000 direct jobs and tens of thousands of indirect jobs in the region.

items: Highway 3 expansion gets underway as St. Thomas prepares for battery plant boom
Construction has started on massive Volkswagen battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont.

blocks.text: To prepare for the arrival of the plant, surrounding municipalities and the provincial government have undertaken infrastructure projects to increase sewer and road capacity for the population boom that was expected in 2027.
Before the plant was announced, the province allowed St. Thomas to annex land from the neighbouring municipality of Central Elgin to make room for the development.
In August 2025, PowerCo Canada announced it had awarded two major construction contracts for the project. Construction began in October 2025, with work starting on the foundations for the facility.
St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who has championed the factory as a major driver of economic growth for his city, told CBC News he's unfazed by the two-year delay.
"They've picked a great local Canadian general contractor and in doing so, they had to adjust the [opening] date," said Preston.

items: PowerCo begins hiring blitz for positions at St. Thomas EV battery gigafactory

blocks.text: PowerCo has been hiring workers in the St. Thomas area since August 2025. Preston estimates roughly 500 people are currently employed by the company in the surrounding area.

He also cited "the number of employees they already have working and living in the city of St. Thomas, the amount of construction that's going on in that site each and every day" as reasons for maintaining confidence in the project.
Preston also pointed to Yarmouth Yards, a large industrial park developed by St. Thomas, which is being populated by industries that are complementary to battery production.
Provincial officials also welcomed EllisDon's selection as general contractor.

In a written statement to CBC News, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade said the contract "represents a major milestone as they work towards the start of production that will create thousands of direct and indirect jobs across the supply chain."
The ministry's statement didn't address the two-year delay.

"We look forward to continuing to work with PowerCo as they progress on their $7-billion gigafactory in St. Thomas that will position Ontario at the forefront of innovative battery and automotive production for decades to come," it said.
Area MP raises concerns
Andrew Lawton, the Conservative MP representing Elgin—St. Thomas—London South, called news of the delay disappointing and questioned Volkswagen's commitment to the plant.

“I realize that Volkswagen is saying it's just about pace and not about the overall commitment. But ultimately, it is about the commitment because we were expecting this to be moving forward at a speed that we're just not seeing,” Lawton said.
Lawton also said he wants to know what the federal government is doing to move things along and ensure Volkswagen remains committed.

"We saw $13 billion worth of federal subsidies put forward to this and the promise — the expectation — was 3,000 well-paid local jobs, not to mention the construction jobs. All of this has been thrown into jeopardy right now."
EV market shifts affect Ontario auto plans
The market conditions cited by PowerCo come as automakers across Ontario have adjusted plans for electric vehicle production amid changes in EV demand.

In April 2025, General Motors cited lower-than-expected demand when it announced plans to halt production of the Chevrolet BrightDrop electric delivery van at its CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll. Hundreds of workers were laid off.

items: Hundreds of workers laid off at Ingersoll, Ont., assembly plant as GM halts production
Honda more definitively halting $15B EV plant development in Ontario, according to reports

blocks.text: Honda also delayed plans for a $15-billion EV plant in Alliston in 2025 before ultimately cancelling the project. The company said it would continue to assess the EV market.
At the same time, Canadian EV sales have shown signs of growth.
Statistics Canada data released in June showed the number of new EVs purchased by Canadians had increased by more than 20 per cent compared with the same period a year earlier.
Canadians bought 8,672 new EVs in January, 12,547 in February and 21,574 in March before sales fell to 17,795 in April.

articles.title: Houthi advances in Yemen drive displacement, deepen humanitarian crisis
articles.summary: With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with…

image.caption: The conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has prompted a humanitarian displacement crisis which is compounded by a lack of aid fundingImage: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mohammed Musleh is still in shock. Following the Houthi capture of the port town of Mokha earlier in September, his family had to flee their home without time to pack.

"We have no idea what will happen now," the 46-year-old told DW. His wife, Muna, is also worried, as the family couldn't bring their personal identification documents. "The Houthis told us to leave, basically immediately. We had no time to take anything," she said.

For now, the family and their two young daughters are staying with relatives in Aden, the largest city controlled by the government in southern Yemen. "We tell our kids in the meantime that we hope to return home soon," the couple said.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Council, the leadership body of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said that recent battlefield changes would not alter the government's goal of restoring state authority nationwide.
However, given the latest advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and their territorial gains in Yemen, a return of the Musleh family to their home in Mokha is unlikely for now.

Since late July, the Iran-backed Houthis have expanded their areas of control from the north and center of the country to much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, seizing territory from forces of the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict continues to escalate, along with an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis are currently pushing further into the country toward the strategic Kahboub Mountains. The mountain range is significant as it overlooks areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Staying at home or leaving Taiz?
The mountains are also only around 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Taiz, which is under government control.

blocks.caption: Yemeni government forces and Houthi forces are fight over control of the strategic Kahboub Mountains near Taiz Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Fatima, a mother in Taiz, has been telling her children that the sounds of shelling are from fireworks. "We are scared and we are also worried as gas has already become unavailable and prices are rising. Merchants are no longer coming into Taiz," she told DW, asking not to publish her full name for fear of reprisal.

Rania and her children have also decided to stay at home in Taiz for now. "But we fear that if the Houthis tighten their grip on the city of Taiz, we will find ourselves under siege again," she said. She also doesn't want to use her first name, and vividly recalls the "suffocating blockade of 2015 and 2016, when the entry of food and goods was cut off."

During the previous war between the Iran-aligned Houthi group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, Houthi forces blocked most routes into the government-controlled city of Taiz for almost two years. The restrictions on food, medical supplies and humanitarian aid drove up prices and left people on the brink of famine.
Growing displacement numbers

The World Health Organization said this week that at least 674 people have been killed and 2,998 injured since fighting escalated in August. However, due to the ongoing clashes, the death tally may already be higher, as fighting is ongoing.

The conflict has also prompted mass displacement of more than 132,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration. In recent days, more than 90,000 people found refuge in Aden, Lahj, Abyan and Al Dhale'e governorates and even in Marib, the UN refugee agency's Yemen representative Armen Yedgaryan saidon Tuesday.
He also predicted that intensifying fighting could drive more mass displacement, with growing numbers of people expected to flee to Djibouti, Somalia and other countries, as well as within Yemen.

blocks.caption: According to the IOM, at least 132,000 people have been displaced, and numbers are likely to grow in the coming period of the conflictImage: IOM Djibouti/AFP

blocks.text: "Conditions for displaced people are increasingly severe as they arrive at already congested displacement sites in urgent need of shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection, placing additional pressure on fragile services and infrastructure," he said.

Even before the latest escalation, more than 5.2 million people were internally displaced in Yemen, and the current fighting is deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis in the country, the UN refugee agency added.
Around 22 million people require humanitarian assistance, including internally displaced people and around 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia.

blocks.caption: The UNHCR's Yemen operation is only 18%  funded in 2026, leaving aid organizations without funds to respond to the latest escalationImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Displaced Yemenis help other displaced Yemenis

"I was in the Al-Kud site, a camp for internally displaced people or IDPs, in Abyan governorate on Sunday," Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) in Yemen, told DW. "317 families have arrived since the fighting began, increasing the number of people from 1,460 to 2,629 people," she said.
However, there is no funding to support them. "These IDPs are surviving purely off the generosity of other IDP families."

She told DW that she met Mustapha, a man who was displaced from his hometown of Mawza seven years ago during the previous war in Yemen. He has been living at the IDP site ever since. "He told us he was hosting 22 families in his shelter, all people from his hometown in Mawza. Together, they share a single latrine. When I asked how they were all eating, he said they share one meal together every other day."
Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi meanwhile released a video message in which he told Yemenis in western and southern provinces that they are not the target.
However, Yemeni political analyst Hisham Al-Omeisy said these are empty words.
"The Houthis may measure this offensive in kilometers gained and territory seized, but Yemenis are measuring it in homes abandoned, families torn apart, and lives lost," he told DW.

"There is something profoundly cruel about pursuing military gains while ordinary Yemenis are once again being condemned to fear, hunger and displacement," Al-Omeisy said, adding that "the lines on the map may change, but the blood, grief and shattered lives behind those lines belong to real people. Yemen's civilians cannot continue to be treated as collateral damage in the Houthis' pursuit of power."
Yemen's conflict has displaced tens of thousands of people

articles.title: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says
articles.summary:
Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’

Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months,…

blocks.text: Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.

In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.
The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.

Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.

blocks.caption: The Starlink station in Wola Krobowska, Poland, April 2026. Photograph: Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/Reuters

blocks.text: Gawkowski said it had not been established who ​was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack.
“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.
Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.

Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.

In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.
A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.

“Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.
“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.

The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.
The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.

The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.
There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.

Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.

articles.title: House wraps up budget talks on more agencies
articles.summary: Budget deliberations for fiscal year 2027 of at least seven more agencies have been terminated by the House of Representatives, which is expected to finish such hearings this week before the General…

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 12:00am

Among the agencies whose proposals and period of sponsorship and debate were finished were the Departments of Education (DepEd), Energy (DOE), Transportation (DOTr), Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), Civil Service Commission (CSC) and Commission on Higher Education (CHED).
Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Budget deliberations for fiscal year 2027 of at least seven more agencies have been terminated by the House of Representatives, which is expected to finish such hearings this week before the General Appropriations Bill is approved on second reading early next month.

DepEd’s budget allocation of P975.9 billion for next year under Secretary Sonny Angara got the House’s green light. This represents 13.55 percent of the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget for 2027, according to Rep. Maria Carmen Zamora.

“Once again, this single largest allocation of any department in the government as part of the education sector, is consistent with the mandate of the Constitution. It affirms that this House continues to treat education not as an expense but as the nation’s most important investment,” she said.

The House also terminated debates on DOE’s P5.58-billion allocation, DOTr’s P300.96 billion, DSWD’s P241.2 billion, ERC’s P944 million, independent constitutional CSC’s P4.04-billion budget as well as CHED’s P35.45-billion spending plans for next year.

DOE-ERC budget sponsor Rep. Arnie Fuentebella said the budget, including its attached agencies, is a forward-looking investment in the government’s capacity to ensure energy resilience amidst global uncertainties.
As for DOTr, Reps. Edwin Ongchuan and Reynante Arrogancia said the allocation is not only for infrastructure, but is also about making easier and efficient the travel time of the commuting public.

The P148.63-million 2027 budget of the Career Executive Service Board, which is under the CSC – has been approved, as lawmakers vow to support operations of human resource governance, professionalization, workplace cooperation and administrative justice.

articles.title: PSA: Bangsamoro polls random manual audit 99.9% accurate
articles.summary: The Random Manual Audit conducted for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao parliamentary election yielded an overall accuracy rate of 99.99561 percent, based on the results from all 21…

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 12:00am

Data from the PSA’s summary report on variance and accuracy rate showed that the audit covered 100 percent, or 21 out of 21, of the selected sample clustered precincts under the BARMM parliamentary polls.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Random Manual Audit conducted for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao parliamentary election yielded an overall accuracy rate of 99.99561 percent, based on the results from all 21 BARMM sample clustered precincts audited as of Sept. 23, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.
The audit found no variance between the automated election system (AES) results and the manual count for two of the three positions reviewed.

For the regional parliament political party race, the AES and manual audit both recorded 7,614 votes, resulting in an accuracy rate of 100 percent. Similarly, the AES and manual count for the member of parliament from the sectoral group for settler communities both tallied 12,006 votes, also posting an accuracy rate of 100 percent.

The only discrepancy was recorded in the district representative to the Bangsamoro parliament race, wherein the AES count showed 7,592 votes while the manual audit recorded 7,591 votes, reflecting a variance of one vote and an accuracy rate of 99.98683 percent.
The PSA reported that the overall variance across the audited positions amounted to a single vote.

The random manual audit is conducted to verify the accuracy of election returns generated by the automated election system by comparing them with manually counted ballots from randomly selected precincts.

The 80 winners in the Bangsamoro parliamentary polls will be formally sworn in on Oct. 30 and will later select the head of the regional government. Their mandate will cover a five-year period, with their term scheduled to conclude on June 30, 2031.
The BARMM conducted its inaugural parliamentary elections on Sept. 14, drawing 2,018,478 voters, or an equivalent of 84.34 percent of the region’s 2.393 million registered voters.

Meanwhile, President Marcos congratulated interim BARMM chief minister and Bangsamoro Federalist Party chairman Abdulraof Macacua for what the administration described as the “successful” conduct of the first parliamentary polls on Wednesday at Malacañang. – Alexis Romero

articles.title: Warships from ASEAN, other states sail in West Philippine Sea
articles.summary: Eleven warships from Association of Southeast Asian nations member states and other partner nations sailed the waters of the West Philippine Sea on Wednesday as part of this year’s ASEAN…

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 12:00am

The Philippine Navy’s BRP Jose Rizal led the maritime activity off the coast of Zambales where the international event aimed at sustaining and strengthening regional security cooperation is being held.
Armed Forces of the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines — Eleven warships from Association of Southeast Asian nations member states and other partner nations sailed the waters of the West Philippine Sea (WPS) on Wednesday as part of this year’s ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) Experts’ Working Group on Maritime Security (EWG-MS).
Among the ASEAN warships that participated were the BRP Tarlac also from the Philippine Navy and one military vessel each for from Singapore and Brunei.
For the PLUS countries, India and New Zealand had two warships while Australia, the United States, and Japan sent one military vessel each.
The participating warships showcased various drill formations in the WPS, an activity that China did not participate in despite also being a PLUS-member state.

Reports said when a Chinese warship appeared from a distance apparently to monitor as the ASEAN-PLUS military vessels were sailing towards the exercise area near Panatag (Scarborough) Shoal or Bajo de Masinloc within the Philippine exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
The Philippine Navy communicated with it through radio, welcoming and inviting it to join but received no response.

Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. led the official opening of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS with a Joint Cooperative Activity (JCA) and Future Leaders’ Program (FLP) last Monday in Olongapo City, Zambales.

Co-hosted by the Philippines and Japan, the activity will feature a series of harbor and sea phase activities involving personnel, naval assets, ships and aircraft from eight ADMM-Plus countries from Sept. 20 to 26 with observers from fellow ASEAN member states and dialogue partners.

“We hope that this exercise will be foundational in two things: number one, learning the procedures or getting familiar with the procedures and working together and cooperation; and secondly, develop, at an early stage, networking, trust and cooperation amongst all the participants and your respective defense establishments and navies,” Teodoro said.

“Our collaboration and cooperation not merely in response but in early prepositioning, working together and in detection becomes more critical,” he stressed, adding that an important avenue for effective and efficient response are free open sea lanes of communication.

The Philippine Navy earlier announced that as co-chairs of the EWG on MS for the 2024–2027 cycle, the Philippines and Japan will lead the two engagements which will bring together participating navies from ASEAN Member States and Plus partner countries to advance practical cooperation and strengthen maritime security collaboration.

“The JCA will be conducted in two phases: the Harbor/Shore Phase and the At-Sea Phase. It will feature cooperative activities designed to strengthen practical maritime security cooperation and confidence-building among participating navies,” it said.

articles.title: Monsod criticizes senators over stand on vote threshold
articles.summary: A framer of the 1987 Constitution called out Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Camille Villar, who objected to the proposal to lower the number of votes needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte…

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — A framer of the 1987 Constitution called out Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Camille Villar, who objected to the proposal to lower the number of votes needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.

Former Commission on Elections (Comelec) chairman Christian Monsod, who helped craft the 1987 Constitution, said Cayetano and Villar may be wrong in challenging the majority ruling of the Senate impeachment court.

Cayetano and Villar were among the six senators who boycotted the voting to modify the original threshold of 16 out of the 24 senators set by impeachment trial presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero.
Excluded in the voting on Wednesday were senators who are facing charges, detained, in hiding or on sick leave even if the two-thirds threshold mandated by the 1987 Constitution remained.
Thirteen senators voted in favor of the motion – stating that 14 votes out of 20 senators are needed for a conviction – while one, Escudero, was against. Six others did not participate in the voting.

Cayetano tried but failed to block the proposal, arguing that a vote to favor lowering the number of senators qualified to vote to convict or acquit could violate the provision in the 1987 Constitution that requires “No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate” in an impeachment trial.
When asked about Cayetano’s argument in an interview over radio dzBB yesterday, Monsod said, “He’s wrong.”
Monsod said the Senate can continue the impeachment trial against Duterte amid plans by some senators to boycott the proceedings.
“As long as there is a quorum, the Senate can continue. If they plan on doing that (boycott), it’s for headlines only. They talk like they know everything, especially Cayetano,” he said.

Monsod took a swipe at Villar’s opinion seeking respect for their colleagues currently being detained. She turned emotional in defending her fellow senators whom she said have not been convicted of the charges pressed against them.
“She does not understand the law,” he said.

Monsod noticed the difference in views of Camille and her brother Sen. Mark Villar, who voted to adjust the denominator in the voting threshold. “I don’t know whether they are playing the political game.”

Meanwhile, Monsod maintained the Anti-Plunder Act or Republic Act 7080 explicitly mandates that government officials charged with plunder shall be suspended from exercising the functions of their office.

In addition, the lowering of what he called the “denominator” in the voting threshold should also include a “fugitive from justice because once he is arrested, he is already prevented from exercising his power.”

The 24-member Senate is currently down to 20 with the absence of detained Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, both facing plunder and graft charges, and Sen. Ronald dela Rosa who remains in hiding while facing arrest by the International Criminal Court (ICC).

On Sen. Loren Legarda, who is on a prolonged medical leave, Monsod said: “We will see whether she should be included in the denominator or not… because she participated in the deliberations before she left for that leave.”
In recalling how the 1987 Constitution was created, Monsod said they changed the provision on the voting threshold in an impeachment trial from three-fourths to two-thirds.
He also believed the Supreme Court (SC) “should not interfere in the definition of the powers” of the Senate, which creates its own rules.
Not indicative of guilty verdict
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the 13 votes to lower the conviction threshold was not indicative of the verdict in the Vice President’s impeachment trial.
In a chance interview yesterday, Gatchalian denied that the 13 votes were “reflective” of the verdict, adding that the senators will decide based on the evidence presented during the trial.
“No. Because when it comes to the verdict, it’s about the evidence, it’s about the testimonies, it’s about how the prosecution and defense will present their cases,” said Gatchalian.
“The defense is trying to prove that the allegations have no basis. It’s complicated. We have yet to reach the final voting,” Gatchalian said.
Asked if the outcome of the threshold voting meant that the numbers were enough to convict, Gatchalian said: “Nothing is certain.”
Airtight evidence

House prosecutors vowed to do their best in persuading senators to convict the Vice President based on the airtight evidence they will present moving forward and regardless of the final voting threshold.

“We are not here to count the votes, we are not vote-counters here. We have to present the evidence needed to convict the VP based on the Articles of Impeachment that we have filed,” Rep. Terry Ridon, a member of the House prosecution team, said.
Lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro said it’s still a long way to go before the senators cast their votes. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Delon Porcalla

articles.title: CEO who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax is no longer CEO
articles.summary: The Michigan tourist who recently went viral over a Facebook photo where she and three family members appeared to be wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts has parted ways with her employer.

image.caption: A map labelling Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' is displayed in the White House after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change its name on Aug. 27. (Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada
The Michigan tourist who recently went viral over a Facebook photo where she and three family members appeared to be wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts has parted ways with her employer.
Jane Smith no longer working for Michigan's Family First Credit Union
Jane Smith, the former CEO of Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, is no longer employed there, according to a statement posted on Wednesday to the company's website.

"We are reaching out to inform you that Jane Smith is no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately," reads the statement addressed to "Family First Credit Union Members and Community" and signed by the chair of the board of directors.

The statement continues to say that chief operations officer Jason Acosta is now serving as interim CEO. It does not provide any further information about why Smith is no longer employed, or whether the decision to leave the company was hers.

CBC News has reached out to Smith, Acosta and the credit union's marketing team, and not yet heard back. But the company apologized in a statement posted to the Family First Credit Union Facebook page on Wednesday.
"We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community," the post reads.

"We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first."
'Like our sweatshirts?'

The news comes in the wake of the backlash over a photo Smith had posted to Facebook on her way to Halifax, in which she and three family members pose wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts that Smith later said were AI-generated.
"Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will," said the Sept. 11 photo originally posted by Smith, and later shared by her sister, followed by "lol lol."

items: Michigan tourist who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax says it was AI
'Lake America' change highlights Canada's reliance on U.S. tech

blocks.text: Judging by the reaction online, just weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid the trade war between the two countries, Canadians were not lol-ing.
In a previous interview with ABC12 News in Michigan, Smith said the image was AI-generated and meant to be a joke.
Republican mayor rejects Trump's Lake Ontario name change
"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the news outlet.
"However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun at the fact that, you know, one of the Great Lakes's names were getting changed."
She further explained that the sweatshirts weren't real, saying she ran a photo of them through ChatGPT to add the "Lake America" gear, then posted it to her private Facebook page with an AI label.
When they arrived in Halifax, it was her sister who reposted it publicly, added the comment and didn't include the AI warning, Smith said.
"We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts."

There's been ongoing backlash over Trump's proposed name-change on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will call it Lake Ontario "now and always." In the U.S., three members of Congress have introduced a bill aimed at stopping Trump's renaming, titled "Hands off our Great Lakes."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: At Trump meeting, Xi Jingping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
articles.summary: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade

blocks.text: Xi Jingping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course.

At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could avoid military conflict between the two competing superpowers.

“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialog, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.

“We should coexist in peace,” he said. “China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”

With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.

His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.

Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was US president.

Trump declared that he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”

He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

articles.title: Ukrainians in UK fear cut to funds for Homes for Ukraine hosts could make them homeless
articles.summary:
Scheme set up after Russian invasion in 2022 paid £350 a month to people hosting Ukrainians but this will reduce to £100 next year

Ukrainian refugees fear they could be left homeless after…

blocks.text: Ukrainian refugees fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments to them from £350 to £100.
The scheme was launched after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has provided support for 181,000 of the 234,000 Ukrainians who have since sought sanctuary in the UK.

Now the government has said it will cut the hosting payments and reduce contributions to local authorities which are paid a sum for each arrival to meet costs associated with the delivery of the programme.

A written statement to parliament from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government on 15 September said funding would be reduced from £5,900 to £3,300. The changes will come into effect from 1 January 2027.

Tetiana, a 73-year-old Ukrainian refugee who has been hosted for two years and four months, said she was devastated to read the government’s letter circulated to hosts in the last few days informing them of the changes.

“I feel that this financial change could impact on my host’s ability to host me. If the hosting comes to an end I don’t know where I will go and how I can start again. I can’t work because of my age and because I have mobility problems. I fled from Kharkiv which is close to the Russia frontline so I can’t go back to Ukraine. I don’t know what I will do. I’m at a loss about what my options will be. This change has created a lot of uncertainty for me. I don’t know how I would be able to pay rent if hosting finishes for me.”

Nataliya Rumyanetseva is hosting her mother, the first Ukrainian to arrive in the UK after the war started. She said the changes were likely to have a significant impact. “When refugees arrive here from Ukraine they are shell shocked and need time to adapt and learn the language. If hosting changes to become a more commercial rental arrangement I think that’s cruel.”

One host who lives in Greenwich said he did not know if he would be able to continue hosting because of the drop in payments. “I’ve been a sponsor since May 2022. I was dismayed to learn that thank you payments are reducing to just £100. I lost my job within months of becoming a sponsor and these payments have become an absolute lifeline even though I did not volunteer for this scheme for the money. I genuinely worry about the consequences of this change for Ukrainians in the UK.”
One option the government proposes is that hosts can switch to landlord status and charge refugees rent.

A host who lives in Cardiff and is hosting a Ukrainian who has enrolled on a course of study said: “The situation feels like a cheap shot from the government. We, in good faith, opened our home to someone in need. That person, in good faith, planned for a life in the UK. And the government in what seems like very bad faith, saw an easy way to claw money back from people who aren’t in a position to stop them.”
The government says it has so far provided more than £1.81bn for the scheme.
The Home Office has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Nigeria, US agree to boost mining investment on sidelines of UN General Assembly
articles.summary: On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the US inked a new mining deal. Nigeria is home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

image.caption: Nigeria already exports raw minerals to be refined overseas [FILE: May 2018]Image: Stefan Heunis/AFP

blocks.text: Nigeria and the US have agreed to "deepen" American investment in the West African country's mining sector.
The deal was signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City, Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced on Thursday.
"This is an important step in strengthening Nigeria-US cooperation around our mineral resources, valued at about $700 billion (€796 billion)," Alake said.
"The framework covers geological data and exploration, mineral development and processing, infrastructure, and technical capacity,"he added.
'We want more local processing'
Although known for its vast oil reserves, Nigeria is also home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.
Lithium, in particular, is in high demand globally as an essential component in the batteries are powering the green energy transition.

Alake said the agreement, which was signed on Wednesday, would be used to identify viable projects. He hinted that local jobs could be created by onshoring the refining of minerals, which until now have largely been exported as ore.
Would you drink this? Nigeria’s toxic gold river

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value," Alake said. "We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses."
However, these goals come as Nigeria's mining sector remains mired by safety concerns and environmental concerns.

articles.title: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam
articles.summary:
Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’

Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has…

blocks.text: Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears.
The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary.

“Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile.

He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.”

blocks.caption: A moon bear at the bear sanctuary in Tam Dao national park, Vietnam. Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPA

blocks.text: His concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned in Animals Asia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears.

Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.”

blocks.caption: Rick Wakeman plays piano at bear sanctuary

blocks.text: Wakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.”

Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years.

blocks.caption: Wakeman performing for the rescued bears. Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPA

blocks.text: Of the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.”

He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and to urge the government to get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.”

He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.”

blocks.caption: Bears playing at the sanctuary. Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPA

blocks.text: Wakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.”

Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.”
Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”

articles.title: About 40 calves dead in structure fire at beloved B.C. highway stop D Dutchmen Dairy
articles.summary: D Dutchmen Dairy says an overnight fire has devastated three structures on their farm and killed around 40 of their calves.

image.caption: Bianca Colonna and her husband assess the damage to one of the structures lost in the fire at D Dutchmen Dairy early Thursday morning. (Jacqueline Gelineau/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Updated
D Dutchmen Dairy says an overnight fire has devastated three structures on their farm and killed around 40 of their calves.
Longstanding family business started in 1978
A well-known ice cream shop and family dairy farm in Sicamous, B.C., has lost multiple structures and dozens of animals in an overnight fire.
Bianca Colonna, whose parents run D Dutchmen Dairy, said the fire started at around 1 a.m. PT, burning three buildings including a barn housing about 40 calves, which all died in the flames.
"So in the words of my mom — her babies passed away last night," she said.
The animals were like family, she said, and each one had a name.
"My four-year-old son hugged and kissed every calf."

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior

blocks.text: D Dutchmen Dairy was established in 1978 by Chris and Nellie Dewitt, according to its website.
Located just off the Trans-Canada Highway, the business has become a popular roadside stop over the years, known for its ice cream and farm animals.
The ice cream shop was not burned, but it is closed as the family assesses its next steps.
Colonna said the fire moved quickly in the old wooden barns, but that firefighters were able to save the milking parlour and cow section.
They even rescued one cow who fell down in the havoc of the night.
"They said, 'We're not going to let her burn,'" Colonna said.
The cause of the fire isn't yet known, and the business is asking for people to avoid the farm at this time.
'Not just a business': mayor
Sicamous Mayor Colleen Anderson said the fire was "devastating," calling the business "iconic."
"Not just a business but family friends, community supporters. Just a big part of Sicamous," she said.
Laurie Kubos of Askew's Food, which sells milk from the farm, said she has many memories of stopping at the dairy farm as a child growing up in neighbouring Revelstoke.
"It was a big deal," she said.
Both said the entire community was rallying around the family-owned business, which has been a major support of charities and organizations over the years.
A community fixture for nearly 50 years

Owner Jake Dewitt, the son of the business's founders, said in an interview with CBC News in 2021 that 180,000 customers stopped at D Dutchmen each year. At peak times, the business employed 25 workers, according to Dewitt.

He attributed the stop's popularity to its "beautiful yard and store," its quality products and its ice cream — which he said is particularly well-known in Alberta, where most of their customers come from.
Reacting to news of the fire Thursday, Jennifer Tirschman, executive director of the Sicamous and District Chamber of Commerce, emphasized what an important role D Dutchmen has played in the area.
"They're part of the very fabric of the soul of this community," she said.
She noted that many people have memories of going to D Dutchmen over the years.
"We're all very saddened to hear about the devastating fire that has occurred, and the community is here to support them in any way we can."
With files from Lauren Vanderdeen, Jacqueline Gelineau, Justin McElroy and Andrew Kurjata

articles.title: Palestinian president, denied visa to speak at UN, addresses leaders in pre-recorded video
articles.summary: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the UN General Assembly on Thursday, delivering pre-recorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied him and other top…

image.caption: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly via pre-recorded video in New York City on Thursday. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the UN General Assembly on Thursday, delivering pre-recorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied him and other top Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.
Israel's Netanyahu will speak in person on Thursday afternoon

"The Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times in its history," Abbas said, citing long-term military occupation in the West Bank and the war in Gaza. Israel, he said, "has targeted all of the basic necessities of life."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was scheduled to speak in person early in the afternoon. As Abbas spoke, the Israeli delegations' seats in the General Assembly hall sat vacant.
In his speech, Abbas once again implored the international community to take more vigorous action and speak out more loudly against Israel.

"How much longer will some states continue to remain silent against Israel or supply it with the weapons it uses against our people? The world has witnessed the tremendous cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank," Abbas said. "What is the international community waiting for in order to protect the Palestinian people?"

Though negotiations have not taken place for years, Abbas urged the international community to push for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Netanyahu has said no Palestinian state will be established while he is Israel's leader and has argued that the Palestinian Authority is not a partner for peace.
Israel set to oust Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. signs off, defence minister says

The international community has backed U.S. President Donald Trump's plan for a group of apolitical administrators to govern Gaza under the Board of Peace. But Abbas said the territory could not remain politically separate from the West Bank and East Jerusalem for the long term.
He said the Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem and the West Bank needed to be governed by "one state, one government, one law and one legitimate entity authorized to bear arms."
Abbas recorded the video on Wednesday.

Since 2005, the now-90-year-old Abbas has led the Palestinian Authority, which is the internationally recognized representative of the Palestinian people. But his support among Palestinians has withered during years of corruption and the sometimes-violent advance of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Under Abbas, Palestine has been recognized as a country by a majority of UN member states. But on the ground in the West Bank, the mostly symbolic moves have not affected Israel's decades-long military occupation. Throughout the war in Gaza, Abbas and the authority have been largely sidelined from negotiations over its future in favour of a transition process shepherded by the U.S.-backed Board of Peace.

items: Trump's 'Board of Peace' earmarks $2.45B US in blueprint to rebuild war-torn Gaza
Canada pledges $100M for Palestine at United Nations General Assembly

blocks.text: The Palestinian Authority was created under a series of peace agreements with Israel in the 1990s and administers semi-autonomous areas of the West Bank, while relying heavily on foreign aid.

It was ousted from Gaza after Hamas won parliamentary elections in 2006 and violently seized control. Abbas was elected to what was supposed to be a four-year term in 2005. The authority has not held presidential or legislative elections since 2006.

Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the 1967 war, and the Palestinians want both as part of their future state. The Palestinians and much of the international community view the settlements as illegal and as an obstacle to creating a viable, contiguous Palestinian state.

articles.title: White House 'repeatedly violated' court order to restore press access, say media outlets
articles.summary: Employees from CNN, Politico and MS Now reported being denied entry, with some having passes confiscated.

blocks.text: Three US media outlets have requested an emergency court hearing, accusing the White House of having "repeatedly violated" a judge's order to restore their access in a stand-off with President Donald Trump.
Employees from CNN, Politico and MS Now reported being denied entry on Thursday morning, with some having their credentials confiscated, while others were granted access.
Judge Timothy Kelly ruled in the early hours of Thursday that Trump's ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".
Trump initially said he banned the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security.
It was unclear whether the refusal to admit some reporters on Thursday morning was because of an administrative lag as the White House potentially worked to comply with the judge's order.
The standoff was expected to impact TV coverage as Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday morning ahead of a state dinner.
CNN said some of their journalists had been denied entry, including senior White House reporter Betsy Klein. But a producer was allowed to enter, the outlet reported.
Politico said one of its reporters was denied access to the White House and had his press credentials confiscated.
MS NOW reported that its White House reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were barred and had their passes taken, but another MS NOW producer was allowed in.
The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.

articles.title: 105-year-old investigated for crimes at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
articles.summary: The suspect is alleged to have been an accessory to murder at the Stalag 326 camp, where tens of thousands of Soviet PoWs died.

blocks.text: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.
The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.
A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.
That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.

No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.

More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.
But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.

One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region.
Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.
Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

articles.title: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
articles.summary: News that an automated AI agent hacked a government IT system raises big questions about regulating the tech.
articles.byline: Henry Moore, Liv McMahon and Chris Vallance

blocks.text: The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight.

On 18 June one of OpenAI's agents went rogue during a test exercise - the company has said it was supposed to "look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation".
In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.

OpenAI said it only realised the breach had happened at all in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity", and the company sent an email to a generic Australian government inbox some weeks later.
That email seems to have gone unnoticed for five days before it was escalated to Australia's cyber-security experts on 10 September.
The prime minister described the breach as "obviously unacceptable" and said OpenAI took "way too long" to inform Australian officials.
Analysts have also raised concerns over OpenAI's almost three-month delay in noticing and reporting the breach via email.
"The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cyber-security firm TrustDecision told the BBC.
Australia has said this incident is the first of its kind, and experts agree it might be.
As far as we know, hacks carried out by AI agents are still quite rare occurrences - but then again, it is largely up to companies themselves to disclose them.
Hacks like this have happened before. In July, OpenAI agents went rogue during a test and infiltrated tech start-up Hugging Face's internal systems.
The AI agents decided that ignoring the limits on what should be done to achieve their goal was the best course of action.
This is what the industry calls "misalignment" - broadly defined as when AI machines do not act in humanity's best interests, such as by bending the rules.
It is a problem that is fundamental to making AI safe, and it is proving challenging.

To put it simply, the type of AI models at play here - known as large language models - are designed to predict the likeliest output to a given input, rather than consider the consequences of that output as a human would.
Companies attempt to prevent negative consequences by placing "guardrails" on the AI but, as the Australian government found out, that is not always enough.

Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC this sort of hack would likely "grow in severity and in frequency", adding: "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."

Niusha Shafiabady, professor of computational intelligence at the Australian Catholic University, said this incident had shown the need to "judge autonomous AI by its behaviour under pressure, not by the promises in a product launch".
"The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision," she said.
"Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures."
The explosive rise of AI has left governments scrambling to put protective measures in place, with some calling for companies to be forced to build ways to disable their own tech into its systems.
One idea backed by some AI firms and lawmakers is a "kill switch" - a way to simply to turn the tech off in a crisis.
OpenAI is reportedly, external already working to build automated tools which can shut down its systems if needed.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, former deputy prime minister and Facebook executive Sir Nick Clegg said the kill switch remains an unproven idea.
"There isn't a room with a little fuse box [where] you just pull out the fuse and everything winds down," he said, with AI tools underpinned by global infrastructure.
Cyber-security experts said the systems protecting Australia's Medicare were just not strong enough, and a skilled human hacker could have got around them.

But other experts say that is not the point - and that this was the latest case of AI agents ignoring laws around how to safely access online information, and perhaps the most serious yet given the information was under government control.

As warnings mount about the potentially devastating impact of AI, many in the industry and in governments around the world are openly wondering about what national and international regulations might be needed to keep it in check.
Meanwhile some scientists, experts and workers have dismissed the bleak projections as vague, hypothetical, or an effort by large AI developers to ensure their dominance.

As it stands, AI companies largely regulate themselves - but this week, 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns.

However, the US and China, two nations at the forefront of AI development, have so far resisted calls for greater regulation, raising questions over whether this hack will be the first of many, or the wake up call many experts want it to be.
"The immediate harm here appears limited, but the governance lesson is not," says Dr Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney.

"As AI agents become more capable and autonomous, those capabilities need to be matched by proportionate containment, real-time monitoring, clear accountability, independent oversight, and much faster incident reporting."
Additional reporting by Tom Gerken and Joe Tidy
