articles.title: Extremist parties are thriving ― and that scares people
articles.summary: Far-right and far-left parties are celebrating success after success, leaving moderate politicians in the dust and worrying many Germans. Political psychology helps us understand what's behind…

image.caption: The far-right AfD, seen here celebrating their win in Saxony-Anhalt, has won over many voters. For many others, however, their rise is cause for concern.Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 6, Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt held elections for its state parliament. The big winner: The right-wing AfD (Alternative for Germany) party, which garnered 43.8% of the votes; more than ever before.
It's still unclear who will govern the state because the AfD does not have an absolute majority.
But it was a landslide win for the AfD, whose Saxony-Anhalt branch is classified as right-wing extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, and that worries many Germans.

The day after the election, Chancellor Friedrich Merz from the conservative CDU said he was "deeply shocked" by the election results. "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany."
Merz's CDU lost more than half its share of the ballot compared to the last state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The CDU dropped from 37.1% in 2021 to 17.2% in 2026.
Two weeks later, at state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 20, the CDU didn't even make the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
It was the first time ever for the CDU; they got only 4.9% of the vote in the northeastern state. The strongest party was once again the AfD with 38.2%.

That same day, in the city state of Berlin, the socialist Left Party won the election and will likely govern Germany's capital. In Berlin, the CDU was the second-strongest party and the AfD came in third.
Why Germany's political center is losing ground
Germans worried about rise of far-right, far-left parties
These state elections show that parties on the extreme ends of the political spectrum are growing stronger in Germany.

The country has experience with both extreme right- and left-wing governments: the Nazis that led Germany into World War II and the Socialist Unity Party (SED) that ruled then-East Germany from 1949 until 1989.
A return to extreme politics is a scary proposition for some people.

In a representative monthly survey called "What worries the world?", the polling institute Ipsos found that almost one-fifth of Germans (18%) said they were worried by growing extremism in the country when they asked about 1,000 people between the ages of 16 and 74 years in March and April 2026.
Generally, people in Germany are concerned about where their country is going. In the Ipsos survey, 82% said they saw Germany as moving in the wrong direction.
How to measure a country's mood
Asking people about their fears or worries is just one way to take the nation's temperature.
But there are many ways to measure politically relevant emotions in the population.

Kerstin Pahl, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, told DW that possibilities include quantitative and qualitative surveys, as well as analyzing online discourse and the content people share on social media. It's also possible to read a nation's sentiment by observing real-life displays of emotions, like public protests and demonstrations.
For researchers like Pahl, it's also interesting to see how political issues can come to symbolize much more than their material or factual meaning.
"People may see their region's ailing infrastructure not just as proof of a lack of investment, but also as a sign that they have been forgotten [by their leaders]," said Pahl.
Affective polarization: Political opponents become the enemy
Extremist parties winning a higher percentage of the votes is what we see on the surface. Below that lie two kinds of societal polarization: Affective and ideological polarization.

"Affective polarization is a growing hatred for the political opponent. Most studies investigated this in the context of the US between supporters of the Democrat and the Republican Party," Eva Walther, head of the social psychology department at the University of Trier in western Germany, told DW. "When this happens on the party level, it's a problem."
MAGA moves to meddle in European politics
Politicians of different parties often have to work together and reach compromises. They don't need to like each other, but they should treat each other with respect, Walther said.
"When this respectful attitude starts crumbling, it's a problem for democracy," she added.
Ideological polarization: Which problem is the most pressing?
The other phenomenon, ideological polarization, is when society is split into distinct groups based on what issues people view as the most pressing problem for them.
For example, many people to the right of the political center in Germany see migration as the biggest problem, while many people to the left of the political center say it's the climate crisis.
When different crisis situations occur at the same time, such as migration and climate change, researchers refer to a "polycrisis."
Polycrises intensify ideological polarization, making it even harder for societies to find a common way forward.
"At the moment, we have the climate crisis overlapping with an affordable energy crisis, more of an economic problem," Walther said.

In the eyes of those for whom the climate crisis is the most urgent issue, fossil fuels should be abandoned as soon as possible. But for those most concerned with affordable energy, relying only on renewable energy sources would needlessly raise prices.

blocks.caption: What's the more urgent problem: climate change or the affordable energy crisis? The answer depends on where you fall on the political spectrumImage: Eckhard Stengel/imago images

blocks.text: People want politicians to take their problems seriously
The belief that a politician is competent and willing to tackle major challenges, to act, is a big factor in how much people trust democracy.
But that's also what makes overlapping crises so hard to manage: No matter which problems politicians attempt to solve first, one part of the population will be disappointed.
"Polycrises make it difficult for politicians to act, which means that people have less trust that politicians can solve the problems important to them," Walther said.
Right-wing extremist parties, however, aim to "satisfy people by giving them simplified answers to complex problems," added Walther.
This leads people to believe that extremist politicians can solve their problems ― which in turn leads to growing polarization.
But politicians from democratic parties can learn from clinical research to tackle this dilemma, according to Walther.
"When a person is in pain and goes to see a doctor, it's important that the doctor recognizes the patient's pain," she said.
Even if the doctor can't instantly solve the issue and make the pain go away, showing that they take the issue and the patient seriously is crucial. And the same goes for politicians.

"They need to make people's needs the first priority in their daily work," Walther said. "People want to be seen, so it's important for politicians to make it clear that they see and understand their problems."
Whether it's a doctor failing a patient or politicians failing the electorate, patient and electorate are likely to scream — and that's a signal we can all read.

articles.title: How renewed fighting in Tigray could spread across the Horn of Africa
articles.summary: Fighting has resumed in Ethiopia's Tigray region. In an interview with DW, Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.

image.caption: Tigrayan forces seized three local airports and launched attacks in Ethiopia's Afar and Amhara regions with allies there this weekImage: AFP

blocks.text: Fighting has erupted again in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive on September 23, with fighting also reported in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara.

The escalation threatens the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war between Ethiopia's federal government in Addis Ababa and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
But the central question is bigger than the return of war to Tigray: could the conflict connect with the wars and rivalries already destabilizing the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?
Martin Plaut, British journalist and Horn of Africa expert, argues that the conflict could spill beyond Ethiopia's borders.

"If a conflict were to spill over, it is quite possible that a conflict involving Eritrea and Ethiopia could then involve Sudanese forces as well, which could drag the whole region into a war," he told DW in an exclusive interview.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again

Jalale Getachew Birru, a senior analyst for East Africa at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also stresses that the conflict cannot be viewed in isolation. ACLED is an independent conflict-monitoring and research organization that collects and analyses data on political violence and armed conflict around the world.
“The Ethiopia[n] case is not [an] isolated case for the Horn of Africa. It involves the neighboring countries as well, and it’s being displayed across the Horn of Africa countries," Birru told DW.

Her assessment points to a broader regional dynamic: Ethiopia's conflict is unfolding alongside shifting alliances and competing interests in neighboring Sudan and Somalia. ACLED's current analysis likewise places the renewed Tigray conflict within a wider pattern of instability across the Horn of Africa.
The risk is not based on a single regional alliance. It comes from the fact that several conflicts are already geographically and politically connected, Birru noted.
African Union urges restraint
The African Union (AU) also expressed deep concern about the possibility of further destabilization.
In a statement on September 23, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf warned that new political and military alliances risk reversing the progress made since 2020.

The AU called for an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions, renewed direct talks under the Pretoria agreement and restraint by Ethiopia's neighbors. It also tasked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's High Representative for the Horn of Africa, with supporting diplomatic efforts.
The AU's intervention reflects concerns that the crisis could have wider regional implications, including the possibility that it could interact with conflicts beyond Ethiopia's borders.
Old enemies, new alliances

The TPLF recently joined six other Ethiopian armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Among them is the Amhara Fano movement, which fought against the TPLF during the previous war.

The alliance is not a unified military force. Its members have different political objectives and territorial interests. But its formation could leave the Ethiopian government facing several fronts at once.

The fighting in Afar, a northeastern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Djibouti, is particularly significant. The region contains the main transport corridor linking landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti, through which much of Ethiopia's international trade passes. Sustained fighting there could therefore threaten a vital economic lifeline.
And beyond Afar lies Eritrea.
Eritrea's potential role

During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Since then, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, Eritrea's capital, have deteriorated. Ethiopia's ambitions for access to the Red Sea have added to Eritrea's security concerns.
"The war could certainly escalate, and Eritrea could become involved," Plaut said.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups opposed to the government, while Asmara has denied such allegations. The extent of any direct Eritrean involvement remains difficult to establish independently.
Sudan: where conflicts could collide

Sudan has been at war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has drawn in regional powers and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.
Plaut argues that Ethiopia and Eritrea are already indirectly involved on opposing sides.

"The Ethiopians are on the side of the RSF and Hemedti," he said, referring to its commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. "There has been strong evidence that there is a base in western Ethiopia which is supplying and training RSF fighters," Plaut added. DW has not independently verified that claim.
Explainer: How did Ethiopia's Tigray war start?
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has faced allegations of supporting the RSF, which it denies. Plaut identifies Eritrea, Egypt and Saudi Arabia as supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces.
"So both Eritrea and Ethiopia are already playing a role, indirectly, in the war," he said.

If Ethiopia and Eritrea were to enter direct hostilities, Sudan's rival forces could have incentives to exploit the new situation, Plaut noted. Fighting could put additional pressure on Sudan's eastern frontier and alter supply routes and military calculations.

Plaut sees the danger of a chain reaction: "Because you have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces, this could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."
"So the whole thing becomes a generalized conflict in the region," he said.
The Red Sea connection
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

Eritrea and Djibouti lie on its western side, Yemen on the eastern side. The war in Yemen has already shown how insecurity around the Red Sea can disrupt international shipping and draw in outside powers.

Eritrea's location and its control of the port of Assab give it strategic importance far beyond Tigray. Any major deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations could therefore affect the wider security architecture of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also developed extensive political, economic and security interests across the Horn of Africa. Their interests overlap in some areas but diverge in others, particularly over Sudan.
The danger is escalation, not inevitability

None of this means that a regional war is inevitable. There is no evidence of a single military alliance stretching from Tigray to the Gulf. Ethiopia's armed groups have competing interests, Eritrea may avoid direct intervention, and Sudan's warring parties have their own priorities.
But conflicts do not need a common command structure to become interconnected.
Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds

The Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. The Pretoria agreement stopped the large-scale fighting, but many of the political and territorial disputes underlying the conflict remained unresolved.
Today, Tigray is again at war while Ethiopia faces several armed movements, Eritrea is a potential military actor, and Sudan is already engulfed in civil war.
Plaut warns that the humanitarian consequences could again be severe.
"There's certainly a danger of this becoming an extremely bloody conflict," he told DW. "After all, six hundred thousand people died in the last one in Tigray."
But he does not predict that the previous death toll will necessarily be exceeded. "Let's hope that it doesn't go in that direction," he said.

articles.title: Fears of return to war as Tigray rebels launch offensive against Ethiopian army
articles.summary:
Fighting escalates after TPLF forms new rebel coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government

There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by rebels…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by rebels from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara , and the formation of a new rebel coalition aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

Fighting from 2020 to 2022 between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) killed about 600,000 people. Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse (AFP) there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.
TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital, Addis Ababa.

The federal army said it had killed 272 TPLF soldiers as they launched attacks in multiple parts of North Wollo Zone in Amhara. The figure has not been independently verified, and no casualties were given for the federal army or civilians.

Analysts say TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that’s now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.
TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.
The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.
On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks.
An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria Agreement.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: 'I'm sorry, I drank it': Mother recalls daughter's last words at Kenneth Law's sentencing hearing

image.caption: Kim Prosser, mother of Ashtyn Prosser-Blake, holds a picture of her son outside the courthouse in Newmarket, Ont., on Thursday. Ashtyn was 19 years old when he died in 2023. (EVAN MITSUI/CBC)

blocks.text: 2 days of powerful, harrowing statements from family and friends
For two days, a courtroom in Newmarket, Ont., heard more than 70 impact statements from loved ones of victims of poison seller Kenneth Law.
Family members and friends came to court to express their grief in person or provided statements to the Crown to be read out. Others, mostly those from the U.K., provided a video recording.
Court also heard from people who had taken one of Law's products but survived.
The victims remembered in the statements ranged in age, but many were just teenagers or young adults, with the youngest aged 14.
The statements touched on similar themes, including how much families had cherished their loved ones and how their lives had been devastated by their deaths.
Family members who appeared in person often broke down in tears, with some saying their lives were now split between the time before the death of their loved one, and after.
On Thursday, court heard from one mother who described how her 21-year-old daughter lay dying in her arms after ingesting sodium nitrite from a package she received from Law.
"The only words she repeatedly said were, 'I'm sorry, I drank it.' Those words will remain with me for the rest of my life," the mother said.

Another mother said her 11-year-old daughter still texts her deceased father, while another described how the toxicity of her daughter’s body forced emergency officials to wear hazmat suits in order to move her.
Family members also directed words at Law, saying they were unable to comprehend how he could deliver deadly substances to vulnerable people, and describing his actions as "despicable."
Over the two days, Law sat in the prisoner's box, staring ahead, not appearing to show any reaction or emotion to the dozens of victim impact statements that were heard.
Crown and defence are now scheduled to return to court on Nov. 27 for sentencing submissions.

articles.title: Donald Trump hosts Xi Jinping for state dinner with tech titans.
articles.summary: Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with the two having toasted each other at a lavish state dinner after their summit meeting. America's top tech bosses were also…

image.caption: Donald and Melania Trump host Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng LiyuanImage: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

blocks.text: September 25, 2026
What you need to know about Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington so far

blocks.caption: Trump hosted Xi at a lavish state dinner in the White House that was also attended by the CEOs of US tech firmsImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump on Thursday rolled out the red carpet for China's Xi Jinping on the Chinese president's first state visit to Washington in over a decade.

Ahead of the meeting, Xi said the US and China "should be partners rather than rivals," while Trump hailed his "truly great friendship" with the Chinese president. However, no breakthrough was expected in the trade tensions between the world's two largest economies.
The talks centered on the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to a statement by Beijing. The US has not provided details about the meeting.
After the talks, Xi attended a lavish state dinner with Trump and US tech executives, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Tesla's Elon Musk.
Trump described the event as the "hottest ticket in town" and said the "entire tech world" and "entire banking world and a lot more" would attend.
On Friday, Xi is scheduled to visit the National Archives, where the US Declaration of Independence, Constitution and Bill of Rights are held.

articles.title: EU to condemn war in Ukraine at G20 even if Putin attends
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to the G20 summit in Miami by the United States. Multiple members of the group have called for Moscow's exclusion over its invasion of Ukraine.

image.caption: Putin has been formally invited to the G20 summit in Miami in mid-December [FILE: September 2025]Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union said on Thursday that it would continue to condemn Russia's war in Ukraine at the G20 summit in Miami scheduled for December.

It said that it would do this regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin attends after being invited by this year's hosting country, the United States. The Kremlin has said that Putin would "consider" Washington's invitation.
The Russian leader did not attend the G20 summit in 2023 in New Delhi, India and the 2022 summit on the Indonesian island of Bali despite being formally invited by the hosting countries.
Also on Thursday, eight people were killed in a wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.
What did the EU say about Putin's possible attendance at the G20 summit?
The EU said it would continue calling for an end to the war in Ukraine.
"Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion [of Ukraine] and to call for it to end," EU spokesman Olof Gill said.
"What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue, irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting."
Gill said that Russia remained a member of the G20 group and that it had "the right to participate" in its meetings.
Both the European Union itself and three of its individual member states — France, Germany, and Italy — are members of the G20 group.

blocks.caption: Putin and Trump last met in person in August 2025 in Alaska, which was the Russian leader's first visit to a Western country since Moscow launched its invasion of UkraineImage: Jeenah Moon/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is the US position on Putin's attendance at the G20?

Ukraine's allies — including G20 members France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and Canada — have called for Russia's exclusion from the group since Moscow launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington was inviting Putin after his meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
"We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with [US President Donald Trump], but with other world leaders," Rubio said on Wednesday. "We hope that's an invitation he'll accept."

Putin's last visit to the United States was to attend a summit meeting with Trump in Anchorage, Alaska in August 15, 2025, also marking his first visit to a Western country since the start of the war in Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Russian air strikes hit Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine on Thursday, according to Ukrainian authoritiesImage: Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP

blocks.text: Russian strikes kill 8 in Kharkiv, Kyiv
At least six agricultural workers were killed and 12 others were wounded in a strike on the northeastern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.
The regional prosecutor's office published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse following the attack.
Ukrainian authorities said that the warehouse had been hit by a small-sized cruise missile of the "Banderol" type.
Meanwhile, at least two people were killed across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, Prime Minsiter Serhiy Koretsky said.
Strikes were also recorded in and around the southwestern port city of Odesa, with officials reporting they sparked a fire at a shopping mall.

articles.title: Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help
articles.summary:
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime

The family of 21-year-old twins who have been

blocks.text: The family of 21-year-old twins who have been sentenced to death and decades in jail for protesting against the Iranian regime have appealed to the United Nations for help for the young women.
A formal “submission of information” relating to the case of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi has been submitted by British human right lawyers on their family’s behalf.
The move could lead to the UN’s human rights council opening talks with the Iranian regime about resolving the case if it is found to involve human rights violations.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, told the UN’s general assembly in New York this week that the country was “ready for dialogue and diplomacy”.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps eight months ago after they joined nationwide protests against the regime.
They were tried over charges that included moharebeh (waging war against God) for taking to the streets of Isfahan, in central Iran, on 8 and 9 January.
At the end of August, Taraneh, along with nine others, was sentenced to death. Romina received a 25-year prison sentence.
The girls’ family are seeking to appeal against the sentences but human rights groups have raised concerns that Taraneh’s execution could be fast-tracked.

The women are being held in Dowlatabad prison in Isfahan, where the twins’ family claim that Taraneh was threatened with being forced to watch the rape of her sister if she failed to sign a confession to her alleged crimes.
The sisters have been held in isolation but are said to have been able to hear each other’s screams as torture was inflicted upon them.
Neither of the women have been seen by their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, or other members of the family since their sentencing.

After the Guardian highlighted the case, the women’s cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, an IT engineer who lives in the US state of Utah, said Taraneh was told that she would only be allowed to eat leftovers of other prisoners’ meals as punishment.
Nourmohammadi, 43, said he had turned to the UN out of desperation.
after newsletter promotion
Taraneh is said to be in need of surgery due to injuries inflicted during interrogation.

Nourmohammadi said: “Turning to the United Nations is not something I ever wanted to have to do. I am simply asking the international community to help ensure that Taraneh and Romina receive the basic rights that every human being is entitled to: a fair process, protection from torture and abuse, access to medical care and legal counsel, and the right to have their cases genuinely reviewed.

“Taraneh is facing the death penalty, and Romina is facing decades in prison. They are young women who should be thinking about their futures, not whether one sister will be executed and the other will spend the best years of her life behind bars.
“They are my family and I will continue to use every peaceful and legal avenue available. I ask the United Nations to stand with them before it is too late – especially for Taraneh.”
A submission to the UN through its “special procedures” can lead to a formal request by the international organisation to a member state for an explanation and action.

Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 16 women. Hundreds of protesters have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.

articles.title: AI systems shifted their answers toward both left- and right-leaning users in a study. Could sycophantic chatbots deepen political divides?
articles.summary: A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.

image.caption: Researchers looked at an array of models and found they shifted their political answers to mirror the views of a hypothetical userImage: Philip Dulian/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A recent wave of headline-grabbing warnings from AI luminaries has fueled fears the technology could escape human control and wipe out humanity. But before artificial intelligence (AI) turns on humanity, it could contribute to humans turning on one another.

Researchers at Brazil's State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) found that popular chatbots shifted their answers when prompted with hypothetical users' political views. The scientists warn that users could mistake this tailored agreement for an independent assessment, potentially deepening polarization.
How chatbots become 'ideological chameleons'
Each was tested under three conditions: with no information about the user's politics, with a prompt describing a left-leaning user and with one describing a right-leaning user.

When no information about the user's ideology was given, 20 of the 21 models produced answers that fell on the left of the researchers' political scale, although several were close to the center. Grok 4.1 was the only model that fell on the right.
Why do people tell ChatGPT their problems?
When information was provided, every model shifted its answers toward the political orientation described in the prompt.

"The most striking finding was how widespread this behavior was," study co-author Zanoni Dias, a UNICAMP computer scientist, told DW. "All 21 models we evaluated shifted their expressed positions toward the user's stated political orientation, although the magnitude varied substantially."
The researchers described the models as "ideological chameleons" and developed a "chameleon index" measuring how far each shifted.
Meta's Llama 3.1 8B and DeepSeek V3.2 changed their responses least. Google's Gemma 3 27B and OpenAI's GPT-5 Nano showed some of the largest shifts.
When personalization becomes political flattery
Adapting an answer to its audience is not inherently problematic. A chatbot might change its vocabulary, examples or level of detail depending on the user.
But the models changed more than their language or tone: Their political positions shifted.
"The key distinction is between adapting how an answer is communicated and changing the substantive judgment being expressed," Dias said.
Can we trust whenever AI gives us an answer?
"We did not instruct the models to agree with the user or to answer as a partisan representative. Nevertheless, their judgments shifted toward the user's side."
The researchers interpret this as political sycophancy: AI systems reflecting what users appear to want to hear.
A possible explanation is that chatbots are trained to favor answers human evaluators rate highly. If agreeable answers get better ratings, models may learn to echo users' views.
How AI could create a private echo chamber

Social media can reinforce beliefs by repeatedly recommending algorithmic content, but a chatbot could go even further. It could create a more personalized echo chamber, generating arguments for a particular user, answering their objections and refining its case throughout the conversation.
Yet users may mistake these tailored responses for impartial analysis, unaware that what a chatbot knows about them may shape its responses.
"The concern is that the same system could validate opposing political positions for different users, with each person interpreting that validation as an independent assessment," Dias said.
Research by Stanford University behavioral scientist Zakary Tormala suggests people may be particularly receptive to arguments they believe came from AI.

"People tend to see AI as more informative, more objective, less biased and less interested in persuading them than another person would be," Tormala told DW. "This can lower people's defenses and make them more receptive to hearing out what AI has to say."
That trust could make political flattery more influential.
How AI simulates human connection

"Hearing their own views validated by others is well known to increase people's certainty about their beliefs," Tormala said. "Once people become more certain, they do tend to become more resistant to persuasion."
Whether AI validation has the same effect remains unproven, he added, but it is plausible.
Could validation deepen polarization?
The UNICAMP study did not test whether political mirroring could really change users' beliefs or behavior. It measured only changes in the models' responses.

"Our study establishes a change in model responses under controlled conditions," Dias said. "It does not establish that users became more polarized, radicalized or likely to engage in conflict. Those are distinct outcomes, and the steps connecting them cannot be assumed."

Petter Tornberg, a University of Amsterdam researcher who studies AI and political polarization, agreed that the study cannot show an effect on users. He also questioned whether models would give the same answers outside the test setting.
He cautioned against assuming that chatbots would necessarily reinforce users’ views. In some conversations, they might help people reconsider them.
Tornberg said a private conversation with a chatbot differs from a public argument on social media.

"They can often provide fairly rational and evidence-based explanations without the social identity dynamics of public political debate," he told DW. "So it is at least possible that in some contexts these systems could be depolarizing rather than polarizing."
Can an AI chatbot really become my friend?
Whether AI narrows or deepens divisions may therefore depend on whether it challenges users or simply tells them what they want to hear.
How political mirroring could be reduced
Dias said developers should test their models with users of different political views to see whether they assess evidence consistently.
They could train models to disagree respectfully, acknowledge uncertainty, correct unsupported claims and present competing views fairly.
That would not mean forcing every answer toward the political center.

"The broader design goal should be to help people examine their beliefs," Dias said, "making evidence, uncertainty and competing considerations visible, while allowing room for legitimate political disagreement."

articles.title: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks in first comment on fresh fighting
articles.summary: The military says its soldiers inflicted casualties as fears grow of a resumption of a full-blown civil war.

blocks.text: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday.
The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons.
The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume.
On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police.
The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.

A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray.
"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying.
The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.
That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the governemnt.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere.
"Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash.

"People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash."
Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash".
With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC.

articles.title: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO for his country but rejects calls to increase defense spending
articles.summary: The US and NATO want Czechia to spend more on defense. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis says Prague cannot afford faster increases, despite growing warnings about the threat from Russia.

image.caption: Babis announced on Monday that the Czech state will run a deficit of 386 billion crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion) next yearImage: Michaela Rihova/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO, demanded in Prague last week. "We ⁠expect our allies to step up," he said.

The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising.

Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania, has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington.

While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases.

blocks.caption: US Ambassador to NATO Matthew G. Whitaker (pictured here in Iowa earlier this month) has made the US position clear to Prague: Czechia 'must remain committed to increasing defense spending'Image: Tim Evans/REUTERS

blocks.text: That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row.
Warnings of a growing threat
Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question.
A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood.
Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies.
Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack.

Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB).
Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow.
The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing.
However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action.
Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year.
Prague's priorities
Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22.
The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion).
While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities.

The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

"The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system."
That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees.
"None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes.
Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
'We don't want World War III'
The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine.

Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace.
"We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict.
It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media.

The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views.

Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget.

"A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions."
Strategic understanding
The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel.

Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?"
However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target.

"Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role.

articles.title: 'Pope fever' takes hold as Pope Leo visits France
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV is expected to draw large crowds during his visit to France. As part of his trip to Europe, he's also set to address the continent's future and some of the challenges ahead.

image.caption: Saint-Etienne Cathedral draped with a welcome banner for Pope Leo XIVImage: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP

blocks.text: France is gripped by "Pope fever." Since the 1905 French law on separating church and state, the country has embraced secular traditions. But over the next few days, the streets will tell a different story.

From Friday, Pope Leo XIVwill spend four days in France, visiting the capital Paris, Lourdes and Metz. All his public events have been sold out for weeks. Organizers expect around one million people to fill the streets of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air mass at the Place de la Concorde.

"The pope is popular among both believers and nonbelievers," political scientist Olivier Roy told DW. He added that Leo XIV's conflict with US President Donald Trump in particular had lent him "a moral standing that extends far beyond the Catholic Church."
Paris gears up for influx

And massive crowds are expected. Some 600,000 people who were able to get tickets will fill the entire Champs-Elysees, going right up to the Arc de Triomphe. Many more are expected to show up without tickets. Authorities have announced that a number of metro stations will be closed. Across the city, churches have been draped with large portraits of the pope and Vatican flags. Security forces are gearing up for a major challenge.

With France's presidential elections just over six months away, the visit comes at a delicate time. The left, Roy said, "appreciates Leo's personality but is skeptical about the state's involvement in organizing the reception."

Those on the far right, he continued, welcomed the visibility of Catholicism but had objected, for example, to an interfaith meeting planned in the eastern city of Metz, which they say places Islam on an equal footing with Christianity.
Because of the separation of church and state, the president will not be able to attend the large public masses.

blocks.caption: Pope Benedict XVI celebrated an open-air mass at the Invalides in ParisImage: Osservatore Romano/ansa/epa/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Leo's visit is likely to boost the pope's profile in the country, which last saw a papal state visit in 2008, when Benedict XVI (2005-2013) traveled to Paris and Lourdes, the world-famous pilgrimage site in the southwest of the country. He drew smaller crowds than those expected for Pope Leo.

Pope Francis (2013-2025) visited Strasbourg in 2014 and Ajaccio in Corsica in 2024 on one-day trips, and in 2023 he spent a night in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille. But each time, he came for a specific occasion rather than visiting the country as a whole. In his speeches to the European Parliament and Council of Europe in Strasbourg, he criticized the migration policies of what he described as an "aged and weary" Europe.
Roy described the contrasting perspectives of recent popes. John Paul II (1978-2005), he said, viewed Christianity as "primarily European," while Francis saw it as "more shaped by the Global South."

This, Roy argued, explained Francis' "certain disregard for Europe." Leo was likely to assume the middle ground, while extending his predecessor's message, Roy said: "He affirms the universality of the Catholic Church, while also recognizing Europe's weight within that universality."
Europe's key role for the pope

For Augsburg-based church historian and papal expert Jörg Ernesti, Europe has remained "the most important political point of reference for popes since the late 19th century," despite the growing internationalism of Catholicism Ernesti pointed to the demographic shift: In 1900, more than two-thirds of all Catholics lived in Europe, he said; today, the figure is only around 20%. This internationalization had also shaped the College of Cardinals, albeit with a time lag. "While Europeans have historically always made up the majority, they now account for just 39%."

During his four-day visit, Leo is scheduled to deliver 15 speeches and homilies. Most of those in Paris will be aimed at wider French society and its political leaders, while the large masses and events in Lourdes will focus primarily on France's Catholics.

blocks.caption: In April 2026, Pope Leo received French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte Macron, at the VaticanImage: Vatican Media/Catholic Press Photo/ipa-agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: The most keenly awaited speech is one scheduled for the final day in Metz, which French President Emmanuel Macron will introduce. It is titled "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity."
The choice of Metz itself is symbolic. Once a center of the Carolingian Empire, the city has changed language and allegiance several times over the centuries, at times being German, at others French.

Leo will be able to invoke the name behind the Robert Schuman Convention Center. Born in Luxembourg, Robert Schuman (1886-1963) was a French statesman who had inherited his father's German citizenship at birth. In the aftermath of World War II, he was an early advocate of Franco-German reconciliation. He pushed for a new, united Europe and in 1958 became the first president of the newly established European Parliament. After his death, he was buried in a small church in Scy-Chazelles, near Metz.

blocks.caption: Robert Schuman's tombstone in a church in his hometown Scy-ChazellesImage: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP

blocks.text: For Pope Leo, Roy said, "Europe is a real entity that must be sustained and developed beyond nationalism." That, he said, "has always been the message of the Catholic Church since World War II. It is Schuman's message."

Roy will be watching closely to see whether, and how openly, Pope Leo criticizes populism and nationalism in his call to strengthen the EU and whether he will speak about a form of nationalist Catholicism found in France. He said that defenders of the traditional Latin Mass were not infrequently "identitarian nationalists or even close to far right circles."
Leo to meet abuse survivors

It is hard to imagine a papal trip without mention of the long-running issue of abuse. When Pope Benedict visited France in 2008, he did not take the chance to meet any survivors of sexual abuse in the French Catholic Church. His successors did, though the institution has been slow to confront its past amid a spate of new scandals.

blocks.caption: This grotto is at the heart of religious life in Lourdes. According to legend, the Virgin Mary appeared several times to a young woman in 1858Image: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This time round, a meeting with survivors is on the pope's agenda in Lourdes. But something else has changed. During the pontificates of Benedict and Francis, those who met with them were usually not named. At times, it appeared that access to the Vatican came in exchange for silence. In France, the seven survivors who will meet Leo have spoken out together ahead of the meeting, with five of them also making their names public.

"Dialogue does not mean approval," they said. "Being received does not mean giving up our demands." The issue is likely to remain a thorny challenge for the Catholic Church — in France and elsewhere for a long time to come.
This article was translated from German.
Why the Catholic Church is seeing a new wave of converts

articles.title: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat
articles.summary: The satellite station is used in part to provide internet coverage to neighbouring Ukraine, the government says.

blocks.text: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army".
He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented.
Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.
It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries.
In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.
Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation.
Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary.
The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational.
The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.

Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad".
On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.

Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In Ukraine, Kharkiv and Kyiv experienced the worst of Russia's attacks overnight into Thursday.
In Kharkiv, six people were killed and twelve others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said.
It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women.
Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine have become more devastating in recent months because of their new jet-powered drones, which are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight them are too expensive.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help.

He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land."
He said Ukraine would seek to target the Russian energy sector over the winter.

The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources.
Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war.

articles.title: Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now likely unconstitutional, judge rules in restoring temporary access – US politics live
articles.summary: Judge rules Trump’s ban of journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico ⁠likely unconstitutional

blocks.text: Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now likely unconstitutional, judge rules in restoring temporary access
Good morning and welcome to the US politics live blog.

We start now with breaking news from the late night hours: a federal judge has temporarily restored White House access to journalists from CNN, Politico and MS Now after president Donald Trump banned them due to their coverage of his administration.
US district judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organizations filed ‌contesting the ban that the president announced ​on 18 September, saying it was ⁠likely unconstitutional.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and issued a temporary restraining order that will be in effect for 14 days. Such orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.
In other news today:

items: US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping meet in Washington for high-stakes talks that expect to cover their competing economies, trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan.

Benjamin Netanyahu will speak at the UN general assembly today where he is expected to attack New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, a vocal critic of the Israeli prime minister who has repeatedly described him as a war criminal. You can follow live coverage of the Israeli prime minister’s address here.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 13m agoTrump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now likely unconstitutional, judge rules in restoring temporary access

blocks.text: Donald Trump has been raging about a story first reported by MS Now on Wednesday that he is seeking to rename the Ford Theatre in Washington DC, a site infamous for the assassination of president Abraham Lincoln, after himself.
Last night he posted on Truth Social about the news item, blaming “Dumocrats” for the “ridiculous lie.”
This morning, hours after the late night ruling from the judge that temporarily reinstated CNN, Politico, and MS Now, Trump (again) said:

double quotation markThe Dumocrats make up lie after lie. The new one is that I want Ford’s Theater named after me. That’s where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. Who would want that? I don’t! It is FAKE NEWS started by MSDNC AND CNN.

This is his first mention of the day of his lesser-favored media outlets. He has not acknowledged the judge’s ruling to restore them access to the White House – yet. We’ll bring you more lines as they come in.
Some more background information on this ongoing situation between the Trump administration and the White House press correspondents:

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, saying the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They requested a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out. Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be ⁠able to constantly write or ​report ​FICTION and LIES,” ​and justice department lawyers ​had ‌sought to ​justify ​the ban on national security grounds. A Justice Department lawyer told the judge the Trump administration provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the ​press passes in letters sent to the news outlets ​on Tuesday. But the judge signaled skepticism of that argument, ​noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed. In a legal filing on Tuesday, the ​Justice Department argued that access to the ‌White House is a ​privilege, not an entitlement, and that the ​president has the authority to suspend access by news organizations.

articles.title: EU finally clinching trade deals with Southeast Asian states
articles.summary: After years of arduous negotiations, the EU is closing on a string of bilateral trade deals with countries in Southeast Asia. And yet, a bloc-to-bloc agreement between the EU and ASEAN remains a…

image.caption: The Philippines is one of the many ASEAN countries pursuing closer ties with the EUImage: Ezra Acayan/AFP

blocks.text: The EU and several Southeast Asian nations are nearing the finish line on bilateral trade deals, and if the current deadlines hold, the European bloc will have agreements in place with six out of 11 ASEAN states by the middle of next year.

Free trade agreements with Singapore and Vietnam are already in force. Negotiations with Indonesia have concluded, and Jakarta aims to sign the agreement in October, with implementation targeted for early 2027.
Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US

Talks with Thailand, relaunched in 2023, have reached nine negotiating rounds, while Malaysia resumed negotiations in early 2025 after a 13-year pause. Both are expected to be finalized by the end of the year or early 2027.
Earlier this week, the EU and the Philippines announced that they had reached "substantial agreement" on their free trade agreement, putting it on course for formal conclusion in the coming months.
Trade up by more than half in single decade
Speaking to DW, Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, described EU engagement with ASEAN on trade and investment issues as "at an all-time high."
EU-Southeast Asia goods trade reached €274.9 billion ($313.7 billion) last year, up around 6% from the previous year and more than 50% from the €177.9 billion recorded in 2016, according to EU data.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is now the EU's third-largest goods trading partner outside Europe, behind only the United States and China.
The Philippines is chair of ASEAN — these are its goals

This week, Manila hosted both the ASEAN–EU Business Summit and the 22nd meeting of ASEAN economic ministers and the EU's trade commissioner. The two blocs pledged greater cooperation to protect themselves from rising geopolitical tensions, including unilateral trade actions and regional conflicts, that "collectively threaten the rules-based international order."
Why is Southeast Asia so important for Europe?

Brussels is expanding its network of trade agreements globally as it looks to expand to new markets and form more resilient supply chains. Southeast Asia, in turn, sits at the center of supply chains for semiconductors, electronics, electric vehicles and batteries, with investment pouring into data centers, renewable energy and digital services.
EU-Mercosur free trade deal: Who gains the most?
An article published this month by the International Monetary Fund said ASEAN's 11 economies already form a $4.5 trillion bloc, growing at more than 4.5% a year.
Such economic expansion, combined with multinational firms' efforts to diversify production beyond China, has made access to Southeast Asian markets more attractive for European companies.

Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW that geopolitical and geo-economic changes are also accelerating cooperation between the two regions.

US President Donald Trump's "protectionist and erratic trade policies" have acted as a crucial catalyst, he said, while the EU's strategy of "de-risking from China" and diversifying supply chains boosted Southeast Asia's strategic importance.

A stronger partnership with European nations also plays in favor of Southeast Asia governments, who have long tried to maintain broad economic relationships with competing powers rather than becoming excessively dependent on China, the United States or any other single partner.
EU companies push for an ASEAN-wide deal

The EU-ASEAN Business Council, said Humphrey, is calling for a region-to-region economic framework with a clear pathway to an eventual region-to-region free trade deal, "something European business has consistently called for."
"This would adopt a modular approach, perhaps starting with a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and an Investment Protection Agreement," Humphrey told DW.

The idea is not exactly new — the EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-to-region agreement in 2007, but the talks bogged down over enormous differences between ASEAN economies and disagreements over the agreement's scope.
The talks were put on ice by mutual agreement in 2009, after which Brussels switched to negotiating bilateral deals with individual ASEAN members.

The main difficulty preservers to this day, as ASEAN includes Singapore, one of the world's wealthiest economies, alongside developing and least-developed members, making it difficult to agree on common commitments acceptable to Brussels.
"In addition, meeting the EU's high social, labor and environmental standards is difficult for the less-developed ASEAN members," said Gerstl.
Is the Commission ready to up the stakes?

Yet, even without an immediate prospect of a full region-to-region agreement, completing the current bilateral deals would give the EU preferential trade arrangements with most of ASEAN's largest economies and demonstrate that Southeast Asia has moved higher up Brussels' trade agenda.
For Humphrey, however, that should be the starting point rather than the endpoint. The concern, he said, is the European Commission might not be willing to move towards region-to-region agreements.

"With 2027 marking the 50th Anniversary of EU-ASEAN relations, we remain hopeful that the Commission will take this milestone seriously and ramp up work on a region-to-region economic architecture," he told DW.
"Failing to do so will only make ASEAN think that the EU does not take the region seriously."

articles.title: Tensions between India and Bangladesh are in focus after Dhaka skipped the BRICS summit in Delhi
articles.summary: Bangladesh's absence from the BRICS summit in New Delhi has raised fresh questions about strained ties. Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's exile in India remains a major obstacle to normalizing relations.

image.caption: Bilateral ties have improved since Rahman took office but are still far from normalizedImage: Mahmud Hossain Opu/AP Photo/picture alliance; Patrick van Katwijk/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: When India hosted a BRICS leaders' summit in New Delhi earlier this month, a notable absentee was Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

The Indian government says Rahman received two invitations: one to attend a BRICS outreach session as the chair of a regional group of nations around the Bay of Bengal, known as BIMSTEC, and another for a bilateral visit to India.
Invitation or snub?
But in Dhaka, these invitations were viewed as a snub, as Rahman was not formally invited to the summit proper in his capacity as prime minister, but only as the chair of BIMSTEC.
This represents a departure from Bangladesh's previous prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, who was invited as premier to previous BRICS summit events, even though Bangladesh is not a member.
The case is the latest example of the frosty ties between the two South Asian neighbors that have developed since Hasina's ouster in 2024 following huge protests and a deadly crackdown.
Hasina fled to India, and last year was sentenced to death after being convicted in absentia of crimes against humanity over the response to the protests.
Bangladesh has called on India to extradite Hasina so that she can face justice.
Hasina has rejected the verdict, calling it politically motivated.

After her ouster in 2024, bilateral relations entered their worst period in years — visa services were curtailed as disputes mounted over her presence in India as well as the management of the border and alleged forced returns without due process of undocumented, mostly Muslim, Bengali-speaking migrants — known as "push-ins."
India forces Bengali-speaking Muslims into Bangladesh

Since Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won February's election, that drift has partly reversed. India resumed tourist visas in June and appointed Dinesh Trivedi as its new high commissioner.
But while a bilateral summit is being discussed for November, Hasina's exile in India remains a major obstacle to normalizing relations.
Former Indian diplomat Ajay Bisaria told DW that Bangladesh had "missed a trick" by staying away.
"It was a chance to engage not just with India but with other global leaders," he said. "But the lost ground is easily recovered."
Has the India-Bangladesh relationship fundamentally changed?
Both sides, he added, would need to manage the "irritant" of Hasina's presence in India. A positive bilateral summit later this year could reset ties, he added.
Humayun Kabir, a former Bangladeshi diplomat, said the relationship is not what it was before Hasina fled to India.
"Ties were one-sided before the uprising, and Dhaka is now looking for something different," Kabir told DW. "There has to be dignity and equality."

Dhaka is willing to engage, but New Delhi must create a congenial atmosphere for a Rahman visit, Kabir said, including by keeping Hasina from making "provocative" remarks and acknowledging the court verdict against her.
Zafar Sobhan, a Bangladeshi political analyst, told DW that Bangladesh will now engage only on equal terms.

"It was hoped that with the exit of the (Mohammad) Yunus-led interim government, New Delhi could mend ties with the elected BNP government," he said. "However, both sides are held hostage by hardliners, giving them limited room for maneuver."
Sobhan said the best way for India to rebuild trust with authorities in Bangladesh is "not to allow Hasina to destabilize Bangladesh with provocative statements."
"Failure to rein her in is seen as an act of unfriendliness," Sobhan explained.
Others read Rahman not taking part in the BRICS summit more sharply.
Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, founder of the Mantraya Institute, called it "clearly a snub", even though Dhaka cited procedural problems with the invitation.

She said the episode must be viewed alongside the unresolved Hasina question, stalled talks on the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty — which is set to expire in December — and Bangladesh's deepening ties with China and Pakistan.

"The BNP is clearly on its way to diversifying its relations amid China's growing overtures and India's hard postures," D'Souza told DW, describing it not as a pivot away from India but a "recalibration toward hedging and greater autonomy."
Sreeradha Datta, a Bangladesh expert at the Jindal School of International Affairs in India, offers a more cautious take.
"India will always remain an important neighbour for Bangladesh," Datta told DW, "but India holds few advantages over Dhaka, and both sides understand that."
"It's too early to suggest the two neighbours have moved apart," she said. "Delhi and Dhaka seem measured in their overtures to each other."
The China factor

That caution matters because the China relationship is not new. Beijing has spent a decade building its economic and strategic presence in Bangladesh, spanning infrastructure, energy, trade and defence, since Dhaka joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2016.
China is now Bangladesh's largest trading partner and a major defence supplier.

Beijing also pledged support for Bangladesh's long-delayed Teesta initiative, a major river-management and infrastructure project to control floods and improve water supply on the Teesta River, which flows between India and Bangladesh.
Despite years of talks, Bangladesh and India failed to sign a Teesta water-sharing treaty.
On his June visit to Beijing, his first overseas trip in office, Rahman leaned into that relationship, securing agreements on trade, investment, infrastructure and defence.

"It is normal for a mid-sized state like Bangladesh to seek relationships with Beijing and other nations," D'Souza said, warning that heavy-handed pressure from India could push Dhaka further that way.

D'Souza advises New Delhi to separate the bilateral agenda from the Hasina question, offer Rahman a concrete package on water, trade and connectivity, and hold firm red lines on any Chinese military presence near the Siliguri corridor and the Bay of Bengal.
Shahab Enam Khan, a Bangladeshi scholar of international relations, pushed back on the idea that improving ties is only in Dhaka's interests.
"If anyone should worry about this relationship, it is New Delhi," Khan told DW, citing India's trade surplus and its dependence on Bangladeshi goodwill for its own security.
India, he said, treated the 2024 uprising "as the loss of a client rather than a neighbour's political transition," pointing to suspended visas, closed land ports and shelter for Hasina.
"Bangladeshis took it as a message that Delhi's goodwill depended on who held power in Dhaka," Khan said.
Rebuilding trust, he said, means ending Hasina's party activity in Delhi, resolving bilateral disputes, and lifting post-2024 trade restrictions.
What India still holds

Geography still complicates any clean break. Bangladesh and India share a 4,096-kilometer (2,400-mile) border, the longest either country has. Bangladesh still depends on India for trade routes, transit, electricity, fuel, medical travel and regional connectivity. The two countries also share 54 rivers.
But those dependencies are also friction points.
The 1996 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty expires in December, the Teesta dispute remains unresolved, and alleged Indian push-ins of undocumented migrants across the border remain a sore point.
Bisaria sees some balancing of its ties between India and China as "natural."
"India can live with that, as it does with its other neighbours," he said.

The real question, then, may not be whether India is losing Bangladesh outright, but whether it is losing its old ability to shape the relationship on its own terms with an increasingly assertive Dhaka.
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere

articles.title: India news: Cockroach party demands Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation
articles.summary: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke has alleged that the removal of more than 130 million names from draft electoral rolls is designed to benefit the BJP and weaken opposition parties. DW has more.

image.caption: Abhijeet Dipke called Kumar 'the biggest threat to India's democracy' and demanded his resignation [FILE: October 27, 2025]Image: Jitender Gupta/ANI

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy
